Hardware requirements 
   •  Any desktop workstation or laptop with an internet connection is sufficient. The procedures were tested on a MacBook Pro (MacOS Tahoe 26.1) with a 12-Core central processing unit (CPU) and 24 GB of random-access memory (RAM). For minimal performance, we recommend using 4 CPUs with at least 18 GB of RAM for analyses.   
 Software requirements 
   •  Operating system: Linux, Windows, or MacOS    •  IDE: An integrated development environment. We recommend Visual Studio Code, which can be accessed at  https://code.visualstudio.com/download .    •  Docker desktop: A platform for docker container management, which can be accessed at  https://docs.docker.com/desktop/ .    •  Nextflow: A workflow system for creating scalable, portable, and reproducible workflows, which can be accessed at  https://www.nextflow.io/docs/latest/install.html . The version used here is 25.10.0.   
   Installation of Docker desktop  Install Docker desktop from the official website:  https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/ . Once downloaded, open the application and go to Settings > Resources and change the CPU setting to a minimum of 4 and the memory setting to a minimum of 18 GB.    Installation of Nextflow  Install Nextflow by following the instructions on the official website:  https://www.nextflow.io/docs/latest/install.html . You can check if Nextflow is correctly downloaded and available by typing the following in your terminal:  nextflow info     Cloning the repository  Open a terminal and navigate to the directory you want to place the repository in, then run:   > git clone 
  https://github.com/NovoNordisk-OpenSource/nnclinssoap.git      Downloading the demo case data  Inside your IDE of choice, open the cloned repository. In the terminal, run the following:   > bash ./setup_test_data.sh  You should see the download start in the terminal. Building the docker images  Start by making sure Docker desktop is open. Then, inside your IDE of choice, open the cloned repository. In the terminal, run the following:   > cd docker && bash ./build_all_images.sh -v docker  Build progress is shown in the terminal and Docker desktop. Building all images takes around 3 to 6 h.     Methods  This section describes how to use NNclinSSOAP with the provided demo case data, ensuring an easy-to-follow introduction to usage. For users who wish to customize their analysis, use other data, or run the pipeline in an HPC, the repository is open-source and contains more detailed documentation.  We divide the methods in 2 procedures, which can be performed sequentially or independently. Procedure 1 describes the preparation and steps needed for running the sc/snRNA-seq workflow. Procedure 2 covers the preparation and steps needed for running the SpatialXenium workflow, with an option to incorporate the annotated Seurat object generated from Procedure 1 as input for cell label transfer. Expected Results  The result of following both procedures is a transformation of raw sc/snRNA-seq data into an integrated and annotated Seurat object, and raw Xenium data into a spatially resolved cell object and map. This can aid in answering clinical questions, giving the user a deeper understanding of the analyzed tissues both at a cellular expression and a structural level, as is the case in the demo case data in this paper, highlighting differences between healthy and cancer kidney tissue.  When the procedures are executed with the supplied demo data using the specified software versions, parameters and settings, deterministic tables and files are expected to be reproducible. Stochastic visualization steps such as UMAP may show minor layout differences while preserving the same biological topology and interpretation. If the paper is followed using a personal dataset, the same types of outputs are expected, but results will differ according to the input data.   Sc/snRNA-seq (procedure 1)  Executing the sc/snRNA-seq workflow (Procedure 1, step 2) generates an nf-core results folder. The demo case dataset has been run with the cellranger aligner [ 31 ], so the results are the standard cellranger outputs. The special addition is the BCO object that has been generated since the plugin is included when running the nextflow pipeline.  In the second part of the workflow (Procedure 1, steps 4 and 5), each script produces a variety of plots and output files, which are organized into dedicated folders—see Box  2  for a summary of the results file structure.    •  Quality Control (QC): QC plots document the standard Seurat workflow, starting from reading the counts matrix and progressing through to the creation of the final Seurat object (see Fig.  3 A to D). A separate folder is generated for each sample’s QC outputs, while the integrated Seurat object is stored in the parent directory.    •  Cell Annotation: This step generates visualizations such as UMAPs displaying annotated clusters and violin plot displaying the annotation scores, along with an updated Seurat object that contains cell type assignments (see Fig.  3 E and F).    •  Differential Expression analysis: For each cell type, the pipeline outputs a normalized counts CSV file, a CSV file with differential expression results, and a volcano and line plot summarizing key findings (see Fig.  3 G and H).      Box 2.   Example file structure from Procedure 1.5   
     
     SpatialXenium (procedure 2)  Executing the SpatialXenium workflow (Procedure 2, step 4) produces several key outputs that can be used for clinical interpretation of the tissues analyzed, shown in Fig.  4 . By using Nextflow, reports covering errors, timing and resource usage have automatically been created. An example results file structure is shown in Box  3 . To aid with technical and clinical interpretation, key outputs from Quality Control (QC), gene expression and cell type analysis are described in further detail below:    •  Quality Control: The QC plots (see Fig.  4 A and B) summarize how many genes and reads are captured per cell and how these values are distributed across the dataset. This allows users to identify low-quality cells, technical outliers, or regions with suboptimal capture efficiency before drawing any biological or clinical conclusion, ensuring that downstream patterns (e.g. “immune poor” areas) are not artifacts of poor data quality.    •  Gene Expression: The gene expression visualizations (see Fig.  4 C and D) show how the selected markers from  assets/genes.txt  are distributed both in UMAP space and across the tissue. Clinically, these plots help confirm that canonical markers (for example, tumor, immune, or stromal genes) are expressed in the expected tissue compartments and spatial niches, supporting interpretations such as tumor–stroma interactions, immune infiltration patterns, or localization of specific disease-relevant pathways.    •  Cell Type: The cell-type plots (see Fig.  4 E and F) resulting from the label transfer display the predicted cell types in UMAP space projected back onto the tissue, with cells below the chosen probability threshold set to “Ambiguous”. This makes it clear which assignments are robust enough to support biological or clinical interpretation, which should be treated with caution. In a clinical context, these maps can be used to explore how specific cell types (e.g., cytotoxic T cells, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells) are spatially organized within lesions, margins, or normal tissue, and how this architecture might relate to disease severity or therapeutic response.       Conclusion  NNclinSSOAP offers a GxP-ready framework for scalable processing and analysis of single-cell and Spatial Transcriptomics data for clinical research and trials. Its modular design and automated provenance capture ensure transparent, reproducible, auditable, and fully traceable analyses suitable for regulated environments, e.g., clinical trials. Together, these features provide a practical, unique, and extensible foundation for deploying multimodal transcriptomics across mechanistic studies and clinical trials. Human adult and pediatric multimodal transcriptomic atlas of progression from pressure-loaded to failing right ventricle. Right ventricular failure (RVF) independently predicts mortality in heart failure, yet its pathophysiology is poorly understood. Here we present a multi-modal atlas of human right ventricular pressure loading and failure, including bulk (n = 142), single-nucleus (n = 11) and Xenium spatial (n = 9) transcriptomics in adults, plus pediatric (n = 14) and mouse pulmonary artery banding cohorts. Subclustering resolved 34 cell subtypes across 12 lineages along a two-phase trajectory. Phase 1 (non-failing to pressure-loaded) accounts for most of the transcriptional change detectable by bulk and single-nucleus RNA sequencing and is marked by loss of resident macrophage identity, fibroblast activation, endothelial expansion and erosion of tissue-protective programs. Phase 2 (pressure-loaded to RVF) produces little change in bulk RNA sequencing but is resolved by spatial transcriptomics, engaging multi-lineage fibrotic, endothelial-activation and cardiomyocyte-reactivation programs, with a gain of extracellular matrix (collagen, laminin, thrombospondin) signaling over a stable cell contact adhesion baseline. Mitochondrial respirometry revealed respiratory dysfunction in adult and mouse RVF but not pediatric RVF. Multi-lineage remodeling of the cardiac microenvironment emerges as the central molecular program of RVF, meriting further study as possible disease-modifying targets. Main  The normal right ventricle (RV) is morphologically and embryologically unique from the left ventricle (LV), precluding the categorical extrapolation of our understanding of left-side pathophysiology to the right heart  1  . Historically, cardiac research has focused on left ventricular failure (LVF), delivering multiple approved therapies, with less attention to RVF  2  . Although the most common cause of RVF is pressure overload secondary to LVF, RVF can also arise from diverse other causes  3 – 5  . Independent of etiology, RV dysfunction portends a poor prognosis: patients with LVF and concomitant RV dysfunction have approximately a two-fold increased mortality risk  6 – 8  .  Advances in LVF therapy have been driven by targeting critical pathways such as the renin−angiotensin−aldosterone system (RAAS)  9  . Attempts to generalize these therapies to the RV have been clinically unsuccessful. Neurohormonal blockade, a cornerstone of LVF therapy, has little efficacy in RVF  9  . There is, therefore, a need for exploratory research to identify RVF-specific therapeutic targets.  We conducted a multi-platform transcriptomic study of failing and non-failing human RVs, integrating bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) (142 individuals), single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) (11 individuals) and Xenium spatial transcriptomics (nine sections), with mitochondrial respirometry, flow cytometry and histological validation. We placed these findings in broader context by comparing to a mouse pulmonary artery banding (PAB) model, pediatric single-ventricle RVs, LVF and a published pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) RV transcriptomic dataset. Recent human cardiac snRNA-seq atlases remain LV centric  10 – 14   or include limited RV in genetically defined cohorts  15  . Although some include non-failing (NF) RV tissue  11 , 14 , 16  , none has stratified pressure-overload RVF progression or integrated bulk, single-nucleus and spatial modalities on matched patient tissue. Here we present, to our knowledge, the first such integrated atlas and propose a two-phase model in which multi-lineage erosion of protective programs occurs in various cell types during the transition from NF to preserved RV in the context of LVF (NF → pRV) and is followed by a pRV → RVF transition that is comparatively muted in bulk RNA expression changes but engages a broader multi-lineage signal elicited in Xenium spatial pseudobulk analyses.    Results   Cohort and multi-platform approach  From the Penn Human Heart Tissue Bank, we collected transmural RV samples from adult NF organ donors and LVF transplant recipients, the latter substratified  17 , 18   into pressure-loaded but preserved systolic function (pRV) and failing (RVF) groups (Fig.  1a  and Supplementary Tables  1 – 3 ). We applied bulk RNA-seq ( n  = 142), snRNA-seq ( n  = 11; 61,398 nuclei) and Xenium spatial transcriptomics ( n  = 9 sections; 625,305 cells; 477-gene panel); a mouse PAB model at 2-week and 2-month timepoints; a pediatric snRNA-seq cohort ( n  = 14; 10 hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS)-palliated RVs stratified by normal function or RVF and four controls); and a cross-etiology comparison with a published PAH RVF bulk dataset  19  .    Fig. 1   Study overview and bulk RNA-seq of human RVF.   a , Cohort schematic across three platforms: bulk RNA-seq (NF  n  = 29, pRV  n  = 78, RVF  n  = 35), snRNA-seq (NF  n  = 4, pRV  n  = 4, RVF  n  = 3) and Xenium spatial transcriptomics (NF  n  = 3, pRV  n  = 3, RVF  n  = 3).  b , PCA embeddings of normalized and transformed counts from RV samples show prominent differences between NF and pRV/RVF samples but relative similarity of pRV and RVF samples.  c , UMAP for dimension reduction of WGCNA results. Points correspond to genes. Distance metric computed from WGCNA topological overlap matrix. WGCNA identifies 29 gene expression modules within bulk data. Top-5 hub genes corresponding to the given module are labeled. Gene Ontology (Biological Processes) enrichments for top-100 hub genes are overlaid for key modules.  d , Gene Ontology enrichments for WGCNA modules. Point size corresponds to Enrichr combined scores, and color corresponds to multiple comparison-adjusted  P  value. Enrichment was tested with Fisherʼs exact test. Gene sets are the top-100 hub genes per module ranked by kME.  e , WGCNA module score violin plots across NF/pRV/RVF for the 14 of 29 bulk modules with a significant module eigengene shift in at least one adjacent transition. Left-sided comparison corresponds to NF versus pRV, and right-sided comparison corresponds to pRV versus RVF. The NF versus RVF comparison is not shown for simplicity. Exact Bonferroni-adjusted  P  values for the significant contrasts are M1 NF → pRV 6.7 × 10 −14 ; M2 NF → pRV 6.7 × 10 −14 ; M3 NF → pRV 4.9 × 10 −8 , pRV → RVF 5.3 × 10 −5 ; M4 NF → pRV 1.3 × 10 −5 , pRV → RVF 1.7 × 10 −4 ; M5 pRV → RVF 0.027; M8 NF → pRV 0.0062; M10 pRV → RVF 5.5 × 10 −5 ; M11 NF → pRV 2.7 × 10 −6 , pRV → RVF 0.010; M12 NF → pRV 2.0 × 10 −11 , pRV → RVF 0.0091; M14 pRV → RVF 2.4 × 10 −4 ; M20 NF → pRV 8.1 × 10 −7 , pRV → RVF 1.3 × 10 −4 ; M25 NF → pRV 1.6 × 10 −8 , pRV → RVF 9.2 × 10 −5 ; M26 NF → pRV 0.024, pRV → RVF 1.9 × 10 −4 ; M28 NF → pRV 1.2 × 10 −9 . All other displayed contrasts are non-significant (adjusted  P  ≥ 0.05). Module eigengene values are shown per bulk RNA-seq sample. Module eigengenes were compared between groups with a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Bonferroni adjustment across the modules. Significance brackets on the panel denote the Bonferroni-adjusted  P  value: NS, not significant ( P  ≥ 0.05); * P  < 0.05; ** P  < 0.01; *** P  < 0.001; **** P  < 0.0001. The 15 modules with no significant shift in either adjacent transition are not displayed. The full per-module table is provided in Source Data Fig.  1 .  f , Cross-cohort concordance dot plots between RV failure (RVF versus NF) and PAH for concordantly downregulated and upregulated pathways. Concordant gene sets were defined as genes changing in the same direction in both cohorts at DESeq2 Benjamini−Hochberg  P  adj  < 0.1 and |log 2 FC| > 0.1. Pathway enrichment used one-sided Fisherʼs exact test with Benjamini−Hochberg adjustment. Down, downregulated; OAS, oligoadenylate synthetase;  P  adj , adjusted  P  value; PC, principal component; Up, upregulated; var, variance explained.   Source data                      Bulk RNA-seq reveals the transcriptomic landscape of RV failure progression  Principal component analysis (PCA) of bulk RNA-seq separated NF from pRV/RVF but poorly separated pRV from RVF (Fig.  1b ). Differential expression (DE) yielded many NF versus pRV/RVF differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with strong NF → pRV and NF → RVF fold change (FC) correlation (Extended Data Fig.  1a,b  and Supplementary Data  1 ). Prominent DEGs common to pRV and RVF included cardiac stress ( NPPA ,  NPPB ), chemokines ( CXCL8 – 11 ) and extracellular matrix (ECM)/angiogenic genes. Pathway enrichment highlighted immune, complement and inflammatory terms (Supplementary Data  2 ), suggesting that immune populations dominate the bulk signal. Many DEGs exhibited stepwise changes from NF → pRV → RVF, with 115 stepwise-increasing genes enriched for T cell chemotaxis, and 161 stepwise-decreasing genes enriched for mitochondrial ribosomal components (Extended Data Fig.  1c–f  and Supplementary Data  3 ). Fewer significant DEGs were identified from pRV → RVF analysis, indicating that most transcriptional remodeling precedes functional decompensation. pRV-upregulated genes enriched for oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS); RVF-upregulated genes were immune dominated (Extended Data Fig.  1g,h  and Supplementary Data  2 ).                    We also evaluated DE by weighted gene correlation network analysis (WGCNA)  20   to capture broader co-expression signals, resolving 29 gene modules, almost all of which were differentially expressed across states (Fig.  1c–e  and Supplementary Data  4 ). Two OXPHOS modules (M25 and M26) declined monotonically across NF → pRV → RVF at the module eigengene level, whereas the large resident macrophage module M1 ( CD163 ,  MRC1 ,  VSIG4 ) was highest in NF and fell sharply from NF to pRV before plateauing. In the opposing direction, an adaptive immune module (M8; T/B cell and major histocompatibility complex class II (MHC-II) genes) rose significantly from NF to pRV (Fig.  1d,e  and Supplementary Data  4 ).  To test cross-etiology generalizability, we compared our bulk data to a published PAH-associated RVF transcriptome  19  . RVF versus NF yielded 235 concordantly downregulated genes (respiratory electron transport (ETC), complex I biogenesis) and 214 concordantly upregulated genes (interferon (IFN) α/β, antiviral signaling), establishing mitochondrial decline and IFN activation as etiology shared (Fig.  1f ). By contrast, the complement cascade was divergent between cohorts, downregulated in our RVF but upregulated in PAH RVF, identifying complement activation as an etiology-specific response (Extended Data Fig.  1i  and Supplementary Data  5 ).    Single-nucleus transcriptomics resolves 34 cell subtypes across 12 lineages  Single-nucleus RNA-seq of 11 RV samples (Supplementary Tables  4  and  5 ) yielded 61,398 nuclei (2,912 genes per nucleus) and 12 major clusters (Fig.  2a,b  and Supplementary Data  6 ). Composition shifted progressively with disease: loss of cardiomyocyte nuclei and expansion of endothelial cell (EC) nuclei from NF → pRV → RVF (Fig.  2c ). This compositional shift parallels reports from LVF snRNA-seq atlases, although, notably, the non-myocyte expansion here is endothelial predominant without the fibroblast expansion typical of LVF  12  . Bulk WGCNA modules were assigned to dominant lineages (Fig.  2d ). Single-nucleus RNA-seq subclustering resolved 34 subtypes across 12 lineages: 10 cardiomyocyte, seven fibroblast, five EC, six myeloid and six lineages retained at lineage level (pericyte, smooth muscle, adipocyte, epicardial, neuronal/glial and natural killer/T) due to low counts (markers in Figs.  6b  and  7b , Extended Data Figs.  2b  and  3b  and Supplementary Data  7 ). Pseudobulk DESeq2 within each subtype across three pairwise comparisons (Supplementary Data  8  and  9 ) identified fibroblasts as most transcriptionally responsive (1,083 DEGs pRV versus NF; 806 DEGs RVF versus NF), followed by cardiomyocytes (248; 464). This difference partially reflects lower inter-patient dispersion among fibroblasts. Cardiomyocytes instead show downregulation of α-myosin heavy chain ( MYH6 ) and the lamin-associated gene  MLIP , with reactivation of the fetal gene program ( NPPA ,  NPPB ,  ACTA1 ) evident at the bulk tissue level. More broadly, cardiomyocytes coordinately downregulate nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes spanning fatty acid oxidation (FAO), the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, OXPHOS subunits and the mitoribosome as well as the biogenesis regulators PGC-1α ( PPARGC1A ) and ERRα ( ESRRA ). In non-cardiomyocyte lineages, glutathione/thioredoxin redox-buffering genes ( GCLC ,  GCLM ,  GSR ,  TXNRD1 ,  SRXN1 ,  SLC7A11 ) are coordinately downregulated, as is the secreted glutathione peroxidase  GPX3 , which has been causally linked to RVF  25  . The myeloid pool downregulates homeostatic receptors ( CD163 ,  VSIG4 ;  MERTK  at trend) while inducing conventional dendritic cell markers  CD83 ,  CD1C  and  FCER1A . There is also downregulation of the TGFβ co-receptor  TGFBR3  (ref.   26  ) across all seven fibroblast subtypes and fibroblast activation ( SFRP4  (ref.   27  ),  THBS4  (ref.   28  )). In ECs, pRV was already marked by an erosion of homeostatic, anti-oxidant and vasoprotective programs—notably, the IL-33 receptor  IL1RL1/ST2  and the matrix metalloprotease inhibitors  TIMP3  and  TIMP4 , with the counter-regulatory RAAS enzyme  ACE2  declining in parallel. snRNA-seq additionally revealed a type I IFN response ( IFI44/IFI44L ,  MX1/MX2 ,  OAS3 ,  RSAD2 ,  STAT1 ) that the Xenium panel cannot resolve as the IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) are off-panel. The one represented chemokine,  CXCL9 , was concordantly induced. Mural cells added early destabilization to the shared vascular-protective loss. We noted downregulation of the structural genes  ELN  (elastin) and  DES  (desmin), the resting stromal metabolic enzyme  ADH1B  and the genes  TIMP3 ,  TIMP4 ,  IL1RL1 / ST2  and  ACE2 , with snRNA-seq adding loss of  SMAD3 .    Phase 2 is focal and cell type specific, not platform driven  Phase 2 lineage-level significant genes are 39 in Xenium, 61 in snRNA-seq and five in bulk (unique gene symbols per contrast), concordant in direction across platforms where detectable (Fig.  4b ). The signal concentrates in two lineages. In cardiomyocytes, Xenium reveals a BMP/TGFβ superfamily signaling program ( BMPR2 ,  BMPR1A, FSTL3 ,  BAMBI  up). This simultaneous upregulation of receptors and their inhibitors is cardiomyocyte restricted and opposite to the receptor loss of function of heritable PAH. In ECs, phase 2 resolves as an EndoMT/angiogenic destabilization program ( SNAI1 ,  ADAMTS1 ,  ANGPT2  up; directionally concordant in snRNA-seq). CCR2 −  macrophage remodeling remains graded rather than a discrete phase 2 step. Module-level analysis (Fig.  4c ) resolves two cross-platform concordant programs. A cardiomyocyte OXPHOS module set (M10, M25, M26) is progressively downregulated, whereas myeloid inflammatory, cytokine and immunoglobulin modules (M8, M13, M15) are coordinately induced. Both programs agree in direction between bulk and snRNA-seq when scored within their cell type of origin. The lineage-level DEG count asymmetry is summarized in Fig.  4d .     Spatially constrained cell−cell communication reveals stage-specific signaling  Cell−cell communication inference (CellChat  29  , applied to per-patient snRNA-imputed Xenium expression under Xenium-derived spatial constraints; Supplementary Data  14 ) revealed a progressive reorganization of myocardial signaling across the NF → pRV → RVF axis (Fig.  4e,f ). In every condition, the highest-probability pathways were contact-mediated adhesion programs (PTPRM, NCAM, ADGRL, CDH), consistent with the dense cellular packing of myocardium and serving as a stable baseline rather than a disease feature. Layered on this baseline, RVF showed a selective gain of ECM signaling: COLLAGEN, LAMININ and THBS, which were low or absent among top-ranked interactions in NF and pRV, rose to prominence specifically in RVF. This matrix signaling gain is concordant with the emergence of the matrifibrocyte-like fibroblast state and frames fibroblast-to-stroma communication as a defining feature of RVF.    Cardiomyocytes demonstrate mitochondrial dysfunction in RV failure  Subclustering snRNA-seq resolved 10 cardiomyocyte subtypes (Extended Data Fig.  2a,b  and Supplementary Data  7 ), which are defined by distinct functional gene programs by subtype Gene Ontology enrichment and exhibit opposing proportional changes in NF compared to disease states, with subcluster distribution similar between pRV/RVF (Extended Data Fig.  2c,d ). SpaGE-imputed label transfer corroborated subtype mapping at single-cell spatial resolution (Extended Data Fig.  2e ). Three subtypes expanded in diseased RVs: CM BetaMHC (fetal sarcomere), CM HAND2 (RV-specifier  HAND2  and endothelin receptor  EDNRA ), and CM RORA, with a trend towards expansion in CM NPP ( NPPA / NPPB ). This represents reactivation of fetal, developmental and stretch-stress programs. Fibroblasts activate early in RV failure  Fibroblasts were the most transcriptionally responsive snRNA-seq population (1,083 pRV versus NF DEGs; 806 RVF versus NF DEGs). Subclustering snRNA-seq resolved seven literature-grounded subtypes (Extended Data Fig.  3a,b ): Fb Resident, Adventitial, Elastogenic, Interstitial, Stressed, Pro-fibrotic and Anti-fibrotic, with fibroblast subtype proportions generally stable across disease states (Extended Data Fig.  3c ). The snRNA-seq trajectory was front loaded and consistent with Xenium (Extended Data Fig.  3d ): in phase 1, there was downregulation of the TGFβ co-receptor  TGFBR3  along with  GPX3  and the matrix/elastogenic genes  ELN  and  TIMP3 . Simultaneously, the canonical myofibroblast/matricellular markers  THBS4  (ref.   34  ) and  ACTA2  (ref.   35  ) and the activated fibroblast marker  SFRP4  were induced.  None of the snRNA-seq, bulk or panel-filtered Xenium data yielded significant fibrogenic DEGs in RVF versus pRV at the lineage level. Xenium fibroblast subtype resolution exposed a focal phase 2 program restricted to activated/matricellular subsets involving  THBS4 ,  TNC  and  PRG4  (snRNA-seq directions concordant, not significant) (Extended Data Fig.  3e ). Two literature-defined module scores anchored the two-phase split: the Koenig et al.  10   donor fibroblast identity signature collapsed sharply at NF → pRV with no further drop at decompensation (Extended Data Fig.  3f ), whereas the Fu et al.  34   matrifibrocyte commitment signature was flat at NF → pRV and trended upward only at pRV → RVF (Extended Data Fig.  3g ). This suggests that fibroblast identity erosion is phase 1 specific, whereas fibrogenic commitment is phase 2 specific. Cross-platform similarity (Extended Data Fig.  3h,i ) was strongest for Stressed and Interstitial subtypes. Spatial neighborhood analysis (Extended Data Fig.  3j–l ) placed FB Stressed, Matrix, Intermediate and CILP in myeloid-enriched niches (Xen FB Matrix–myeloid Pearsonʼs  r  = 0.93). Massonʼs trichrome/Sirius Red histology confirmed progressive fibrosis (+5.9% area per stage; Extended Data Fig.  3m ). In RVF, the fibrotic myocardium niche occupies a smaller fraction of section area (Fig.  3g ). This does not necessarily represent less fibrosis, as niche proportions are compositional. They describe how section area is partitioned between neighborhoods, not how much matrix each neighborhood contains. The rising histologic collagen burden (Extended Data Fig.  3m ), the pRV → RVF gain of ECM signaling (Fig.  4e ) and the matrifibrocyte commitment trend (Extended Data Fig.  3g ) all measure matrix content or fibroblast state and are compatible with fibrotic remodeling intensifying within existing neighborhoods while the stressed myocardium and vascular niches expand their share of the section. Fibroblast subclusters identified from previous LV studies were similarly recovered (Extended Data Fig.  4a–d ), indicating conserved fibroblast biology across ventricles.                      Mural cells lose vasoprotective programs in RV failure  Mural snRNA-seq subclustering (Extended Data Fig.  3n ) separates pericytes from smooth muscle. Pericytes undergo phase 1 loss of vascular-protective programs spanning metabolic, homeostatic, anti-protease, anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidant functions (gene lists in Extended Data Fig.  3o  and Supplementary Data  8  and  9 ), concordant across bulk, snRNA-seq and Xenium pseudobulk. The loss is largely pericyte restricted. Pericyte snRNA-seq additionally showed downregulation of the TGFβ co-receptor  TGFBR3  and the hypoxia pathway gene  HIF3A . We quantify the protective program loss by a curated pseudobulk module score ( TIMP3 ,  IL1RL1 ,  GPX3 ,  ELN ; Extended Data Fig.  3p ), whose NF/pRV/RVF trajectory parallelled the fibroblast module. At the lineage level, mural cells did not demonstrate significant phase 2 changes, whereas sublineage analyses by snRNA-seq pseudobulk reveal IEG/AP-1 stress and partial contractile reversion as the dominant gene groupings (heatmap in Extended Data Fig.  3q ). Xenium subtype resolution (Extended Data Fig.  3r ) resolves focal subset-restricted hits:  MYH11  loss in Pericyte_KCNJ8, Pericyte_THBS4 and VSMC_Inflamed;  CNN1  induction in VSMC_Arterial; and  NR4A3  induction in VSMC_Inflamed (cross-platform concordance in Extended Data Fig.  3s ), supporting a focal phase 2 program rather than a pan-mural shift.    The immune compartment remodels in RV failure with resident macrophage identity loss and cumulative inflammatory transition  Myeloid subclustering yielded six snRNA-seq populations (Fig.  6a–c  and Supplementary Data  7 ): CCR2 −  resident macrophage, inflammatory macrophage (iMac), monocyte/monocyte-derived, TREM2 + , dendritic and proliferating; mast cells were only identified by Xenium. CCR2 −  resident macrophages expressed the conserved TLF framework ( TIMD4 ,  LYVE1 ,  FOLR2 )  36  . iMac cells retained resident markers while strongly expressing immediate-early genes ( NR4A1/  NR4A2/NR4A3 ,  FOS ,  EGR1 ) and, more modestly, NF-κB target cytokines ( CCL3 ,  CCL4 ,  IL1B ) while also lacking monocyte lineage markers, reflecting an activated-resident rather than a recruited-monocyte state. TREM2 +  cells expressed a lipid-associated signature  37   implicated in phagocytosis of cardiomyocyte-ejected dysfunctional mitochondria  38 , 39  .  Pseudobulk DESeq2 identified CCR2 −  resident macrophages as the most responsive myeloid population (169 pRV versus NF snRNA-seq DEGs; 10 Xenium). Phase 1 featured cross-platform loss of resident/scavenger markers ( VSIG4 ,  CD163 ). No individual significant DEG emerged from snRNAseq analysis of pRV → RVF, but the inflammatory transition appeared cumulative from NF → pRV → RVF. From NF → RVF, resident macrophages induced the NR4A immediate-early family, the activation marker  CD83  and coordinated MHC-II induction ( HLA-DRB1  significant), supporting increased antigen presentation capacity. Myeloid WGCNA (Fig.  6d–f ) recapitulated this pattern: RVF-upregulated M8 enriched for MHC-II master  CIITA   40  , whereas the RVF-downregulated  NR3C1  target-enriched M1 module captured the same coordinated resident identity loss. After co-embedding RV and LV (from Koenig et al.  10  ) myeloid cells (Extended Data Fig.  4e,f ), the same resident/scavenger markers,  VSIG4  and  CD163 , fell in both ventricles (Extended Data Fig.  4g,h ), identifying erosion of resident macrophage identity as a shared, chamber-independent feature of heart failure.  Within the myeloid compartment, the dominant transcriptional change was a coordinated, pan-myeloid downregulation of GR transactivation targets. The canonical GR transactivation targets  FKBP5 ,  TSC22D3 ,  ZBTB16  and  KLF9 — together with  ANGPTL4 —were concordantly downregulated as an early stepwise shift  23  , established at the pre-failure (pRV) stage and sustained in RVF (Fig.  6g,h  and Supplementary Data  17 ), and this decline was consistent across myeloid subtypes rather than confined to a single population. In parallel, MHC-II/antigen presentation genes, led by the master regulator  CIITA , were induced with the same early kinetics. Critically, this rewiring was program specific rather than a generalized inflammatory activation, and two innate immune axes that commonly accompany myocardial stress were explicitly unchanged across disease stage. The NLRP3 inflammasome, a canonical driver of heart failure inflammation, showed minimal induction of its sensors, adaptor, caspases or effector cytokines ( IL1B ,  IL18 )  41 , 42  . Likewise, the type I IFN/antiviral ISG response, increasingly reported in failing and inflamed myocardium, remained flat, arguing against an IFN-driven component to the myeloid response  43 , 44  . Thus, the failing RV myeloid compartment shows a focused, coordinated shift in GR target gene expression, in the absence of inflammasome or type I IFN activation. Comparison with failing LV (dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM)) myeloid cells shows that this configuration is only partly conserved across ventricles: MHC-II/antigen presentation induction is shared, and the type I IFN response stays low in both, whereas the loss of GR target gene expression and the absence of inflammasome activation are RV specific. LV DCM myeloid cells instead retain GR target expression and show inflammasome induction (Extended Data Fig.  4i ).  Spatial Xenium refined myeloid taxonomy into eight subpopulations, adding Mac C1q and Mast Cell. Residents distributed broadly, and iMacs co-localized with monocytes at the tissue periphery—a spatial pattern that cannot by itself distinguish phenotypic transition of resident macrophages from monocyte-derived recruitment (Fig.  6i ). TLF marker retention in iMacs, iMac non-expansion (not significant by Kruskal−Wallis) and CCR2 −  contraction are consistent with phenotypic transition, but the iMac/monocyte spatial co-occurrence and absence of imaging-based lineage tracing leave the relative contribution of resident cell transition versus monocyte recruitment unresolved.    ECs suppress anti-oxidant programs and activate in RV failure  EC snRNA-seq subclustering yielded five clusters (Fig.  7a,b  and Supplementary Data  7 ), including an endocardial population ( LEPR ,  NPR3 ). snRNA-seq showed EC expansion in pRV/RVF driven by capillary and arterial ECs, with relative contraction of endocardial and lymphatic ECs (Fig.  7c ). Xenium favored arterial expansion with stable capillary proportions, reflecting platform-specific recovery biases. High-dimensional WGCNA (hdWGCNA)  45   resolved seven EC modules (catalog in  Methods  and Supplementary Data  18 ), with ecM1/ecM4/ecM7 (capillary/arterial/venous EC programs) being upregulated in RVF (Fig.  7d–g ).  Phase 1 EC resolved into two cross-platform programs (Fig.  4a,b ). Phase 1 loss of homeostatic features included suppression of vasoprotective genes ( IL1RL1 , the dominant anti-oxidant  GPX3 ,  ACE2  and  EDN1 ). ISGs rose in parallel, with concordant induction of  IFI44L ,  RSAD2 ,  IFI44 ,  OAS1 / OAS2 / OAS3 ,  MX1 , and  STAT1  by snRNA-seq and bulk (not included in the Xenium 477-gene panel). We curated 13 phase 2 EC candidate genes spanning five functional programs: angiogenic destabilization ( ANGPT2 ,  MYC ,  ADAMTS1 ), EC stress ( STC1 ,  NR4A1 ,  NR4A3 ), EC activation ( ACKR1 ,  PLA2G2A ), mesenchymal ( SNAI1 ), and EC identity ( VWF ,  PECAM1 ,  MECOM ,  CA4 ), and we tested cross-platform concordance in EC pan-pseudobulk (RVF versus pRV; Fig.  7h,i ). The functional phase 2 program validated cleanly: angiogenic destabilization (3/3 Xenium-sig + sn-concordant), the isolated  SNAI1  event,  ACKR1  biphasic reduction in phase 1 and recovery in phase 2 and  CA4  capillary identity erosion; EC stress IFN effector genes (IEGs) were direction concordant but false discovery rate (FDR) modest at the lineage level. Three EC identity/activation candidates ( VWF ,  MECOM ,  PLA2G2A ) showed Xenium signal without snRNA-seq direction concordance.  At the sublineage level, cardioprotective  NRG1  was strongly induced in endocardial ECs in phase 1 (Fig.  7j ). The arterial specifier  MECOM   46 , 47   visually trended up in arterial ECs snRNA-seq in phase 1 (Fig.  7k ; notably, phase 2 in Xenium); because  MECOM  regulates arteriovenous specification in human cardiac endothelium, adult  MECOM  induction may explain capillary/arterial-biased expansion.    A mouse PAB model recapitulates some but not all aspects of human RVF  PAB isolates the RV-specific consequence of sustained pressure overload, the hemodynamic insult shared with pulmonary hypertension and other right-sided afterload diseases, in the absence of pulmonary vascular and systemic confounders or LV failure. We profiled snRNA-seq of sham ( n  = 3) and PAB with mild or severe RVF ( n  = 3,  n  = 4; stratified by RV dilation (RV end-diastolic area); Supplementary Table  7 , Extended Data Fig.  5a,b  and Supplementary Data  19 ). Most cell populations were recovered except adipocytes  48  , with EC expansion and cardiomyocyte contraction across disease states paralleling the human dataset (Extended Data Fig.  5c ). EC expansion was largely arterial in mice versus capillary/arterial in humans (Extended Data Fig.  5d,e ), and human EC hdWGCNA modules embedded consistently. Myeloid cells (<2% of total cells) separated into MHC-II - high and resident macrophages. PAB-induced shifts in RV myeloid cells were broadly discordant with human RVF. Across single-nucleus myeloid cells, PAB did not reproduce the human antigen presentation response: the M8 antigen-presenting module was not induced (Extended Data Fig.  5f ), and the pooled MHC-II module score was unchanged across severity (Extended Data Fig.  5g ). Also,  NR3C1  (GR) target genes showed no repression (Extended Data Fig.  5g ). Because antigen-presenting macrophages are a minor fraction of RV myeloid cells, we tested MHC-II directly in residents with two orthogonal assays, both of which showed active suppression in PAB RV resident macrophages. Flow cytometry showed that surface MHC-II (I-A/I-E geometric mean fluorescence intensity) on CCR2 −  resident macrophages declined in a severity-dependent manner ( P  = 0.013) even as leukocyte, myeloid, macrophage and resident macrophage frequencies remained unchanged across severity (Extended Data Fig.  5h ). Genetic pulse−chase fate mapping ( Cx3cr1 -CreER; Rosa26 -tdTomato) with flow-sorted bulk RNA-seq of long-lived resident macrophages confirmed MHC-II suppression in PAB RV resident macrophages (Extended Data Fig.  5i  and Supplementary Data  20 )  49  . Thus, the antigen presentation/MHC-II program induced in human RVF resident macrophages is instead suppressed in the mouse PAB RV, establishing inter-species divergence of the RVF myeloid signature.                    In summary, comparing pediatric to adult RVF, we found that:    Gene expression modules are largely concordant between adult and pediatric RVs.    Overall, there is substantial, but not perfect, concordance in the transcriptional changes during RVF.    Endothelial expansion is seen in both cases of RVF, although it appears driven by venous ECs in pediatric hearts versus capillary ECs in adult hearts.    Mitochondrial gene expression is mostly unchanged in pediatric RVF, unlike adult RVF. Consistent with this, mitochondrial respiration also appears unchanged.    Myeloid MHC-II expression is induced in both cases.      RVF and LVF share core transcriptional programs  Cell-type-resolved LV concordances have already emerged from the fibroblast (Extended Data Fig.  4a–c ) and myeloid (Extended Data Fig.  4d–i ) analyses above. To consolidate that picture and extend it to the bulk module and transcriptome scale, we leveraged the same Koenig et al.  10   human LV snRNA-seq dataset across the full RV WGCNA module set, which showed that RV modules were broadly conserved in LV with concordant NF-versus-DCM trends (Fig.  8g ). Findings that were common to RVF and LVF included induction of the contractile/cytoskeletal/focal adhesion module M2 (Fig.  8h ); repression of the nuclear-encoded ETC mitochondrial modules M10, M25, M26 and M28 (Fig.  8i ); and NF-versus-failing pseudobulk cardiomyocyte FCs (Fig.  8j ). One chamber-specific divergence emerged from the myeloid comparison: the RV iMac population uniquely retained TLF residency markers that were not reported in the Koenig et al. LV inflammatory macrophages. This is consistent with, although it does not prove, an RV iMac hybrid resident-like state.  Thus, the core heart failure programs (mitochondrial suppression, inflammatory activation and myofibroblast activation) are shared between RVF and LVF.     Discussion  We integrated bulk, single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomics with orthogonal mitochondrial respirometry, flow cytometry and histology to construct a multi-lineage atlas of human RVF, from which a two-phase model emerges. Phase 1 (NF → pRV) carries the dominant transcriptional burden in bulk and snRNA-seq pseudobulk and features tissue-wide erosion of protective programs, resident macrophage identity loss, fibroblast activation, endothelial expansion and anti-oxidant suppression and pan-tissue  FKBP5  loss. The compensated-to-decompensated (pRV → RVF) transition is best framed as a transcriptional set-point shift in phase 1 (approximately 95% of platform-resolved DEGs) followed by qualitatively distinct, lineage-specific phase 2 programs that include cardiomyocyte oxidative stress, EC  ANGPT2 / ADAMTS1  induction consistent with vascular remodeling and fibroblast matricellular activation.  A central and unanticipated finding is that the pediatric single-ventricle RV resists the mitochondrial failure that characterizes adult and mouse pressure overload. In adult RVF, a coordinated decline in nuclear-encoded mitochondrial transcripts, accompanied by suppression of the ERRα/PGC-1α biogenesis program, parallel impaired complex I + II respiratory function. The mouse PAB RV showed the same concordant decline: cardiomyocyte mitochondrial transcripts were coordinately downregulated (gene set enrichment, consistent with the decreased ETC gene expression reported by Hwang et al.  53  ) alongside reduced respiratory capacity, although the per-animal transcriptional effect was modest relative to the functional deficit. By contrast, pediatric HLHS-palliated failing RVs were metabolically spared. Mitochondrial transcripts were neither induced nor significantly suppressed, and respiratory capacity was preserved (Fig.  5h ). The cross-cohort respiratory pattern (Fig.  5j ), with deficits in adult and mouse but not pediatric single-ventricle RVF, together with the transcriptional data, suggests that the adult and mouse pressure-overloaded RVs undergo coupled mitochondrial transcriptional and functional decline. Conversely, the developing single-ventricle heart sustains respiratory function.  A notable feature of the RV myeloid compartment was a macrophage population marked by an immediate-early gene program, including  NR4A1 ,  NR4A3 ,  DUSP2 ,  FOS  and  JUN , which we designate as iMac. Because induction of these transcription factors is a recognized consequence of enzymatic tissue dissociation in single-cell RNA-seq, such signatures are often dismissed as technical artifact  54  . Several lines of evidence argue against that interpretation here. The program was defined in snRNA-seq, which omits the warm enzymatic dissociation step responsible for the artifact, and was independently recovered by in situ spatial transcriptomics (Xenium), in which transcripts are detected on fixed tissue without any dissociation. Furthermore, the signature was confined to a single macrophage subset and showed reproducible spatial organization, co-localizing with monocytes within discrete tissue foci—a distribution incompatible with a uniform, handling-induced stress response, which would be expected across all cell types irrespective of identity. The iMacs additionally retained resident macrophage markers that were not observed in the inflammatory macrophages of the Koenig et al.  10   left ventricular atlas, suggesting that the RV harbors an activated, resident-like macrophage state localized to sites of monocyte accrual. Whether this state reflects local activation of resident macrophages or in situ adaptation of recruited cells cannot be resolved from cross-sectional human data and will require lineage-resolved models. Regardless of origin, its presence points to a chamber-specific organization of the myeloid response in right ventricular failure.  We found evidence for disruption in GR signaling, with tissue-wide loss of the GR co-chaperone  FKBP5  and a coordinated, pan-myeloid suppression of  NR3C1  transactivation targets, although this evidence is limited to transcriptional state. Because the GR can bind both positive and negative glucocorticoid response elements (GREs) and drive either induction or repression accordingly, downregulation of GRE-associated transcripts does not by itself imply reduced GR activity. Therefore, the direction of GR signaling cannot be inferred from target gene expression alone, and functional validation of altered glucocorticoid signaling will require dedicated studies. However, the PAB model only partially reproduces this human signature ( NR3C1  targets unchanged), limiting its utility for studying RV glucocorticoid biology. Because  FKBP5  loss is observed across both tissue-resident and circulating-origin lineages, the underlying signal could reflect either local microenvironmental modulation of glucocorticoid responsiveness or systemic axis perturbation. Distinguishing these possibilities will require dedicated experimental designs.  The endothelial expansion seen in pRV/RVF across adult human, pediatric human and mice is somewhat unusual among heart failure transcriptomic studies but has been reported in the context of ischemic left ventricular cardiomyopathy  11  . We hypothesize that this reflects coronary microvascular adaptation to RV-specific hemodynamics (a thin-walled chamber perfused throughout systole as well as diastole), driving compensatory capillary/arterial expansion to maintain oxygen delivery in the setting of pressure loading, with adult  MECOM  +  arterial induction and pediatric venous-dominated expansion reflecting different developmental contexts. Phase 2 angiopoietin axis destabilization ( ANGPT2 ,  MYC ,  ADAMTS1 ) suggests that this initially compensatory vascular response transitions toward destabilization at decompensation. Functional validation will require perfusion imaging, vascular casting or interventional EC studies.  More broadly, mouse PAB reproduces the hemodynamic burden of human RVF and converges with human RVF in terms of metabolic and structural programs: suppression of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes, reduced respiratory capacity, cardiomyocyte fetal gene reactivation, endothelial expansion and progressive fibrosis. However, it diverges in immune and hormonal programs, most notably myeloid antigen presentation (MHC-II/ CIITA ) and glucocorticoid signaling and in finer features such as the arterial-biased endothelial expansion seen in mice. The model is, therefore, well suited to studying RV metabolic and fibrotic remodeling but should be applied cautiously to immune or glucocorticoid pathways.  Our atlas can be placed directly against previous cross-chamber and cross-etiology studies. In the NF human heart, the right and left ventricles are nearly transcriptionally identical. The four-chamber atlas of Tucker et al.  16   reported only approximately 24 genes differentially expressed between the ventricles, versus more than 1,000 for each atrial−ventricular contrast, implying that the RV-specific programs we resolve in failure are disease emergent rather than reflections of baseline chamber identity. Against the matched failing-LV/DCM atlas of Koenig et al.  10  , the failing RV and LV share a substantial core transcriptional program (mitochondrial suppression, cytoskeletal remodeling and immune activation)  10 , 12 , 15   with RV-specific divergence in focal programs such as glucocorticoid axis loss and reduced inflammasome induction. A rat pulmonary-artery-banding (RV) versus aortic-banding (LV) model likewise shows broadly overlapping ventricular transcriptomes at baseline (approximately 91% shared) but a distinct, stronger RV disease response, together with a conserved secreted/matrix right-heart-failure signature of approximately 50 genes spanning rat PAB and human chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH)  55  . Notably, isolated afterload modeling argues that RVF and LVF are largely distinct: only 2.2% of human LVF genes overlap the rat PAB regulated set  55  . Our predominantly LVF secondary cohort is the informative exception: its RVF shares the broad cardiomyopathic core of the failing LV, which we attribute to the common myocardial and systemic substrate of LVF-associated RVF rather than to the isolated afterload that drives the RV-versus-LV divergence seen in the banding model.  These comparisons carry translational implications. The shared core molecular pathology between LVF-associated RVF and LVF suggests that the clinical failure of LV-directed guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) in isolated RVF  9   reflects engagement of non-cardiac targets, biomechanical context, chamber geometry or upstream hemodynamic triggers rather than fundamentally divergent molecular pathways. Combined with a parallel plasma LTBP-2 biomarker study  56  , the fibrosis-related RV transcripts identified here may eventually serve as biomarkers of RV remodeling. Overall, the multi-lineage microenvironmental remodeling that we identify nominates anti-fibrotic strategies (notably, TGFBR3), immunomodulatory approaches and direct mitochondrial functional support as plausible RV-specific therapeutic avenues.  Our study has limitations. The snRNA-seq cohort ( n  = 11), although among the largest for human RV, remains modest. We address this through the larger bulk cohort ( n  = 142) and cross-platform concordance for key claims. Xenium was available for  n  = 3 per group, limiting CellChat inference, and is restricted to the 477-gene panel, so off-panel claims (notably,  POSTN ,  FKBP5 ,  TGFBR3  and  MLIP ) rest on bulk and snRNA-seq alone. Also, the phase 2 signal is quantitatively limited across platforms. Endothelial EndoMT and cardiomyocyte reactivation programs will require targeted functional validation. Experimental model and subject details   Mouse models  All animal studies were approved by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocols 805255 and 805309). Method details   Statement on human specimens  This study complies with all relevant ethical regulations and was approved by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Review Board (study number 802781), the Childrenʼs Hospital of Philadelphia Institutional Review Board (study number 22-020464) and the Gift-of-Life Donor Program. Prospective informed and written consent for research use of surgically explanted tissue was obtained from the transplant recipients or from the next-of-kin in the case of deceased organ donors. The consent obtained covers publication of the resulting data: participants, or next-of-kin for deceased organ donors, were informed that the results of the research may be presented at scientific meetings or in publications, with identity not disclosed and only coded identifiers used. In brief, all hearts underwent in situ cardioplegia and were kept in cold cardioplegia or saline until transmural samples were snap frozen in liquid nitrogen (within 4 hours) and stored at −80 °C until processing for mRNA analysis.      Participant demographics  Bulk RNA-seq included 142 participants: NF  n  = 29 (11 male, 18 female; mean age 51.8 ± 16.1 years, range 18−75), pressure-loaded  n  = 78 (61 male, 17 female; mean age 53.6 ± 11.0 years, range 20−69) and RV failure  n  = 35 (21 male, 14 female; mean age 55.0 ± 8.7 years, range 27−69).
