Xenium spatial transcriptomics included nine participants: NF  n  = 3 (one male, two female; mean age 61.0 ± 6.1 years, range 54−65), pressure-loaded  n  = 3 (two male, one female; mean age 54.3 ± 1.5 years, range 53−56) and RV failure  n  = 3 (two male, one female; mean age 47.7 ± 20.0 years, range 27−67). Per-participant sex, age and underlying diagnosis are given in Supplementary Tables  1 ,  4  and  6 . The pediatric single-nucleus cohort comprised 14 participants from two institutions (Colorado  n  = 9, Washington University in St. Louis  n  = 5): NF donors  n  = 4 (two male, two female; mean age 4.9 ± 3.3 years, range 1.3−8.0), single-ventricle participants with protein-losing enteropathy or plastic bronchitis  n  = 5 (three male, two female; mean age 9.6 ± 5.1 years, range 4.8−16.0) and single-ventricle participants with systolic heart failure  n  = 5 (four male, one female; mean age 10.5 ± 8.3 years, range 3.8−23.0). One participant in the systolic heart failure group was 23 years old at collection. All others were under 18.    Bulk RNA-seq: sample stratification  Diseased RVs were stratified into two groups: pRV (right atrial pressure and right atrial to pulmonary capillary wedge pressure ratio—that is, RA ≤ 8 mmHg, RA:PCWP ≤ 0.37) and RVF (RA ≥ 9 mmHg, RA:PCWP ≥ 0.63) based on validated clinical predictors of RVF or death after left ventricular assist device placement  17 , 18  .    Bulk RNA-seq: human sample preparation  Snap-frozen cardiac tissues from the RVs of explanted donors were pulverized in a liquid nitrogen-cooled cryomill. Total RNA extraction was performed using RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen) with poly(A) selection. RNA quality was assessed using RNA 6000 Nano Kit (Agilent Technologies) and 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies), targeting an RNA integrity number (RIN) score >7.0. RNA-seq libraries were prepared using TruSeq mRNA Stranded Kit (Illumina) according to the manufacturerʼs recommended protocol.    Bulk RNA-seq: transcriptome pseudo-alignment  Libraries were sequenced to a depth of more than 20 million reads per sample. Reads were trimmed using Trimmomatic  58  . Trimmed reads were pseudo-aligned to the human transcriptome (GRCh38) using Kallisto  59  . Transcript-level abundances were converted to gene-level counts with tximport, which weights transcripts by length to correct for the length dependence of read counts under the 2 × 150 sequencing configuration  60  . The resultant gene-level count matrices were then used for downstream analysis.    Bulk RNA-seq: differential gene expression  DEGs were detected using DESeq2 (ref.   61  ). To account for inter-subject differences including sex, race, other clinical variables and batch effects, SVA  62   was used to estimate 21 surrogate variables and remove sequencing batch effects—that is, with the model Expression ~ Group + SV1 +…+ SV21, where the tilde represents ‘distributed as’. A joint model was fit over all contrasts, and then pairwise comparisons (for example, NF versus pRV) were conducted for disease states using the Wald test at an  α  value of 0.1. The surrogate variables were fit from demographic and clinical covariates (sex, age, race, body surface area, height, weight, body mass index, thyroid disease, pacemaker status and sequencing and library preparation batch). Those covariates are not released, as they are indirect identifiers. The fitted surrogate variables are deposited with the count matrix so that the published models can be reproduced without patient-level characteristics.    Bulk RNA-seq: WGCNA  The R packages WGCNA  20   and hdWGCNA  45   were used for all WGCNA analysis. Only genes expressed in more than 5% of subjects (or nuclei for EC snRNA-seq) were retained for analysis. For bulk analysis, WGCNA was run on DESeq2 normalized counts and was used to identify gene modules that co-varied among subjects, agnostic of disease state.  The key of EC hdWGCNA module identities is as follows: ecM1 core/capillary identity ( n  = 1,139 genes); ecM2 sarcomeric/cardiomyocyte ambient signature ( n  = 836); ecM3 constitutive RNA splicing/processing ( n  = 647); ecM4 arterial identity ( n  = 125); ecM5 AP-1/NR4A immediate-early stress ( n  = 120); ecM6 peri-vascular/mural-like ECM ( n  = 115); ecM7 venous/inflamed program ( n  = 91). Hubs are in Supplementary Data  18 .  For the bulk WGCNA module catalog (nomenclature), the module identities used were as follows (29 in total; full hub gene lists in Supplementary Data  4 ): M1 resident-macrophage identity (hubs  VSIG4 ,  CD163 ,  MRC1 ,  LAPTM5 ,  HCLS1 ,  FCN3 ); M2 cytoskeletal/focal adhesion + structural/ECM (contractile, multi-lineage); M3 late chromatin/epitranscriptomic ( METTL3 ,  INO80 ,  KANSL1 ,  PHF8 ,  MBD1 ); M4 myeloid/T cell antigen presentation; M7 polycomb/developmental ( EZH2 ,  HOXB8 ,  ITGA4 ,  POLE2 ); M8 MHC-II master,  CIITA -enriched; M10/M25/M26 nuclear-encoded ETC/OXPHOS (M10/M26 also complex III/ATP synthase/ MCUR1 ); M12 cardiomyocyte ( TNNI3 ,  TNNI3K ,  BMPR2 ,  MYH7 ); M13 immunoglobulin repertoire ( IGHG/IGKC ); M14 cardiac transcriptional regulators ( CASZ1 ,  RARA ,  KDM5A ,  MED13L ,  TLE4 ,  DDR1 ); M15 endothelial activation (95 genes, chemokine signaling); M21 TGFβ/Notch/Wnt suppressors ( SKI ,  AXIN1 ,  MIB2 ,  CTBP1 ,  MTA1 ,  ALKBH5 ); M24 complex I/IV hubs; M27 splicing/RNA processing ( SRSF7 ,  SF3B1 ); and M28 mtDNA-encoded ETC ( MT-ATP6 ,  MT-CO2 ,  MT-CO3 ,  MT-CYB ,  SOD1 ). Modules M5, M6 and M16 are referenced descriptively without standalone identities.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: sample selection  Diseased hearts were selected from patients with DCM who had no high-impact variants identified on whole-exome sequencing. To maximize the probability of capturing transcriptional changes, the RVF samples were enriched for severity, possessing decreased diastolic function (RA ≥ 14 mmHg, RA:PCWP ≥ 0.7), decreased systolic function (TAPSE ≤ 1.7) and at least moderate tricuspid regurgitation; pRV samples were comparatively enriched for normal diastolic function (RA ≤ 4 mmHg, RA:PCWP ≤ 0.33), systolic function (TAPSE ≥ 2.2) and trivial or less tricuspid regurgitation. RVF and pRV samples were otherwise well balanced for other clinical and demographic variables (Supplementary Tables  4  and  5 ). For the pediatric HLHS cohort, Fontan/Glenn single-ventricle physiology differs fundamentally from adult LVF secondary pressure overload in onset timing, ventricular morphology and load history; pediatric comparisons, therefore, test molecular convergence rather than direct replication.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: human sample preparation  Samples were prepared as described previously  12  . In brief, frozen cardiac tissues from the RV of explanted donors (approximately 100 mg) were sectioned to 100 µm (Leica, CM1950 cryostat) and then transferred into a 2-ml Dounce homogenizer containing 1 ml of chilled lysis buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 250 mM sucrose, 25 mM KCl, 3 mM MgCl 2 , 1 µM DTT and 0.05% IGEPAL-630 in nuclease-free water). Samples were homogenized with 10 passes of a coarse pestle and then 10 passes of a fine pestle and then incubated on ice for 15 minutes. Large debris was removed by centrifugation at 40 g  for 1 minute (Beckman Coulter, Allegra X-15R swinging bucket centrifuge) before sequentially being filtered through a 50-µm and then a 10-µm filter (puriSelect Life Science) into a 50-ml conical tube. The filters were washed with 6 ml of wash buffer (0.01% BSA, 5 mM MgCl 2 , PBS), and the resultant suspension was pelleted at 550 g  for 5 minutes at 4 °C. The pelleted nuclei were resuspended in 150 µl of cold nuclei resuspension buffer (0.01% BSA, 5 mM MgCl 2 , 0.4 U µl −1  murine RNase inhibitor (New England Biolabs), PBS) and counted on a hemocytometer before dilution to 1,000 nuclei per microliter.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: mouse sample preparation  Samples were prepared similarly as above for the human samples, with the notable exception of an additional fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) step at the end. DAPI (1 µg ml −1 ) was added into the lysis buffer. Instead of resuspension in nuclei resuspension buffer, nuclei were resuspended in FACS buffer (1% BSA, 0.4 U µl −1  murine RNase inhibitor (New England Biolabs), PBS). Nuclei were flowed at the lowest flow rate on a FACSAria III (BD Biosciences) with a 100-µm nozzle. In total, 100,000 DAPI +  singlets were collected. Nuclei were recovered by spinning at 500 g  for 5 minutes and then resuspended in nuclei resuspension buffer before quantification and dilution to 1,000 nuclei per microliter.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: 10x Chromium single-cell gene expression  Nuclei were loaded onto the 10x Genomics Chromium microfluidic platform (Single Cell 3′ solution, v3) for an estimated recovery of 6,000 cells per device. Processing of libraries was performed according to the manufacturerʼs instructions.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: sequencing and alignment  Complementary DNA libraries were multiplexed and sequenced on a NovaSeq 6000 S4 chip (Azenta) to a goal of approximately 75,000−100,000 reads per nucleus. Raw base call files for each sample were demultiplexed and converted to FASTQ files using the 10x Genomics toolkit Cell Ranger 7.1.0 (cellranger mkfastq)  63  . FASTQ files were then uploaded to the 10x Genomic Cloud where Cell Ranger Count 7.1.0 was run on each sample to map them to the human (GRCh38) 2020-A transcriptome or the mouse (GRCm39) 2020-A transcriptome with the include-introns flag set to true. Resultant raw feature matrices were then used for downstream analysis.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: ambient RNA and noise removal  To remove ambient and background RNA contamination, we used CellBender  64  , running remove-background with hyperparameter tuning (primarily of learning rate) to ensure smooth convergence during model training. CellBender-denoised count matrices were then further processed with DecontX  65   to estimate and subtract residual per-cell ambient contamination, and the DecontX-corrected counts were carried forward for all downstream analyses. Some residual cytoplasmic RNA contamination during nuclear isolation can nevertheless produce low-level off-target detection of canonical cell type markers (for example,  RYR2  in non-cardiomyocyte populations); cell type assignment, therefore, relies on relative enrichment over a panel of cluster-defining markers rather than presence/absence of any single gene.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: filtering and quality control  All further analysis was conducted in Seurat  66  . Nuclei with more than 5% mitochondrial transcripts, with fewer than 200 transcripts or with more than 100,000 transcripts were discarded. For each nucleus, the entropy (using the Python package ndd and its entropy function) and the exonic percentage (using scR-Invex) were calculated. Nuclei with entropy below Q1 − 1.5×IQR (first quartile (Q1), interquartile range (IQR)), exon percentage above Q3 + 1.5×IQR (third quartile (Q3)) or mitochondrial read percentage above Q3 + 1.5×IQR were flagged as outliers and removed. For secondary outlier detection, nuclei were then clustered using Seuratʼs built-in graph-based clustering approach (FindNeighbors and FindClusters). Each cluster was fit with an ellipsoid using the sklearn EllipticEnvelope function, and the 5% of nuclei farthest from the cluster centroid were labeled as outliers and also removed. For doublet removal, we elected to utilize a semi-supervised approach, as has been done previously  11  , which was based upon identifying nuclei that simultaneously had gene expression signatures consistent with two (or more) cell populations  11  . Practically, this was done by iteratively clustering nuclei at high resolution, generating  z -score expression profiles for each expected cell population and visualizing the nuclei clusters colored by  z -score using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) embedding. Clusters that demonstrated high expression profiles for multiple cell types were deleted, and then the entire above process was repeated until no further clusters were removed (six rounds).    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: myeloid subtype marker rationale  Myeloid subtype assignments were supported by markers with established functional roles:  F13A1  (coagulation factor XIII) is required for post-infarction cardiac integrity  67  .  MARCO  and  HPGDS  define scavenger populations implicated in non-inflammatory clearance of damage-associated molecular patterns and prostaglandin D 2 -mediated inflammation resolution, respectively  36  .  VSIG4 ,  CD163  and  LYVE1  mark self-renewing tissue-resident macrophage subsets associated with complement-mediated immune quiescence  36   and hyaluronan-dependent maintenance of arterial tone  68  . Initial high-resolution subclustering of CCR2 −  resident macrophages identified three transcriptionally distinguishable subsets (enriched for  HPGDS , a broader  F13A1 / CD209 / VSIG4  signature or  RBPJ ), but these subsets showed no disease-specific expansion (all differences <10% of total resident macrophages) and were combined into a single CCR2 −  resident macrophage population for downstream analyses.  CCR2  transcript itself is sparsely detected in droplet-based snRNA-seq of human heart  10  , a well-described dropout effect that disproportionately affects modestly expressed transcripts. Populations were, therefore, defined by combinatorial marker expression rather than by  CCR2  expression alone.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: sample integration  The 11 single-nucleus datasets were integrated using the R Harmony package  69  . Specifically, the 11 preprocessed (as above) and normalized/scaled (via SCTransform) datasets were first combined via Seurat merge, and then the RunHarmony command was utilized to generate batch-corrected PCA components (50 dimensions). These Harmony-corrected dimensions (rather than raw PCA) were used for all downstream neighbor graph construction (FindNeighbors), clustering (FindClusters) and UMAP embedding (RunUMAP).    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: reference mapping  Reference mapping was conducted using the Seurat version 4 reference mapping pipeline. In brief, both the reference and query datasets were initially preprocessed via SCTransform. The reference dataset was then integrated using canonical correlation analysis (CCA) integration rather than Harmony integration as used elsewhere. Anchors between the reference and query dataset were then identified and used to map query data to the integrated reference dataset.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: differential gene expression  Differential gene expression at the single-nucleus level was performed using the FindMarkers function. The default Wilcoxon rank-sum method was used for statistical testing. Only genes with log 2 FC > 0.1 were retained, and those with adjusted  P  < 0.05 were considered significant.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: pseudobulk differential gene expression  Pseudobulk dataset generation was done by summing counts (from the ‘counts’ slot of the SCTransform assay) for each major cell type using the AggregateExpression function. Differential gene expression analysis was then conducted via DESeq2. For both snRNA-seq and Xenium pseudobulk analyses, multiple-testing correction was performed using Benjamini−Hochberg FDR within each DESeq2 run (per subtype × contrast); no global correction was applied across the full subtype × contrast matrix, in keeping with standard pseudobulk practice where each cell type is treated as a distinct experiment. DEG counts reported throughout this paper use the unified threshold adjusted  P  < 0.05, |log 2 FC| > 0.5 and baseMean > 50 unless otherwise stated.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: enrichment analysis  Pathway enrichment analysis was conducted using the web interface for Enrichr  70   and the R enrichR package. Inputs were genes upregulated or downregulated in the cluster of interest (log 2 FC > 0.1, adjusted  P  < 0.05). Combined score was calculated as  c  = log( p ) ×  z , where  c  is the combined score,  p  is Fisherʼs exact test  P  value and  z  is  z -score for deviation from expected rank.    Bulk RNA-seq: PAH comparison  To compare RVF transcriptional programs across etiologies, we reanalyzed the published PAH RV bulk RNA-seq dataset from Khassafi et al.  19  . Raw count matrices were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus ( GSE240941 ) and processed using the same DESeq2 pipeline as our adult RV bulk data. DEGs from PAH RVF versus PAH NF were compared with our RVF versus NF DEGs to identify concordant and discordant genes. Pathway enrichment analysis (EnrichR) was performed separately on concordant genes (same direction in both datasets) and discordant genes (opposite direction).    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: mitochondrial transcription factor analysis  We assessed mitochondrial biogenesis transcriptional regulators across three analytic axes (per-patient pseudobulk DESeq2 expression, CollecTRI/decoupleR  71   transcription factor activity inference and MitoCarta3.0 (ref.   72  ) module scoring) to disentangle transcription factor transcript level, downstream regulon activity and aggregate mitochondrial program output.   Mitochondrial transcription factor panel  A literature-curated panel of nine mitochondrial biogenesis regulators was analyzed:  ESRRA ,  ESRRG ,  PPARA ,  PPARGC1A  (PGC-1α),  NRF1 ,  NFE2L2  (NRF2),  TFAM ,  POLRMT  and  TFB2M , covering the PGC-1α/ERR/PPAR/ NRF1 / TFAM  axis governing nuclear-encoded mitochondrial gene expression and mtDNA transcription.    Per-patient pseudobulk expression  For each subtype and lineage, raw RNA counts were aggregated per patient × disease state with Seurat AggregateExpression; counts were then modeled by DESeq2 (design = ~group) with apeglm log 2 FC shrinkage and Benjamini−Hochberg correction. Pairwise contrasts (NF versus pRV, pRV versus RVF, NF versus RVF) used the Wald test. Per-patient violin plots show pseudobulk variance-stabilized transformation (VST) expression, with pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum  P  values reported between disease states. Pseudobulk treats each patient as the unit of replication, avoiding the inflated significance produced by treating individual nuclei as independent observations.    Transcription factor activity inference via CollecTRI/decoupleR  Transcription factor activities were inferred from the cardiomyocyte snRNA-seq using the decoupleR R package with the CollecTRI regulon network (decoupleR::get_collectri, organism = ‘human’, split_complexes = FALSE). Per-cell transcription factor activity was estimated by univariate linear modeling (decoupleR::run_ulm) on SCTransform-normalized expression with default minimum regulon size. Per-patient mean activity per disease group was computed and visualized as a heatmap for the curated mitochondrial transcription factor panel; this approach captures downstream regulon-level activation independent of transcription factor transcript abundance. Pairwise group differences were tested by Wilcoxon rank-sum on per-patient mean activities.    MitoCarta3.0 module score  The MitoCarta3.0 inventory of human mitochondrial-localized genes was used to score aggregate mitochondrial program output. Seurat AddModuleScore was applied to the full MitoCarta3.0 gene set on the SCTransform-normalized snRNA-seq cardiomyocyte data; per-cell scores were aggregated per cardiomyocyte subcluster × disease state.    Bulk RNA-seq cross-validation  DESeq2-VST expression values for the same nine-transcription-factor panel were extracted from the bulk RNA-seq cohort ( n  = 142 patients). Disease-state differences were tested by Wilcoxon rank-sum.     Spatial transcriptomics: 10x Xenium  The Xenium protocol was completed using the Xenium Slides and Sample Prep Reagents Kit (10x Genomics, PN-1000460) and associated consumables. The procedure itself was done using the manufacturerʼs suggested protocol ( CG000578 ; 10x Genomics) without modifications. In brief, 5-µm sections of formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) RV samples were mounted onto a Xenium slide (10x Genomics) prior to deparaffinization, decrosslinking, fixation and permeabilization. We specifically chose nine RV samples (three NF, three pRV and three RVF) based on RNA quality and sample geometry (variable sizes but typically 10 × 10 mm) for Xenium analysis. Probes were hybridized, washed, ligated and amplified prior to autofluorescence quenching and nuclei staining. Custom probes were designed based on a manually curated list of 100 cluster-specific marker genes from the snRNA-seq data (using the Seurat FindAllMarkers function). The prepared slides were then loaded onto the Xenium Analyzer (10x Genomics), which was run following the recommended protocol. A total of 477 target genes (377 predesigned from the Human Multi-Tissue and Cancer Panel and 100 custom genes) plus 64 negative control probes (541 total) were included on the panel (design ID: 44Z7X8; Supplementary Data  10 ). Output was visualized via Xenium Explorer (10x Genomics). Default Xenium segmentation recovered fewer cells than transcript-level methods, and Baysor  73   produced visually apparent over-segmentation of large cardiomyocytes. Proseg  74   (version 0.3.0) was, therefore, used for resegmentation with the ‘–xenium’ preset, which leverages nucleus boundary overlap for transcript-to-cell assignment. Transcripts with quality value <20 were excluded prior to resegmentation. Each tissue section was divided into overlapping spatial patches using SpatialData/Sopa  75  , and Proseg was run independently on each patch with default parameters (10 components, initial voxel size 10 µm). Patch-level results were merged with global cell ID remapping to avoid collisions across patches. Cell type annotation was performed using RCTD  76   (spacexr R package) in full mode, using our snRNA-seq dataset as the reference. The snRNA-seq reference was constructed from the 12 major cell type annotations with downsampling to a maximum of 500 nuclei per cell type. RCTD was run with UMI_min = 10 and UMI_min_sigma = 100. RCTD weights were used to assign each spatially resolved cell to its most likely cell type. SPLIT  77   ambient RNA correction was applied to the Proseg-resegmented count matrices. To validate cell type frequency estimates against segmentation-dependent cell size variation, nucleus-level proportions were computed by mapping Xenium DAPI nucleus boundaries to Proseg cell boundaries using polygon intersection, with each nucleus inheriting the RCTD annotation of its maximally overlapping Proseg cell. This provides an orthogonal frequency estimate where each nucleus counts as one unit regardless of cell body size. SpaGE  21   imputation was used to impute the expression of genes not included in the Xenium panel but present in the snRNA-seq reference. Subclustering of spatially resolved cells was performed within each of the 12 major cell types using Seurat (version 5). For each cell type, the SPLIT-corrected count matrix (supplemented with SpaGE-imputed genes) was normalized via SCTransform, reduced to 30 principal components and clustered using the Louvain algorithm at a resolution selected to maximize biological interpretability while minimizing over-splitting. Subtype annotations were manually assigned based on marker gene expression and concordance with snRNA-seq subtypes. Pseudobulk differential gene expression analysis was performed within each spatial cell type using DESeq2. To preserve biologically meaningful transcript abundance differences that SPLIT over-corrects, pseudobulk aggregation was performed on the raw, uncorrected Proseg-resegmented count matrix. Genes with |log 2 FC| > 0.5 and adjusted  P  < 0.05 were considered significant. Spatial niche identification was performed using Seurat’s BuildNicheAssay function with  k  = 100 nearest spatial neighbors. To prevent patient-specific cardiomyocyte subtype variation from dominating niche definitions, all cardiomyocyte subtypes were collapsed into a single label prior to niche computation. Centered log ratio (CLR) transformation was applied to niche proportion vectors to amplify differences in rare cell type fractions, followed by  z -scoring. Mini-batch  k -means clustering ( k  = 15) was performed on the CLR-transformed vectors. Clusters sharing similar compositions were merged into 14 final niches. Niche proportions were compared across disease groups (NF, pRV, RVF;  n  = 3 per group) using Kruskal−Wallis tests with Benjamini−Hochberg correction.    Spatial transcriptomics: CellChat cell−cell communication analysis  To infer intercellular signaling within RV myocardium while retaining spatial context, we combined single-nucleus expression with Xenium spatial coordinates. Because the Xenium panel measured only 477 genes, single-nucleus expression was first imputed onto Xenium cells per patient, using each patientʼs own matched snRNA-seq dataset as the reference, so no expression information was shared across individuals. Cell type annotations were consolidated into 13 broad groups from subclustered labels: ECs, cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, macrophages, pericytes, vascular smooth muscle cells, lymphocytes, myeloid cells (monocytes, dendritic cells and proliferating myeloid cells), adipocytes, epicardial cells, neural cells, lymphatic endothelial cells and mast cells. CellChat  29   was run separately for each patient. For each sample, the imputed expression matrix, lineage annotations and Xenium cell centroids were used to construct a spatial CellChat object with spatial scale factors derived from the Xenium coordinate system. Ligand−receptor interactions were drawn from CellChatDB.human. Overexpressed genes and interactions were identified, and communication probabilities were computed under spatial constraints using the truncated mean method (trim = 0.25). Interactions supported by fewer than five cells were removed. Pathway-level probabilities were aggregated across constituent ligand−receptor pairs. For aggregate network visualization, per-patient CellChat objects restricted to the myocardium niche were averaged across patients within each condition (NF,  n  = 3; pRV,  n  = 3; RVF,  n  = 3) to prevent dominance by any single individual. Edge weights were normalized by the product of sender and receiver cell type proportions to control for compositional differences across conditions. For pathway ranking, summed communication probability across all ligand−receptor pairs was computed per pathway per condition and normalized to sum to 1 within each condition. Analyses were performed in R with CellChat version 3.    PAB procedure  All animal studies were approved by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocols 805255 and 805309). Mice were housed on a normal light/dark cycle (light on from 7:00 to 19:00) with constant access to normal chow and water. PAB was performed in 9-week-old C57BL/6J mice. The anesthetic procedure included induction with ketamine (100 mg kg −1  body weight) and xylazine (10 mg kg −1  body weight) cocktail (intraperitoneal injection), tracheal intubation with a 20-gauge needle and ventilation with a Harvard rodent ventilator (Harvard Apparatus) at a rate of 120−180 breaths per minute and tidal volume of 10 µl g −1  body weight. The main pulmonary artery trunk was dissected from surrounding tissues and constricted with a 7-0 suture tied against a 25-gauge needle to generate a severe RVF. The same procedure including dissection was performed for sham mice apart from pulmonary artery ligature. Close monitoring was performed during procedure and recovery. Meloxicam was administered preoperatively and postoperatively for 48 hours for analgesia, and mice were evaluated daily for 3 days after surgery. The skin sutures were removed 7−10 days postoperatively to avoid irritation and infection. RV remodeling was confirmed by echocardiography at 2-week and 2-month post-surgery timepoints (Supplementary Table  8 ).    PAB resident macrophage bulk RNA-seq  Heterozygous  Cx3cr1 -CreER; Rosa26 -tdTomato mice were fed tamoxifen chow (Inotiv, TD.130856) starting at 3 weeks of age for 1 week. At 8 weeks of age, mice underwent PAB (or sham surgery). Two weeks after surgery, mice were anesthetized with isoflurane inhalation, and their hearts were perfused with 20 ml of cold PBS. The hearts were then dissected, atria were removed and the left and right ventricles were harvested for single-cell isolation. The ventricles were digested as previously described to generate a single-cell suspension  78 , 79  . In brief, ventricles were finely minced in ice-cold PBS until a smooth consistency was achieved. Minced tissues were transferred to Eppendorf tubes containing digestion buffer (RPMI supplemented with 450 U ml −1  Collagenase I, 60 U ml −1  DNase I and 60 U ml −1  hyaluronidase enzymes) and digested at 37 °C on a shaker for 45 minutes. After digestion, samples were briefly vortexed and immediately placed on ice to stop the reaction. Then, the cell suspensions were mechanistically dissociated by pipetting with a 1,000-µl pipettor. The digested solution was filtered through a 40-µm cell strainer and rinsed with neutralization buffer (HBSS without Ca 2+ /Mg 2+ , 2% heat-inactivated bovine serum and 0.2% BSA) to obtain a single-cell suspension. Red blood cells were lysed using ACK lysis buffer. Single-cell suspensions were stained for  CD45  (clone 30-F11; BioLegend, 103132), CD11b (clone M1/70; BioLegend, 101223) and  CD64  (clone X54-5/7.1; BioLegend, 139323). Resident macrophages (CD45 + CD11b + CD64 + tdTomato + ) were sorted by FACS, pelleted and then sent to Azenta for ultra-low-input RNA-seq.    Right ventricular cardiomyocyte mitochondrial isolation from frozen tissue  Mitochondria were isolated from flash-frozen tissue as done previously with modifications  80 , 81  . In brief, frozen right ventricular cardiac muscle was thawed on ice in mitochondrial isolation medium (Buffer A, 50 mM MOPS, 100 mM KCl, 1 mM EGTA, 5 mM MgSO 4 , pH 7.1) for 10 minutes. Thereafter, the cardiac tissue was minced on ice for 3 minutes and then subjected to a 15-minute digestion in Buffer A supplemented with 0.25 mg ml −1  Collagenase II (Worthington,  LS004176 ) while rocking at room temperature. After collagenase digestion, cardiac tissue was centrifuged at 300 g  for 5 minutes at 4 °C. The pellet was then resuspended in Buffer B (50 mM MOPS, 100 mM KCl, 1 mM EGTA, 5 mM MgSO 4 , 2 g l −1  BSA, pH 7.1) and homogenized via a glass-Teflon homogenizer (Wheaton) for approximately five passes and subsequently centrifuged at 800 g  for 10 minutes at 4 °C. The resulting supernatant containing the mitochondrial fraction was collected in a separate pre-chilled tube and centrifuged at 10,000 g  for 10 minutes at 4 °C to pellet mitochondria. The final mitochondrial pellet was washed with Buffer A to remove damaged mitochondria on the exterior of the pellet and then was resuspended in Buffer A. Protein concentration was determined using a bicinchoninic acid protein assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23225). For mouse PAB and pediatric human samples, mitochondria were similarly isolated from flash-frozen RV tissue using the protocol described above. Pediatric samples were obtained from pediatric patients with HLHS (with and without RVF) and from non-diseased pediatric donors with normal cardiac anatomy.    Assessment of mitochondrial electron transport capacity using high-resolution respirometry  Mitochondria isolated from freeze/thawed tissue are fully uncoupled and have been suggested to lose components of the TCA cycle throughout processing; however, they still maintain electron transport capacity  80  . Using high-resolution respirometry (Oroboros O2K), oxygen consumption (     J      O    2       ) was measured in isolated mitochondria from human right ventricular muscle in Buffer D (105 mM K-MES, 30 mM KCl, 1 mM EGTA, 10 mM K 2 HPO 4 , 5 mM MgCl 2 -6H 2 O, 2.5 mg ml −1  BSA, pH 7.2) supplemented with 20 mM creatine at 37 °C. Alamethicin (10 µg ml −1 ) was supplemented to Buffer D during the experiment to ensure complete membrane permeabilization and access to substrates. Then, 5−15 mg of right ventricular tissue homogenate was added to the respiratory chambers at an oxygen concentration of approximately 200 µM. Once a baseline steady-state rate was established, substrates were injected as follows: NADH (1 mM) and cytochrome c (Cyt C) (5 µM), succinate (10 mM), rotenone (5 µM), antimycin A (5 µM), N,N,N′,N′-tetramethyl- p -phenylenediamine (TMPD, 0.5 mM) and ascorbate (1 mM). The mean      J      O    2        after each injection was measured and obtained once a steady-state flux was maintained for 5 minutes. Primary measurements included complex I (NADH + Cyt C), complex I + II (after succinate addition; coupled maximal OXPHOS capacity), complex II (rotenone-resistant respiration; succinate-driven with complex I inhibited) and complex IV (ascorbate + TMPD) maximal electron transfer capacity. Residual oxygen consumption (ROX) was defined as the      J      O    2        remaining after antimycin A addition (complex III inhibitor) and was subtracted from each preceding respiratory state to yield mitochondrial-specific values, in keeping with MITOEAGLE consortium conventions. All respiratory rates were normalized to the mass of starting mitochondrial protein (pmol O 2  s −1  mg −1  mitochondrial protein) for cross-cohort consistency. Inter-group differences were assessed by Kruskal−Wallis test with Mann−Whitney pairwise post hoc comparisons (NF versus pRV, NF versus RVF, pRV versus RVF). Non-mitochondrial respiration (ROX) was independently tested across groups to confirm that observed mitochondrial deficits were not confounded by NADPH oxidase (NOX)-mediated changes in non-mitochondrial O 2  consumption. The same O2K inhibitor titration protocol was applied to pediatric human samples. The pediatric respirometry cohort consisted of pediatric NF controls (non-diseased pediatric donors with normal cardiac anatomy,  n  = 7) and pediatric HLHS-palliated failing RVs ( n  = 9), forming a within-pediatric NF-versus-failing comparison matched for age, ventricular morphology (single-ventricle physiology in the failing arm) and load history.  Mouse PAB respirometry used a different, FAO-focused protocol on intact RV tissue fiber bundle preparations (rather than freeze/thaw-isolated mitochondria), reflecting the smaller available tissue mass and the goal of profiling β-oxidation capacity in the same run. Substrate addition was sequential: pyruvate + malate (complex I leak respiration in the absence of adenosine diphosphate (ADP)), ADP (complex I-driven coupled phosphorylating respiration), Cyt C (outer mitochondrial membrane integrity check; intact outer membrane defined as Cyt C / ADP ratio < 1.10), octanoyl-carnitine (complex I + FAO substrates) and succinate (complex I + II + FAO maximal coupled capacity). Respiratory control ratio (RCR) was calculated as ADP/pyruvate + malate. Inter-group differences (sham versus PAB-mild-RVF versus PAB-severe-RVF) at each timepoint (2 weeks, 2 months) were assessed by Kruskal−Wallis test with Mann−Whitney pairwise post hoc comparisons, in keeping with the adult and pediatric statistical framework.    Immune repertoire profiling  Mouse RV cardiac single-cell suspensions were stained with the following anti-mouse antibodies: CD45-BUV395 (clone 30-F11; BioLegend, 103191), CCR2-BV421 (SA203G11; BioLegend, 150605), Ly-6G − PerCP-Cy5.5 (1A8; BioLegend, 127615), CD11b-PE (M1/70; BioLegend, 101207), CD64-PE-Cy7 (X54-5/7.1; BioLegend, 139313), TREM2-APC (237920; R&D Systems, FAB17291A) and I-A/I-E (MHC-II)-APC-Cy7 (M5/114.15.2; BioLegend, 107627). Antibodies were used at the manufacturer-recommended amounts in a 100-µl staining volume: CD45-BUV395, CD11b-PE and I-A/I-E (MHC-II)-APC-Cy7 at 0.25 µg per 10 6  cells; CCR2-BV421, Ly-6G − PerCP-Cy5.5 and CD64-PE-Cy7 at 0.5 µg per 10 6  cells; and TREM2 − APC at 10 µl per 10 6  cells. Samples were acquired on an LSRFortessa (five-laser: 355 nm, 405 nm, 488 nm, 561 nm and 640 nm) using FACSDiva version 9.1 (BD Biosciences) and were analysed in FlowJo. Compensation was calculated from single-stain controls acquired in the same run. After exclusion of doublets (forward scatter area (FSC-A)/forward scatter height (FSC-H)), populations were gated as follows: leukocytes (CD45 + ); myeloid cells (CD45 + CD11b + Ly-6G − ; Ly-6G −  excluding neutrophils); and macrophages (CD64 +  within the myeloid gate). Macrophage residency was defined by CCR2 alone: CCR2 −  cells as resident macrophages and CCR2 +  cells as recruited and monocyte derived. TREM2 +  macrophages were gated within the macrophage gate. Surface MHC-II was quantified as the geometric mean fluorescence intensity (gMFI) of I-A / I-E on the CCR2 −  resident gate. MHC-II gMFI was analyzed on a log scale (fluorescence intensity is log distributed). Trends across sham, mild-RVF and severe-RVF groups were tested with a batch-adjusted linear model on the per-animal (log transformed for gMFI) values. One sham was excluded for quality control. Gates were drawn separately for each of the two staining cohorts, on the internal negative population of each bivariate plot, and applied identically to every sample within a cohort. The complete gating cascade for a representative animal from each cohort is shown in Extended Data Fig.  9 . The cascade shown is representative of, and was applied identically to, all n = 23 biologically independent animals (cohort 1, n = 12; cohort 2, n = 11).                      Histology  Full-thickness human RV and mouse hearts were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, serially dehydrated in ethanol and paraffin embedded (FFPE). FFPE blocks were sectioned at 10 μm, mounted onto slides and stained with either trichrome or Sirius Red according to the manufacturerʼs instructions. Widefield brightfield microscopy was performed on a Keyence BZ-X810 microscope at ×10 with image stitching using BZ-X800 software. Image processing was performed in Fiji. For mouse slides, a region of interest (ROI) was manually drawn to isolate the RV free wall from the septum. Tissue borders and fibrosis-positive regions were identified using color deconvolution to generate binary masks. Statistical analysis was performed in Prism using Kruskal−Wallis with two-stage linear step-up Benjamini−Krieger−Yekutieli correction for pairwise comparisons.  For cardiomyocyte cross-sectional analyses, slides were stained with Alexa Fluor 488 WGA (Cell Signaling Technology, 1:100) and α-actinin (Abcam, ab68167, 1:200) and DAPI. Donkey anti-rabbit IgG Alexa Fluor 568 was used as secondary antibody (Invitrogen/Thermo Fisher Scientific, A10042, 1:500). Three representative stitched ×40 tile-scan images were acquired per subject in RV regions where cardiomyocytes were predominantly oriented in cross-section. Regions containing predominantly longitudinally oriented cardiomyocytes were manually excluded. Cellpose  82   was used for cell segmentation on processed WGA images using the following settings: diameter 100, flow threshold 0.5, cell probability threshold 0.0, normalization percentiles 1.0−99.0 and dynamic Niter iterations 200. Generated images were subsequently analyzed in CellProfiler  83  . Cardiomyocytes were identified by filtering segmented objects based on α-actinin intensity, size and eccentricity to exclude non-cardiomyocytes, cell aggregates and obliquely sectioned cells. Minimum Feret diameter (MinFerDia) was extracted for each cardiomyocyte as a proxy for cross-sectional cell size (17,864 cardiomyocytes total across the 12 patients). For visualization (Extended Data Fig.  2i ), per-patient median minimum Feret diameter was used. The full per-cell dataset is provided in Supplementary Data  16 .  Statistical analyses were performed in R using linear mixed-effects models to account for the hierarchical structure of the data. Experimental group (NF/pRV/RVF for human studies and sham/mild-RVF/severe-RVF for mouse studies) was modeled as a fixed effect. Subject identity was included as a random intercept for all analyses, and slide was additionally included as a random intercept for mouse studies to account for repeated measurements obtained from the same specimen and histologic section. Pairwise group comparisons were performed using estimated marginal means with Benjamini−Hochberg correction for multiple testing.    Clustering parameters  All clustering analyses used the following parameters unless otherwise specified. For bulk RNA-seq WGCNA, a soft-thresholding power was selected using the pickSoftThreshold function to achieve approximate scale-free topology. For snRNA-seq analysis, SCTransform normalization was applied with mitochondrial read percentage regressed out. PCA was computed using the top 3,000 variable features, and 50 principal components were retained for downstream analysis. Nearest neighbor graphs were constructed using FindNeighbors with  k  = 20. Clustering was performed using FindClusters with the Louvain algorithm. Clustering resolution was selected in a semi-supervised manner: nuclei were clustered at a range of resolutions (0.1−2.0), and the resolution yielding biologically interpretable clusters with distinct marker genes was selected. For the 12 major cell types, the default Seurat resolution of 0.8 was used. For subclustering, a resolution of 0.5 was used for fibroblast, endothelial, myeloid, mural and natural killer/T lineages. Cardiomyocyte subclustering used a resolution of 0.3. For EC hdWGCNA, seven modules were identified using a soft-thresholding power automatically selected via the pickSoftThreshold function to approximate scale-free topology. For Xenium subclustering, 30 principal components were used with resolutions of 0.3 (cardiomyocytes) to 0.5 (all other cell types). UMAP was computed using RunUMAP with n.neighbors = 30 and min.dist = 0.3.   Quantification and statistical analysis  Details of specific statistical analyses for each section, sample sizes and statistical tests used are given in the  Methods  and in the corresponding figure legends. All analysis was done in R using primarily custom-written scripts, which are available with deposited data, and the Seurat package. For pseudobulk DE, DESeq2 was run independently for each cell subtype, and pairwise disease comparison and  P  values were adjusted for multiple testing within each analysis using the Benjamini−Hochberg procedure. Cross-subtype correction was not applied, as each subtype−comparison pair tests an independent biological question.     Software and versions  Analyses were performed in R version 4.3.3. Bulk RNA-seq processing used Trimmomatic version 0.39, kallisto version 0.51.1, tximport version 1.30.0, DESeq2 version 1.42.1 with apeglm version 1.24.0 shrinkage, sva version 3.50.0, edgeR version 4.0.16 and WGCNA version 1.73. Single-nucleus data were processed with Cell Ranger version 7.1.0, CellBender version 0.3.0 and decontX (celda version 1.18.1) and analyzed with Seurat version 5.1.0 (SeuratObject version 5.0.2, SeuratWrappers version 0.3.5), harmony version 1.2.3, hdWGCNA version 0.3.01, monocle3 version 1.3.7, decoupleR version 2.9.7 with CollecTRI, fgsea version 1.28.0, enrichR version 3.3, presto version 1.0.0 and glmGamPoi version 1.14.3. Xenium data were processed with Proseg version 1.1.9 and Sopa version 2.2.10 and analyzed with spacexr (RCTD) version 2.2.1, SPLIT version 0.1.3, SpaGE (GitHub commit edd0fb70; no tagged releases) and CellChat version 3. Histology was analyzed in Fiji/ImageJ version 1.54p, Cellpose version 3.1.1.2 and CellProfiler version 4.2.8. Flow cytometry was acquired with FACSDiva version 9.1, gated in FlowJo version 11.1.0 and reanalyzed with flowWorkspace version 4.14.3 and ggcyto version 1.30.2. Figures were produced with ggplot2 version 3.5.2, patchwork version 1.3.0, cowplot version 1.1.3, EnhancedVolcano version 1.20.0, Nebulosa version 1.12.1 and scCustomize version 3.0.0. Anthropic Claude was used to assist with the implementation and debugging of analysis code and to improve the clarity and readability of author-written text. All AI-assisted code and textual revisions were reviewed and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the final analyses and manuscript. evidence_text:
Spatial Mapping of the Precancer-to-Cancer Transition in Breast and Prostate. Breast and prostate cancers are both hormone-driven adenocarcinomas that undergo analogous invasion programs. Using lightsheet microscopy on intact tumors, we identified transitional junctions between precancerous and invasive regions. We then developed a multimodal serial-section workflow integrating volumetric reconstruction with spatial transcriptomics. Analysis of 319 spatial assays from 51 cases revealed gene expression features and novel structural insights defining the shift from precancer to invasive disease. In breast cancer, loss of MGP and PLAT was associated with invasive transition and promoted tumorigenesis in functional assays. In prostate cancer, GDF15, ALDH1A3, ANPEP, and FASN were upregulated along invasive progression, and their knockdown in PC-3 cells suppressed proliferation and migration. Enrichment of tumor-associated macrophages (SPP1+ and MS4A6A+) along non-triple-negative breast cancer breast cancer transitions highlights immune involvement as a potential driver of invasiveness.

Significance

Our method of defining precise spatial locations of invasive transition allows for the direct interrogation of transition drivers, presenting new therapeutic targets for the two most prevalent cancers and providing a framework for studying spatially defined mechanisms of tumor progression. See related commentary by Jing and Li, p. 1720. Although they originate in distinct organs, there are notable similarities in their development, progression, and underlying biological mechanisms ( Fig. 1A ; ref. 1 ). Both cancers rely on steroid hormones for growth and development, leading to similar therapeutic strategies targeting hormone signaling ( 2 – 4 ). They also share underlying hereditary genetic mechanisms for cancer initiation, such as alterations in BRCA1 and BRCA2 ( 5 , 6 ), and morphologic similarities, particularly in the organization of their epithelial structures. Both tissues are composed of glandular structures with two primary cell layers, an inner luminal cell layer and an outer basal cell layer, and are responsible for secretory functions (production of milk in the breast and prostatic fluid in the prostate; refs. 7 , 8 ). These tissues also share a similar path to tumorigenesis, in which carcinoma typically arises from luminal cells. The surrounding basal layer remains intact during early precancer states, those being ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) in the breast and high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (HGPIN) in the prostate ( 9 , 10 ). Luminal cells in both cancers also typically express hormone receptors, such as estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) in the breast and androgen receptor (AR) in the prostate. During the transition from precancer to malignancy in both tumor types, the basal cell layer is broken, and neoplastic cells spread into the surrounding environment ( 11 , 12 ). As such, precancerous lesions often have an attenuated basal layer, indicating progression toward loss of this barrier. Additionally, DCIS and HGPIN can both display similar epithelial cell patterns, such as cribriform architecture ( 13 ). Despite the clinical importance of tumor progression, the spatial and molecular dynamics of these transitions, particularly in breast and prostate cancers, remain poorly understood. This is, in part, due to the inability of conventional two-dimensional (2D) single-modality approaches to capture the full complexity of tumor topology and tumor–microenvironment interactions in situ . In this study, we developed a new volumetric approach that combines native three-dimensional (3D) and vertically reconstructed 2D data modalities to investigate malignant transition in breast and prostate tissues. We first imaged 14 tissue blocks from four cases with 3D lightsheet microscopy, providing high-resolution 3D immunofluorescence (IF) data for tissue blocks in their entirety. We report differences between the 3D morphologies of precancerous lesions and invasive carcinoma in both cancer types. To investigate the molecular signatures associated with these transitions, we developed a multimodal 3D serial sectioning approach, combining spatial transcriptomics (ST), multiplex imaging, and histologic staining. We assembled a cohort of 319 assays spanning 51 cases, nine of which were serially sectioned, and imaged with a variety of spatial data types ( Fig. 1B ; Supplementary Tables S1–S3). Additionally, we supplemented our 3D serial section cohort with 69 nonserial sections of Xenium, CosMx, CODEX, Visium, and Visium HD data. This 3D serial section approach enables reconstruction of 3D tissue structures from 2D sections, providing a unified framework for analyzing molecular and morphologic changes across 3D space. By leveraging Xenium, CosMx, Visium, Visium HD, and CODEX platforms, we interweave data at varying resolutions and biomarker coverage depth, overcoming important limitations inherent to single-platform analyses. Using this new approach, we reveal mechanisms underlying the progression of DCIS to intraductal carcinoma (IDC) in breast cancer and the transition from normal glands to Gleason pattern 3 (GP3) in prostate cancer. We have identified differentially expressed genes (DEG), spatial relationships, and tumor microenvironment (TME) features integral to epithelial cell state transitions. Furthermore, we have provided functional and mechanistic insights into the potential involvement of some of these genes in the key transitions. In addition to technical pipelines relevant to other cancer types, this study offers a blueprint for understanding breast and prostate cancer progression and suggests potential processes for therapeutic intervention. Results Breast and Prostate Cancer Transition Study Cohort Overview We profiled 319 tumor and normal sections (2D) and blocks (3D) from 51 cases, encompassing breast cancer (112 assays, 21 cases) and prostate cancer (207 assays, 30 cases) as part of the NCI Human Tumor Atlas Network (HTAN; Fig. 1B ; Supplementary Tables S1–S3). The samples were divided into three cohorts based on the assay method and analysis strategy: stacked 3D, native 3D, and 2D cohorts. The stacked 3D cohort comprised 233 assays, including 76 assays from breast cancer and 157 from prostate cancer. Five spatial omics platforms (Xenium, CosMx, Visium, Visium HD, and CODEX), together with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) imaging, were used to reconstruct 3D tumor structures and investigate molecular markers associated with the transition from noninvasive to invasive states (Supplementary Tables S2–S5). We also added additional 2D sections to form a nonserial 2D analysis cohort to increase sample size for DEG analyses, which included a total of 305 sections from 47 cases. Additionally, we performed native 3D assays using fluorescent lightsheet microscopy (FLSM) to trace the glandular structures in 3D and directly observe the transition from noninvasive to invasive states in both breast and prostate cancers. Volumetric Lightsheet Microscopy Reveals Tumor Architecture To investigate the architecture of precancerous and invasive tumor volumes within intact samples, we utilized FLSM to image cleared and immunostained tumor tissues ( Fig. 2A and B ). This analysis included five samples from two patients with breast cancer and nine samples from two patients with prostate cancer ( Fig. 2A , “Methods”). Cytokeratin-5 (CK5) and pan-cytokeratin (PanCK) were used to label basal cells and epithelial cells, respectively, enabling the delineation of normal, precancerous, and invasive lesions in both breast and prostate cancer tissues ( Fig. 2C and D ). This 7 mm by 2.5 mm by 1 mm sample (Supplementary Mov. S1) was filled with large but scattered regions positive with PanCK staining but little to no CK5 staining on the periphery, indicative of IDC and a discontinuous or absent basal layer ( Fig. 2C , yellow arrowhead in E ; Supplementary Mov. S2 and S3). Although IDC regions seem separated and scattered on a 2D section, they are interconnected throughout the tumor sample and can span large volumes (Supplementary Mov. S1, S2, and S4; Supplementary Fig. 1A), consistent with a pattern of invasion and uncontrolled growth in the 3D space. There are also six distinct PanCK-positive areas with CK5 staining surrounding their periphery. Some regions feature a thin layer of PanCK staining within the CK5 boundary, indicative of normal ductal structures in which a single layer of basal epithelial layer surrounds a single layer of luminal epithelial layer ( Fig. 2E , green dashed line). Others feature an enlarged PanCK patch inside of the CK5 boundary, indicative of DCIS regions in which malignant luminal cells in the breast duct start to proliferate but the basal layer is still intact ( Fig. 2E , blue dashed line). DCIS morphology either resembles a large homogeneous mass [ Fig. 2E , region-of-interest (ROI)1] or an enlarged ductal structure ( Fig. 2E , ROI2). For example, the DCIS structure highlighted in ROI1 spans more than 750 μm in the z-dimension, which is the direction perpendicular to the sections ( Fig. 2F ). The regions with intact CK5 + basal layers seem to retain the CK5 layer throughout the volume we observed, which leads us to hypothesize that the invasive lesion exists outside of the sampled region. Nonetheless, DCIS regions can be embedded within IDC regions ( Fig. 2G ; Supplementary Mov. S4). Lastly, we observed one region with multiple DCIS-like areas nested into a single larger structure, with strong CK5 staining interwoven with PanCK-stained precancer cells (Supplementary Fig. S1B and S1C; Supplementary Mov. S5). We propose that the observed structure is a breast lobule filled with neoplastic cells. As lobular carcinoma in situ was not indicated by our pathologist, we hypothesize that the cancer cells originated from DCIS regions outside of the sample but invaded through the ductal system. To investigate differences between high-grade PIN and invasive prostate tumor structures, we focused our detailed analysis on HT957Z1 that has coexisting normal glandular structures, high-grade PIN, and invasive adenocarcinoma. The pathology report of this patient indicates prostatic acinar adenocarcinoma with a Gleason score of 4 + 3. We observe bright but unspecific staining of spherical structures throughout many prostate samples, which we suspect originate from antibodies trapped by corpora amylacea ( Fig. 2D ; Supplementary Fig. S1D and S1E; Supplementary Mov. S6). We postulate that this reflects the overall inflammatory status of the patient. Similar to breast cancer samples, normal prostate ducts and acini are marked by an outer layer of CK5 and a thin inner layer of PanCK (Supplementary Fig. S1E). Some ductal structures feature an enlarged inner PanCK layer (25–50 µm thick rather than the typical ∼10 μm thick) with an intact CK5 boundary, suggestive of high-grade PIN structures ( Fig. 2H , blue dashed line). These high-grade PIN structures are adjacent to, and seemingly connected to, disordered PanCK+ branching structures without CK5 on the periphery, consistent with the invasive pattern of Gleason score 4 ( Fig. 2H , yellow dashed line, and Supplementary Mov. S7). Indeed, the CK5 to PanCK ratio decreased with the transition from 0.4 to 0.1 ( Fig. 2I ). This observed transition offers a detailed view of the architectural changes during the neoplastic transition ( Fig. 2J ; Supplementary Mov. S8). In addition, we observed ductal structures with strong CK5 staining on the basal layer and a lumen filled with PanCK-positive cells, similar to the DCIS morphology observed in breast cancer. These could be IDC of the prostate ( Fig. 2H ; Supplementary Fig. S1F orange dashed line). In summary, FLSM of intact breast and prostate tumors revealed that regions appearing disconnected in 2D are in fact highly interconnected in 3D, with DCIS and high-grade PIN lesions embedded within and/or transitioning into invasive carcinoma. These analyses highlight how basal layer integrity and epithelial expansion define architectural shifts, providing a direct volumetric view of noninvasive and invasive morphology. Gene Discovery Serial Section Workflow and Computational Framework To understand the molecular drivers associated with the structural transition, we devised a multimodal workflow integrating spatial assays across different platforms. Although the archetypical 2D section is blind to transition dynamics in the third dimension, it does provide large amounts of data, thanks to lower imaging costs. With a view to optimizing 2D tradeoffs of cost versus the limited field-of-view provided by 2D spatial assays, we developed an experimental and computational framework for volumetric integration of 2D sections from a tissue block using five platforms, namely H&E, Xenium, CosMx, CODEX, and the Visium family (Supplementary Fig. S2A). The data from the intermingled sections are computationally combined, furnishing a comprehensive view of spatial and structural variations (Supplementary Fig. S2B). Briefly, sections are cut at specific intervals and optimally arranged on slides according to the respective imaging area of each platform. Following imaging, sections are spatially registered using a keypoint workflow, enabling precise computational alignment across sections (arXiv:1511.01154), and the resulting data are annotated for gene discovery (“Methods”). The product is a block-specific atlas of computationally registered sections that can be examined for precancer-to-cancer transitions and interconnected tumor volumes. Single-platform 2D sections are generally unable to fully characterize transitions, unless the transition region is both sufficiently linear and there is a serendipitous match between it and the section orientation (Supplementary Fig. S2B). The computationally registered multisections in our method capture both linear and nonlinear transition regions within the section area, leaving no topologically disconnected image fragments of the transition region. The integration of platform data and the respective genes they cover support further computational inferences of the transition continuum by proximal correlations of expression (Supplementary Fig. S2C). The approach is used here for finding ROI level DEGs associated with cancer transition in volumetric tumor blocks. Effectively, this allows regions, for example, DCIS, microinvasion (MI), and IDC in breast cancer, to be examined holistically along a spatial continuum. We developed two methods to discover genes associated with these interconnected transition regions: path-based and morphology-based (“Methods”). Briefly, in the path-based method, we calculated a single correlation value across multiple spatial platforms within each interconnected 3D volume. The regression was run on expression values for each region along the path of the transitioning epithelial structure. In the morphology-based method, all regions morphologically annotated as noninvasive (e.g., DCIS) were compared WITH the all invasive regions (e.g., IDC) within the same platform. We also supplement these 3D ROI-level DEGs with 2D approaches that involve assessing regions’ myoepithelial intensity using basal layer markers. Using these markers, we are able to assign each region an invasiveness score, which is an indication of the basal layer marker gene abundance for the region and serves as a continuous metric reflecting the degree of morphologic and molecular progression along the transition axis within each ROI. This score was then correlated with gene expression, allowing the identification of cohort-level genes associated with myoepithelial integrity (“Methods”). Transitionary regions in all ROIs were reviewed and validated by board-certified pathologists. Biomarkers for DCIS-to-IDC Transition in Breast Cancer First, we applied our methodology to ascertain biomarkers correlated to the DCIS-to-IDC transition in breast cancer. Nine tissue samples were serially sectioned (“Methods”). Two samples having greater sectioning depths (460 and 120 µm) were selected for ROI-based analysis, as their increased depths enabled visualization of more pronounced morphologic changes along the Z-dimension of the tissue blocks. HT704B1, a 450-µm deep breast carcinoma specimen with regions of DCIS and IDC, was analyzed using five spatial platforms: Xenium ( n = 6), CODEX ( n = 12), H&E ( n = 20), CosMx ( n = 4), and Visium HD ( n = 2; Fig. 3A ; Supplementary Mov. S9 and S10). The 3D analysis of these sections revealed that regions separated in 2D space by more than 5 mm were in fact interconnected in the Z plane ( Fig. 3B ; Supplementary Table S6), underscoring the value of serial sectioning for understanding true morphologic relationships. We analyzed two regions of interest, ROI1 and ROI2, and identified common metabolic, epithelial integrity, and proliferation modules associated with the transition from DCIS to MI and to IDC ( Fig. 3C–E ; Supplementary Mov. S11 and S12). For example, DCIS in ROI1 demonstrated sustained expression of HMGCS2 (R 2 = 0.79, P = 0.003: path-based) and TFF1 (R 2 = 0.82, P = 0.002: path-based), which was lost in the interconnected IDC volume ( Fig. 3D ). Additionally, DCIS in ROI2 demonstrated strong expression of PLAT that significantly decreased at the site of MI ( Fig. 3E ). Both TFF1 and PLAT may play a role in maintaining epithelial integrity, potentially limiting neoplastic cell migration and invasiveness ( 14 – 18 ). HMGCS2 facilitates ketogenesis, enabling the production of lipid-derived energy ( 19 ), possibly enhancing precancerous cells' survival under hypoxic conditions often present in DCIS regions ( 20 ). In IDC, we observed upregulation of two genes involved in cell proliferation, TCIM (FC = 0.60: morphology-based on Xenium; ref. 21 ) and MKI67 (FC = 0.47: morphology-based on Xenium), in ROI1, and angiogenic factor VEGFA (R 2 = 0.74, P ≤ 0.001; path-based; ref. 22 ) in ROI2 ( Fig. 3D and E ). TCIM , acting through the activation of Wnt/β-catenin pathway ( 21 ), may play a role in inducing invasive cancer cell proliferation marked by MKI67 . In addition to HT704B1, we also annotated ROIs in HT206B1, a triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) sample (Supplementary Fig. 3A; Supplementary Mov. S13). In ROI1, we identified an interconnected region transitioning from DCIS to IDC (Supplementary Fig. S3B; Supplementary Mov. S14). In the IDC areas of ROI1, we visualize upregulation of MYC (R 2 = 0.89, P ≤ 0.001; path-based) and MKI67 (R 2 = 0.68, P = 0.006; path-based), both markers of proliferation and invasiveness ( 23 , 24 ). Conversely, DCIS areas showed elevated expression of CDKN1A (R 2 = 0.90, P = 0.05, path-based) and CA9 . In contrast to MYC and MKI67 , CDKN1A is a negative regulator of the cell cycle that may play a role in maintaining a less proliferative phenotype in DCIS areas ( 25 ). Additionally, the upregulation of hypoxia-induced marker CA9 in hypoxic regions of DCIS suggests that CA9 , in addition to the lipid-derived energy provided by HMGCS2 , may support the survival of DCIS cells by facilitating adaptation to hypoxic environments often found in DCIS ( 26 , 27 ). Beyond the aforementioned genes, we identified additional mechanisms shared across multiple ROIs that may help to drive the DCIS-to-IDC transition ( Fig. 3F ; Supplementary Fig. S3C and S4). In DCIS regions, there was higher expression of genes involved in tissue architecture and remodeling ( TFF1 , PLAT , and MGP ; refs. 14 – 16 , 18 , 28 ), ductal formation and differentiation ( KIT and PIP ; refs. 29 , 30 ), and metabolism ( HMGCS2 ; ref. 19 ). IDC regions exhibited upregulation of genes associated with proliferation ( TCIM and MKI67 ; ref. 21 ), angiogenesis ( VEGFA and CP ; refs. 22 , 31 , 32 ), and metabolism ( GLUL and FASN ; refs. 33 , 34 ). Together, these shifts in gene expression reflect the transition from organized, less invasive phenotypes to more highly proliferative and invasive cancer cell states. In HT891Z1, we analyzed two ROIs, ROI1 and ROI2, that capture the transition from a normal gland, through HGPIN, to GP3 morphology (Supplementary Mov. S17 and S18). In HT891Z1 ROI1, the transition showed distinct differences in gene expression along the normal–HGPIN–GP3 axis ( Fig. 4C ). In less invasive and normal regions, we observed higher expression of FAS (R 2 = 0.53, P = 0.026; path-based). FAS , encoding the Fas cell surface death receptor that promotes apoptosis via the formation of the death-inducing signaling complex, initiates a cascade of caspases, culminating in programmed cell death ( Fig. 4D and E ; refs. 35 , 36 ). Conversely, along the normal to GP3 transition, we observed upregulation of GDF15 (R 2 = 0.68, P = 0.006; path-based) and MYC (R 2 = 0.58, P = 0.016, path-based) , whose expression also goes up as breast cancer progresses ( Fig. 4E ). GDF15 , a member of the TGF-β superfamily, has been implicated in bone metastasis and progression to castration-resistant prostate cancer ( 37 ) but not in earlier stages of prostate cancer. Notably, in section Z290 of ROI1, we observed a striking dichotomy between normal and HGPIN expression patterns on the same section. On the right side of the gland, FAS was detected, whereas the left side exhibited elevated expressions of MYC and GDF15 . Subsequent Z-sections revealed these two sides diverging into distinct morphologies, with the right retaining normal features of the prostatic gland and the left progressing toward HGPIN morphology. In HT913Z1, ROI1 shows a normal duct transitioning into GP3 morphology (Supplementary Fig. S5A and S5B; Supplementary Mov. S19). In the normal axis, we observed elevated expression of SORL1 across multiple sections with Xenium (Supplementary Fig. S5C), a gene not previously described in prostate cancer but which plays a role in lipid metabolism and trafficking through interactions with receptors like low-density lipoprotein receptor ( 38 ). In the invasive axis of HT913Z1, we observed upregulation of SERPINA3 , with a distinct expression pattern localized only to specific GP3 areas. SERPINA3 has been implicated in a variety of processes, including mediating apoptosis, autophagy, and aerobic glycolysis, thereby affecting cell survival and metabolic pathways ( 39 ). Additionally, in melanoma, high SERPINA3 expression has been associated with extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, increased invasion, metastasis, and poorer overall survival, suggesting a similar proinvasive role ( 40 ). Finally, we identified pathways shared across multiple ROIs that may help to drive the normal-to-GP3 transition ( Fig. 4F ; Supplementary Fig. S4 and S5C). In areas having essentially normal glandular morphology, we observed upregulation of genes associated with gland differentiation and hormone signaling ( FHL2 and SOX9 ; refs. 41 , 42 ), inhibition of epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT; SORL1 , NTN4 , and FLRT3 ; refs. 43 – 45 ), tissue integrity ( UPK1A ; ref. 46 ), survival ( FAS ; ref. 35 ), and metabolism ( SLC40A1 ; ref. 47 ). In contrast, regions with more aggressive HGPIN and GP3 morphology displayed increased expression of genes involved in migration and angiogenesis ( GDF15 , MYC , and EPHA6 ; refs. 37 , 48 , 49 ), metabolism and cell–cell communication ( ALDH1A3 ; ref. 50 ), tissue integrity ( SCIN ; refs. 51 , 52 ), survival ( SERPINA3 ; ref. 39 ), and cell proliferation and differentiation ( NPDCD1 ; ref. 53 ). In all, changes in the expression of these genes reflect biological transformations that occur from noninvasive to invasive transition in prostate cancer. Impact of the TME on Malignant Transition in Breast and Prostate Cancers In addition to epithelial cell markers, we explored changes in the TME that might facilitate the transition from normal to more invasive epithelial cells. We identified two TME cell types potentially involved in this transition: tumor-associated macrophages (TAM) and cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAF). Using our 2D automated gene discovery workflow ( Fig. 5A ), we identified two markers, SPP1 and MS4A6A , that distinguish TAM populations across different morphologic regions in non-TNBC breast cancer ( Fig. 5B ). In HT704B1 ROI1, we analyzed the expression of SPP1 and MS4A6A throughout the z-dimensional section stack, in which there is a clear association of MS4A6A + TAMs infiltrating DCIS regions, whereas SPP1 + TAMs are more prevalent within IDC regions ( Fig. 5C and D ; Supplementary Fig. S6A and S6B). Interestingly, only luminal cell-of-origin breast tumors displayed this relationship, whereas sections from basal tumors differed in that their SPP1 + and MS4A6A + TME expression was associated with noninvasive morphology. Similarly to TNBC, in prostate cancer, we observed localization of MS4A6A + TAMs with noninvasive morphology. To further evaluate this association in three dimensions, we performed an analysis using all Xenium sections from HT704B1. For each TAM, we computed the shortest 3D distance to the nearest epithelial region. We then quantified the basal-layer intensity score of the corresponding epithelial region as a measure of invasiveness. Across five of the six sections analyzed, SPP1 + TAMs were preferentially associated with more invasive epithelial regions characterized by lower basal-layer integrity scores, whereas MS4A6A + TAMs were more frequently localized near less invasive regions with higher basal-layer integrity scores (Supplementary Fig. S6C). CAFs also exhibit distinct associations with neoplastic cell states and play a critical role in modulating the TME. In non-TNBC breast sections, we observed upregulation of key stromal genes around invasive regions— MFAP5 and ASPN —that contribute to tumor progression ( Fig. 5B and E ). MFAP5 , a fibroblast-secreted ECM glycoprotein, facilitates cancer cell invasion by remodeling the ECM and activating PI3K/AKT and TGF-β signaling pathways, which drive the EMT ( 54 – 56 ). It also enhances angiogenesis by upregulating VEGF , promoting tumor vascularization ( 57 ). ASPN , a proteoglycan secreted by CAFs, regulates ECM stiffness by interacting with collagen and other ECM components ( 58 , 59 ). In summary, the spatial enrichment of SPP1 + macrophages at invasive fronts suggests that inflammatory signaling, ECM remodeling, and immune modulation converge to create a permissive niche for epithelial escape ( 60 , 61 ). In parallel, MFAP5 - and ASPN -expressing fibroblasts contribute to matrix remodeling and proangiogenic signaling, altering both biochemical and biomechanical properties of the tissue. The juxtaposition of these immune and stromal programs with transitioning epithelial cells suggests that malignant invasion arises from coordinated epithelial–microenvironmental interactions. Common and Diverse Mechanisms of Precancer-To-Cancer Transition in Breast and Prostate Tumor heterogeneity presents a major challenge, as no single molecular process is universally shared within a tumor or across all cases. However, our analyses highlight several patterns of gene expression associated with the transition from noninvasive to invasive states in breast and prostate cancers ( Fig. 6A ; Supplementary Fig. S7A and S7B). Broadly, these transition genes fall into three categories: genes enriched in breast, genes enriched in prostate, and genes shared across both cancer types. Figure 6. In breast cancer, genes linked to tissue integrity and remodeling—including MGP and PLAT —were consistently enriched in noninvasive states (DCIS) across multiple samples ( Fig. 6A ; Supplementary Fig. S7A and S7B). Additional markers such as KIT and CA9 also localized to DCIS regions at the ROI-level in HT206B1 (Supplementary Fig. 3). In contrast, IDC was marked by angiogenesis-related genes, with KRT8 and VEGFA enriched at the cohort level and CP enriched within ROI analyses (Figs. 3F , 6A and B ). IF validation further confirmed that MGP protein was significantly upregulated in DCIS relative to IDC (normal vs. IDC: P = 1.29e−4, DCIS vs. IDC: P = 3.81e−8; Student t test; two-sided. Fig. 6B ; Supplementary Fig. S8A; Supplementary Mov. S20). MGP , a γ-carboxyglutamic domain containing protein, plays a critical role in inhibiting soft tissue calcification and maintaining ECM integrity by preventing inappropriate calcium deposition, ensuring ECM flexibility and function ( 62 ). In premalignant states, maintaining ECM organization is essential, as dysregulation—such as increased stiffness from mineralization—may facilitate tumor invasion and progression by altering ECM composition and structure ( 28 , 63 ). Similarly, PLAT protein was significantly enriched in noninvasive breast regions (normal vs. IDC: P = 3.81e−4; DCIS vs. IDC: P = 0.009; Student t test; two-sided. Fig. 6C ; Supplementary Fig. S8B). In prostate cancer, noninvasive regions expressed ECM-related genes such as UPK1A and FLRT3 . ANPEP and ALDH1A3 , linked to cell–cell communications and metabolism ( 64 , 65 ), were upregulated in invasive prostate cancer regions but downregulated in invasive breast cancer areas. We also validated some invasive drivers by IF, including GDF15 ( P = 0.031; Student t test; two-sided. Fig. 6D ; Supplementary Fig. S8C) and ALDH1A3 ( P = 3.46e−6; Student t test; two-sided. Fig. 6E ; Supplementary Fig. S8D), both of which were significantly upregulated in invasive lesions compared with normal glands. GDF15 , a stress-induced cytokine in the TGF-β family, is known to promote EMT and tumor progression ( 37 , 66 , 67 ). Finally, several genes were consistently enriched across both cancer types, including FASN (Supplementary Fig. S8E and F; fatty acid synthase), which promotes tumor progression by supplying lipids necessary for the energy demands of rapidly proliferating cells ( 68 ), and EPHA6 (Supplementary Fig. S8G), a member of the Eph receptor tyrosine kinase family that is involved in cell–cell communications and has been indicated as a metastasis-associated gene in prostate cancer ( 49 ). We then selected candidate transition markers, including those showing consistent trends both at the transcriptional and protein levels, for functional validation in patient-derived cell lines. In breast cancer, we used short hairpin RNA (shRNA)-mediated knockdown of noninvasive enriched tissue remodeling-related genes MGP and PLAT in patient-derived DCIS cell lines ETCC-006 and ETCC-010 ( 69 ). Real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) confirmed significant transcript reduction ( P < 0.005), and functional assays showed significant effects associated with the gene knockdowns ( Fig. 7A ). CCK-8 assays showed that silencing either gene enhanced proliferation across 24- to 120-hour time points after transfection, and wound-healing assays demonstrated accelerated migration, as reflected by greater wound closure at 24 hours ( Fig. 7B–D ; Supplementary Fig. S9). These results indicate that loss of MGP or PLAT promotes proliferative and migratory behaviors, consistent with their protective roles in maintaining DCIS. Figure 7.
