These findings demonstrate that stPainter-derived epithelial states are spatially interpretable, providing hypotheses about functional organization during tumor progression.  Finally, we evaluated the generalizability of stPainter-100 across an expanded spectrum of malignancies by extending our analyses to the remaining SPATCH datasets (OV and LIHC) and multiple independent public Xenium datasets, including PRAD, NSCLC, and CESC (Supplementary Figs.  8 – 11 ). In all cases, stPainter facilitated robust downstream workflows, achieving a level of resolution in major and fine-grained subpopulation identification comparable to that observed in COAD. These results support the robustness and broad applicability of stPainter for facilitating downstream analysis across diverse cancer histologies.     Discussion  High-resolution ST  28   is fundamentally constrained by stochastic RNA capture and restricted gene panels, necessitating the integration of whole-transcriptome scRNA-seq to restore biological signals and enhance data fidelity. However, existing imputation frameworks  12 , 19   are hampered by a sample-specific supervised paradigm that requires tissue-matched references and repetitive retraining for every new experiment, a dependency that severely restricts their scalability and clinical applicability. Here, we developed stPainter, a conditional latent diffusion model that shifts the field toward a pretrained paradigm. By leveraging a massive pan-cancer atlas of 1.3 million cells across 21 diverse malignancies, stPainter shifts ST imputation from a sample-specific supervised setting toward a pretrained inference paradigm without the need for auxiliary matched data or retraining, providing a convenient and effective (Supplementary Fig.  7 ) tool for ST data analysis.  The technical efficacy of stPainter is grounded in its conditional latent diffusion architecture. By encoding cancer-type metadata as a conditional prior ( c ), the model constrains the generative dynamics to a biologically plausible subspace. In contrast to conventional approaches that operate directly in the high-dimensional gene expression space, or require tissue-matched references and dataset-specific retraining, stPainter performs SDE-guided generation within a highly compressed, denoised latent manifold ( z )  26  , iteratively mapping sparse spatial measurements back onto the learned distribution from a pretrained pan-cancer atlas (Supplementary Fig.  5 ). By compressing transcriptomic variability into a low-dimensional latent embedding (e.g., 50 or 100 dimensions), the model establishes a stable basis for unsupervised manifold learning and high-resolution cluster delineation  36  . In parallel, the generative decoder reconstructs a continuous expression matrix spanning the full pretraining gene space, enabling comprehensive downstream transcriptomic analyses. Although these individual components originate from the computer vision community, the core contribution of stPainter is the integration of these components into a reference-free pretraining-and-inference paradigm for single-cell resolution spatial transcriptomics, whose component-level necessity is validated by our ablation experiments (Supplementary Figs.  4  and  5 ).  Single-cell resolution ST provides gene expression profiles analogous to scRNA-seq, yet critical differences in data characteristics necessitate analytical approaches  28  . Unlike scRNA-seq, where enzymatic dissociation can disproportionately impact fragile cell types like epithelial cells  10 , 37 , 38  , Xenium technologies often exhibit higher dropout rates for less abundant populations, such as immune cell genes ( CD8A ,  CD14 ) (Supplementary Fig.  8 ). Furthermore, signal leakage from abundant neighboring cells can mask the transcriptomic signatures of rarer cell types, complicating their accurate identification  10  . stPainter is designed to address these fundamental data quality issues. By enhancing the raw measurements, it expands the assayed gene space to 10,000 genes and mitigates sparsity, generating profiles that are better suited for downstream clustering, marker evaluation, and spatial-domain analysis.  The high levels of noise and sparsity in Xenium data also severely compromise downstream computational tasks, particularly the clustering and identification of fine-grained cell subtypes. Conventional methods like PCA often fail to effectively separate biological signals from technical noise, resulting in poor cluster resolution  10  . While many imputation tools exist, they are often not optimized for clustering tasks and can fail to remove technical artifacts  22  . stPainter provides an alternative representation for clustering. We demonstrate that performing clustering directly on the latent representations learned by our model, rather than on raw or imputed gene expression, produced clearer separation of major cell populations and stronger concordance with marker-supported and reference-supported annotations. The resulting 50- to 100-dimensional latent space robustly captures major transcriptional variation relevant to lineage organization and downstream clustering. This enables the resolution of fine-grained subtypes with clusters that show strong concordance with known marker genes, and provides a useful representation for downstream exploratory analysis, particularly when matched scRNA-seq references are unavailable.  Although stPainter showed consistent performance across the evaluated datasets, several avenues remain for further optimization and exploration. The current framework addresses data sparsity based on patterns derived from scRNA-seq. Future iterations could explore more adaptive and learnable strategies for sparsity processing that dynamically account for sample-specific technical biases and varying capture efficiencies. Furthermore, while the latent representations produced by our model provide a representation for downstream clustering, the biological interpretability of these latent dimensions warrants deeper investigation. Uncovering the specific gene-program alignments within this manifold could provide additional insights into the regulatory logic of the tumor microenvironment. Moreover, transfer-label and CODEX analyses provided complementary evidence for the downstream interpretability of stPainter-enhanced data. Transfer labels were used as reference-supported annotations to assess agreement with established cell-type organization, while adjacent-section CODEX imaging offered orthogonal protein-level support for regional spatial concordance. We therefore interpret these results as evidence of marker- and domain-level biological consistency, rather than definitive same-cell or same-section ground-truth validation. Finally, the current pan-cancer atlas faces an inherent challenge of compositional imbalance, with rare malignancies being underrepresented compared to common cancer types. Integrating broader, more balanced multi-omic datasets may further refine stPainter’s reference-free generalization and enhance its capacity to resolve the intricate biological granularity essential for downstream mechanistic interrogation.    Methods   Ethical statement  This study complies with all relevant ethical regulations. All datasets analyzed in this study were obtained from publicly available, de-identified sources, and no new experiments involving human participants or animals were conducted. Therefore, approval from an institutional review board or ethics committee was not required.    Problem formulation  Formally, we represent a single-cell resolution transcriptomic dataset as a tuple    T  =   (   X  ,  C   )    , where    X  ∈    R    N  ×  G      denotes the gene expression matrix for  N  cells and  G  genes, and    C  ∈    R    N  ×  K      constitutes the one-hot encoding for  K  distinct cancer types. Accordingly, the  i -th cell is characterized by the pair ( x   i  ,  c   i  ). We aim to capture the heterogeneous gene expression patterns intrinsic to different cancer types by pretraining our latent diffusion model stPainter on a comprehensive pan-cancer scRNA-seq atlas reference      T    sc    =   (     X    sc    ,    C    sc     )    , which spans a 10,000 genes feature space  G  sc . Conversely, we define a target single-cell resolution spatial transcriptomic dataset as      T    st    =   (     X    st    ,    C    st     )    , typically restricted to a specific cancer type with a limited gene panel such that  G  st  ≪  G  sc . Our primary objective is to leverage the learned generative priors to transform the raw      T    st      into an enhanced        T   ¯     st    =   (       X   ¯     st    ,    Z    st    ,    C    st     )    . This output comprises the spatially informed expression matrix        X   ¯     st    ∈    R      N    st    ×    G    sc        imputed to the full reference gene space, and a compact latent embedding      Z    st    ∈    R      N    st    ×  L      that encapsulates cellular manifolds.    stPainterarchitecture  The architecture of stPainter is composed of two synergistic components: a VAE for latent space embedding and a GiT for conditional generative modeling. The VAE is first trained to compress high-dimensional transcriptomic profiles into a compact, structured latent manifold that captures essential biological variance. Subsequently, the GiT functions as our core generative module by operating within this learned manifold. It is designed as a conditional diffusion model to learn the complex probability distribution of cellular states based on auxiliary information, such as cancer type. This decoupled, two-stage approach allows stPainter to efficiently handle broad gene-panel data while leveraging the power of Transformer models for precise, context-aware generation.   VAE architecture . Our VAE is inspired by the probabilistic framework of scVI  36   to learn a latent representation  z  while disentangling it from technical nuisance factors. It consists of an encoder-decoder architecture:    The encoder network maps the raw gene expression profile  x  and its cancer type  c  to the parameters of the two factorized latent distributions via distinct output heads:   1    (     μ    z    ,  log    σ    z    2     )   =    Encoder    z     (   x  ,  c   )   ,    (     μ    l    ,  log    σ    l    2     )   =    Encoder    l     (   x  ,  c   )   .    These parameters define the distributions for the biological latent vector    z  ~  N   (     μ    z    ,  diag    (     σ    z    2     )    )     and the scalar library size factor    l  ~  LogNormal    (     μ    l    ,    σ    l    2     )    . The latent variables are then sampled using the reparameterization trick.    The decoder network maps the latent state back to the parameters of the Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial (ZINB) distribution via two distinct output heads:   2   ρ  =    Decoder    ρ     (   z  ,  c   )   ,   π  =    Decoder    π     (   z  ,  c   )   .    These outputs define the normalized gene frequencies  ρ  and the dropout probabilities π. The reconstructed gene count      x   ¯     is then drawn from the distribution ZINB( μ ,   θ  , π), where the mean is given by  μ  =  l  ⋅  ρ  and the dispersion   θ   is a globally learnable parameter.    The hyperparameters of the VAE architecture are detailed in Supplementary Table  3 .   GiT architecture . The GiT is a conditional diffusion model based on the Diffusion Transformer (DiT)  39  . We specifically adapted its architecture to process 1D latent transcriptomic embeddings, enabling it to model intricate dependencies within the VAE-learned cellular manifold:    The input to the GiT is the noisy latent vector  z ( t ). We implement a feature-wise tokenization strategy by treating the latent vector as a sequence of  L  tokens. Each one is projected into a hidden dimension  D  via a learnable linear embedding. Learnable 1D positional embeddings are added to preserve the topological semantics of the latent dimensions, yielding the initial sequence      H    0    ∈    R    L  ×  D     .    The core network comprises a stack of Transformer blocks that iteratively denoise the latent representation. We employ an adaptive layer norm zero (adaLN-Zero) mechanism to rigorously condition the process on the cancer type  c  and timestep  t . For each block, a shared MLP processes the fused condition vector to predict modulation parameters ( γ ,  β ,  α ) that are applied to the Multi-Head Self-Attention (MSA) and Feed-Forward Network (FFN) modules:   3     H    k    ′    =    H    k  −  1    +    α    1    ⋅  MSA    (   adaLN    (     H    k  −  1    ;    γ    1    ,    β    1     )    )   ,     4     H    k    =    H    k    ′    +    α    2    ⋅  FFN    (   adaLN    (     H    k    ′    ;    γ    2    ,    β    2     )    )   .    The regression MLP is initialized to zero, rendering each block an identity function at the start of training to stabilize learning dynamics.    After processing through  n  blocks, the output sequence  H   n   is projected back to the latent space dimension. The tokens undergo a final adaLN normalization, followed by a linear projection back to the scalar dimension. The sequence is then reshaped to yield the predicted noise required for the diffusion process, formally denoted as:   5   ϵ  =  GiT    (   z   (   t   )   ,  t  ,  c   )   .       The hyperparameters of the GiT architecture are detailed in Supplementary Table  4 .    Training and inference of stPainter  The application of stPainter involves two phases: a training phase to learn generative priors from the pan-cancer atlas, and an inference phase to enhance target ST data. The training is sequential: we first train the VAE to create a robust latent representation of cellular states. Then, holding the VAE fixed, we train the GiT to model the conditional distribution of these latent states. For inferencing, we employ a guided generation process based on score-based diffusion, which iteratively refines an initial noisy estimate of the target cell’s latent state to be consistent with both the learned priors and the original measurements.   Generative Modeling with SDE . The generative process of stPainter is formulated through the lens of score-based generative modeling via SDEs  26  . This framework conceptualizes generation as a time-reversed diffusion process. A forward process, defined by a prespecified SDE, systematically perturbs data samples  z (1) from the complex data distribution  p  1  towards a simple prior distribution  p  0  (e.g., an isotropic Gaussian) at  t  = 0 over a continuous time interval  t  ∈ [0, 1]. A standard choice for this forward SDE is the Variance Preserving (VP) SDE:    6   d  z  =  −    1    2    β   (   t   )   z   d  t  +    β   (   t   )      d  w  ,     where  β ( t ) is a positive, monotonically increasing variance schedule defined on  t  ∈ [0, 1], and  w  is a standard Wiener process.  The reverse process is defined as follows. The trajectory of this diffusion can be reversed by solving a corresponding reverse-time SDE  40  :    7   d  z  =    −    1    2    β   (   t   )   z  −  β   (   t   )     ∇    z    log    p    t     (   z   )      d  t  +    β   (   t   )      d    w   ¯   ,     where    d    w   ¯     is a Wiener process running backwards in time, and      ∇    z    log    p    t     (   z   )     is the score function of the perturbed data distribution  p   t   at time  t . Simulating this SDE from a noise sample  z (0) ~  p  0  to  t  = 1 effectively generates a sample from the original data distribution  p  1 . The central challenge is thus to accurately estimate the time-dependent score function, which we accomplish by training our GiT.   Training of stPainter . The training of stPainter is conducted in two sequential stages, ensuring a stable latent manifold is learned before the generative priors are established.    The VAE is first trained on the pan-cancer scRNA-seq atlas      T    sc      to learn a compressed and robust latent representation of single-cell transcriptomes. The objective is to maximize the evidence lower bound (ELBO) of the data log-likelihood, which balances reconstruction fidelity with regularization of the latent space:   8     L    VAE    =    E    q   (   z  ∣  x  ,  c   )      [   log  p   (   x  ∣  z  ,  c   )    ]   −    D    KL     (   q   (   z  ∣  x  ,  c   )   ∣  ∣  p   (   z   )    )   ,    where the first term is the ZINB-based reconstruction loss and the second is the Kullback-Leibler divergence that regularizes the posterior  q  towards a standard normal prior  p ( z ). Upon convergence, the VAE encoder provides a high-quality mapping from gene expression space to the latent manifold.    Following VAE convergence, its encoder is used to project the entire pan-cancer atlas into the latent space, creating a dataset of latent vectors  z  sc . The GiT, parameterized by   θ   and denoted as   ϵ     θ   , is then trained on this latent dataset. Its objective is to predict the initial noise   ϵ   added to a latent vector  z (0) to produce its noisy version  z ( t ), conditioned on the cancer type  c  and timestep  t . This is equivalent to learning the score function and is achieved by minimizing the following objective:   9     L    GiT    =    E    t  ,  z   (   0   )   ,  ϵ  ~  N   (   0  ,  I   )         ∣  ∣    ϵ    θ     (   z   (   t   )   ,  t  ,  c   )   −  ϵ  ∣  ∣    2    2      ,    where  z ( t ) is sampled from the forward process perturbation kernel  p   t  ( z ( t )∣ z (0)) and  t  is sampled uniformly from [0, 1].    The training hyperparameters are detailed in Supplementary Table  5 .   Inferencing with stPainter . During inference with stPainter, we employ a guided generative process based on Stochastic Differential Editing (SDEdit)  41  . This process ensures that the generated profiles are both biologically realistic and faithful to the original, partially measured data. The procedure unfolds in five steps:    First, we align the spatial transcriptomics gene panel  G  st  with the pretraining gene space  G  sc . A binary imputation mask    m  ∈     {   0  ,  1   }       G    sc        is constructed, where  m   g   = 1 if gene  g  is measured in the ST panel and  m   g   = 0 otherwise. The raw ST expression vector  x  st  is zero-padded to the full pretraining dimensionality, and the masked input  x  st  ⊙  m  is used as the starting point for inference.    Second, we obtain a latent representation  z  st  of the masked input  x  st  ⊙  m  by passing it through the frozen, pretrained VAE encoder. This maps the partially observed measurement onto the learned cellular manifold.    Third, instead of initializing the generative process from pure noise (i.e., at  t  = 1), we add a controlled amount of noise to the initial latent state  z  st . This is achieved by simulating the forward SDE (Eq. ( 6 )) starting from  z (0) =  z  st  for a specified duration, up to a time  t  0  ∈ (0, 1]. This yields a perturbed latent vector  z ( t  0 ). The hyperparameter  t  0  critically governs the trade-off between faithfulness to the original measured expression (lower  t  0 ) and the realism of the imputed profile (higher  t  0 ).    Fourth, starting from the perturbed latent vector  z ( t  0 ), we then numerically solve the reverse-time SDE (Eq. ( 7 )) from  t  =  t  0  down to  t  = 0. This is typically performed using a predictor-corrector sampler or a simpler Euler-Maruyama scheme, where each step is guided by the score estimated by our trained GiT,   ϵ     θ   . This step effectively projects the noisy, partial information onto the manifold of complete, realistic cellular states learned from the pan-cancer atlas.    Fifth, the denoised latent vector  z (0) represents the imputed cellular state that optimally balances prior knowledge and measured data. It is then passed through the frozen VAE decoder to deterministically generate the full-dimensional expression profile        x   ¯     st     . Finally, a sparsity-aware postprocessing step is applied: for each gene, values below the  S -th percentile are set to zero, where  S  is the gene-specific zero-value ratio estimated from the pretraining scRNA-seq atlas. This step enforces biologically realistic sparsity patterns in the imputed profiles. The effect of this postprocessing is validated by the wo_sparsity ablation in Supplementary Fig.  4 a, b, which demonstrates consistent performance degradation when this step is removed.    The sampling hyperparameters are detailed in Supplementary Table  6 .    Pan-cancer scRNA-seq atlas processing  We aggregated publicly available scRNA-seq datasets encompassing 21 cancer types, including both primary and metastatic tumors. To ensure broad genomic representation across cancer studies, only genes present in all datasets were retained for integration  42  . Cells were excluded if they exhibited any of the following: mitochondrial gene fraction > 20%, ribosomal gene fraction > 40%, fewer than 300 detected genes, or total UMI counts < 500. Highly variable genes were identified using the  Scanpy  implementation of the normalized dispersion method; the top 10,000 most variable genes were selected as targets for downstream imputation. To evaluate the biological fidelity of the integrated atlas, we applied scVI for batch-corrected integration after quality control  36  . The resulting embedding resolved canonical cell subtypes, confirming the atlas’s suitability for pan-cancer analyses. For the tested multiple myeloma dataset, we used an external scRNA-seq reference recommended in the original study and performed label transfer with TACCO to support subsequent downstream analyses  43 , 44  .    Downstream analysis of ST datasets  To facilitate robust downstream analysis, we first performed quality control by excluding the bottom 15% of cells based on total UMI counts. Gene expression imputation was then carried out using stPainter. Subsequent analyses followed the standard  Scanpy  workflow: after log-normalization, low-dimensional embeddings were derived using both stPainter’s latent representation and PCA. Neighborhood graphs were constructed, followed by UMAP dimensionality reduction and Leiden clustering. Given that cell-type annotations were initially assigned using a transfer-annotation approach, we assessed the concordance between these transfer-annotation labels and the Leiden clusters. To refine annotation resolution, we performed subclustering and re-annotation of major cell populations and validated their identities by comparing marker gene expression profiles with those from reference single-cell transcriptomic datasets of the same tissue type. Major cell populations were annotated based on the expression of canonical marker genes:  CD8A  (T cells),  CD19  (B cells),  MZB1  (plasma cells),  CD68  (myeloid cells),  FCGR3B  (neutrophils),  PLVAP  (endothelial cells),  COL1A1  (fibroblasts), and  PDGFRB  (SMCs).  To evaluate the impact of stPainter imputation on the spatial architecture of the TME, we conducted a spatial coherence analysis based on cell-type annotations. Specifically, we partitioned each tissue section into 100 μm × 100 μm patches and quantified the cellular composition within each patch. Using spatially resolved CODEX proteomics data from adjacent sections as orthogonal protein-level support, we computed patch-wise cell-type proportions and assessed regional concordance using Pearson correlation. This analysis demonstrates that stPainter preserves biologically plausible spatial organization of the TME.  Major lineages, including T cells, epithelial cells, and myeloid cells, were further subclustered and manually annotated via cluster-specific DEGs. The resulting cell type assignments were cross-validated with adjacent CODEX sections by calculating Pearson’s  r  of cell counts within matched 100 μm × 100 μm regions.    Evaluation metrics  To evaluate model performance, we employed a suite of metrics categorized into gene-level and cluster-level.   Gene Metrics . These metrics quantify the similarity between predicted gene expression (     X    ^     ) and ground-truth observations ( X ) across  n  cells.     Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC):  PCC measures the linear relationship between the predicted and observed expression profiles for each gene:   10   PCC    (     x    i    ,      x    ^      i     )   =      ∑    j  =  1    n     (     x    i  j    −    μ    i     )    (       x    ^      i  j    −      μ    ^      i     )       σ    i        σ    ^      i      ,    where  μ  and  σ  denote the mean and standard deviation of expression values, respectively.     Structural similarity index measure (SSIM):  SSIM assesses the preservation of spatial patterns by integrating luminance, contrast, and structural information:   11   SSIM    (     x    i    ,      x    ^      i     )   =     (   2    μ    i        μ    ^      i    +    C    1     )    (   2  cov    (     x    i    ,      x    ^      i     )   +    C    2     )      (     μ    i    2    +      μ    ^      i    2    +    C    1     )    (     σ    i    2    +      σ    ^      i    2    +    C    2     )     ,    where    cov    (     x    i    ,      x    ^      i     )     represents the covariance between  x   i   and        x    ^      i     , and  C  1 ,  C  2  are stabilization constants.     Root mean square error (RMSE):  RMSE quantifies the average prediction error magnitude. To account for cross-platform technical variation, it is calculated on  z -score normalized expression values:   12   RMSE    (     x    i    ,      x    ^      i     )   =      1    n      ∑    j  =  1    n       (       z    ^      i  j    −    z    i  j     )     2      ,    where  z   i  j   and        z    ^      i  j      are normalized intensities. A lower RMSE indicates superior imputation accuracy.     Jensen-Shannon divergence (JS):  JS evaluates the similarity of spatial distributions, computed here as the Jensen-Shannon divergence between normalized spatial probability distributions  P   i   and        P    ^      i     :   13   JS    (     x    i    ,      x    ^      i     )   =    1    2      KL    (     P    i    ∥      P   ¯     i     )   +  KL    (       P    ^      i    ∥      P   ¯     i     )     ,    where        P   ¯     i    =   (     P    i    +      P    ^      i     )   /  2    and KL denotes the Kullback-Leibler divergence.     Cluster Metrics . These metrics assess the model’s capacity to preserve the spatial organization of cell types and tissue domains.     Adjusted Rand Index (ARI):  ARI evaluates the similarity between the clustering of imputed data and ground-truth annotations, corrected for chance:   14   ARI  =      ∑    i  j           n    i  j        2       −      ∑    i           a    i        2         ∑    j           b    j        2         /       n      2           1    2        ∑    i           a    i        2       +    ∑    j           b    j        2         −      ∑    i           a    i        2         ∑    j           b    j        2         /       n      2         ,    where  n   i  j   is the number of shared elements between clusters, and  a   i  ,  b   j   are the marginal sums of the contingency table.     Adjusted Mutual Information (AMI):  AMI quantifies the information shared between two partitions, adjusted for the expected mutual information due to random chance:   15   AMI   =    MI    (   A  ,  B   )   −  E   [   MI    (   A  ,  B   )    ]     avg    (   H   (   A   )   ,  H   (   B   )    )   −  E   [   MI    (   A  ,  B   )    ]     ,    where MI is the mutual information,  H  is the entropy, and    E    represents the expectation.     Normalized Mutual Information (NMI):  NMI scales the mutual information score to the range [0, 1] based on the entropy of the partitions:   16   NMI    (   A  ,  B   )   =    MI    (   A  ,  B   )       H   (   A   )   H   (   B   )       ,        Homogeneity (Homo):  Homogeneity measures the degree to which each cluster contains only members of a single class:   17   Homo   =  1  −    H   (   B  ∣  A   )     H   (   B   )     ,    where    H   (   B  ∣  A   )     is the conditional entropy of ground-truth categories    B    given predicted assignments    A   . A value of 1.0 indicates perfect homogeneity.      Statistics and reproducibility  No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. Sample sizes were determined by the availability of publicly accessible datasets that met the predefined quality-control criteria. All dataset inclusion, exclusion and quality-control procedures are described in the Methods. Randomization and blinding were not applicable because this was a computational study involving no experimental allocation or subjective outcome assessment. Pearson correlation analyses in Supplementary Fig.  17  were performed across six independent cancer datasets ( n  = 6) using two-sided tests. Pearson’s  r  and exact  P- values are reported, and no correction for multiple comparisons was applied. The datasets, preprocessing procedures, model settings and evaluation metrics required to reproduce the analyses are described in the Methods and Supplementary Information. evidence_text:
DeSpaST: deconvoluting spatial transcriptomics signals to cell-level resolution using histology images. Advances in spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies enable spatially resolved gene expression profiling, yet most platforms remain limited to spot-level resolution, where each measurement aggregates signals from multiple cells and obscures cell-specific programs and microenvironmental interactions. Existing computational approaches either provide limited sub-spot refinement or rely on matched single-cell RNA sequencing references that are costly and difficult to obtain. Here, we present DeSpaST (Deconvoluting Spatial Transcriptomics Signals to Cell-Level Resolution Using Histology Images), a dynamic edge-conditioned graph convolutional network that deconvolves spot-level ST data into cell-level gene expression profiles using only paired histology images. DeSpaST extracts nucleus-level morphological features, constructs directed cellular interaction graphs, and integrates spatial and transcriptional information through message passing. Validated across four cancer datasets with orthogonal Xenium, immunofluorescence, ablation, and interslice evaluations, DeSpaST enhances spatial resolution, facilitates downstream cellular-level analyses, and provides deeper insights into tissue biology. Background  Spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies have made significant progress in transitioning transcriptomic research from the cell level to a 2D spatial cell system. This transition is crucial for investigating cell–cell communication, tissue heterogeneity, and the tumor microenvironment, offering new insights into intricate biological processes. In contrast to single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), which requires tissue dissociation, ST technologies profile gene expression and preserve the spatial composition of cells within the native tissue environment [ 1 ]. ST technologies (e.g. 10× Genomics Visium [ 2 ], Nanostring GeoMx DSP [ 3 ], HDST [ 4 ], and Slide-seq [ 5 ]) utilize unique spatial barcodes to label the spatial locations and capture the gene expression at thousands of barcoded spatial locations (referred to as spots) within one experiment [ 6 ]. While these methods achieve high detection efficiency, their spatial resolution is inherently limited. The barcoded spot area (Spot diameter: 10× Genomics Visium: 55 μm, Nanostring GeoMx DSP: 10 μm [ 7 ], and Slide-seq: 10 μm [ 8 ]) encompasses a diverse population of cells, ranging from a few cells up to 200 cells [ 9 ]. To accurately distinguish the mixed-cell populations and uncover biological inferences from the ST data, it is essential to develop computational models that can enhance the resolution of ST data.  Several computational methods have been developed to improve the spatial resolution of ST data. Bayesian-based methods such as BayesSpace [ 10 ] refine gene expression to sub-spot resolution, only yielding modest improvement. Deep-learning-based approaches such as SPOTlight [ 11 ], Tangram [ 12 ], cell2location [ 13 ], and CARD [ 14 ] integrate ST data with scRNA-seq data, mapping related gene expression cells to ST coordinates or reconstructing the ST landscape from various cell combinations. However, the reliance on scRNA-seq data significantly raises the experimental costs and introduces constraints, including limited cell types and potential biases in spatial reconstruction accuracy.  Instead of relying on the scRNA-seq data, integrating histology images with ST data presents a more feasible and promising way to enhance ST resolution. Most ST platforms, such as Visium and HDST, typically provide corresponding histology images, like hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining images, which offer high-resolution morphological and spatial information for individual cells across the tissue sections. Deep-learning-based methods such as TESLA [ 15 ], XFuse [ 16 ], and iStar [ 17 ] have been developed to integrate the histology image with ST data to enhance ST resolution. However, these methods primarily enhance resolution at the pixel level but fall short of achieving cell-level gene expression resolution. Furthermore, these methods focus on extracting pixel level histological features [e.g. pixel intensities in red, green, blue (RGB) channels], neglecting true cell features and cell–cell interactions, which compromises model accuracy. A specialized model that directly incorporates actual cell-level features is necessary to improve the biological application of ST data.  Many fundamental biological questions—including the delineation of cell-type boundaries, characterization of the tumor microenvironment, and inference of cell–cell communication—inherently require cell-level resolution. However, true single-cell spatial assays such as Xenium or MERFISH remain expensive, limited in gene panel size, and not universally available, making spot-level ST the dominant modality in practice. Moreover, matched scRNA-seq data from the same tissue, which several existing deconvolution methods depend on, is not always obtainable and may introduce additional biases when tissue dissociation alters cell-type composition. A computational approach that can reliably infer cell-level expression directly from spot-level ST data and routine histology images therefore addresses a practical and widely encountered gap in the field.  In this work, we developed an innovative model called DeSpaST (Deconvoluting Spatial Transcriptomics Signals to Cell-Level Resolution Using Histology Images), which incorporates the cell level features from histology image with ST data using dynamic edge–conditioned graph convolution neural network ( Fig. 1 , and  Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Starting with a histology image, we perform cell segmentation and explicitly extract cell morphological and spatial interaction features, followed by constructing the cellular graphic interaction structures of the tissue. We then build a graph deconvolution model that combines ST data with these morphological features and interaction structures to deconvolute spot-level gene expression into cell-level gene expression profiles. In contrast to the previous methods that primarily rely on pixel-level information and use convolutional neural network (CNN)-like structures to encode the features, which often failing to capture cell–cell interaction information. DeSpaST leverages the graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to fully capture the cellular interaction topologies by constructing cellular interaction graphic structures. Unlike conventional CNNs, GCNs operate on non-Euclidean data structures, enabling comprehensive modeling of diverse cellular interaction topologies.    Figure 1   Illustration of DeSpaST in uncovering cell-level gene expression. (a) Workflow of DeSpaST: The DeSpaST model integrates histology images with spatial transcriptomics (ST), encompassing cell segmentation, extraction of cell features, construction of cellular graphic structures, and the application of Graphic Convolution blocks for the precise deconvolution of cell-level gene expression. (b) Illustration of DeSpaST's application to human breast cancer tissue. Two genes  ERBB2  and  MS4A1  are shown as examples. From left to right includes H&E image, H&E image with pathologist annotations, DeSpaST  ERBB2  gene expression, Visium  ERBB2  gene expression, TESLA  ERBB2  gene expression, DeSpaST  MS4A1  gene expression, Visium  MS4A1  gene expression, and TESLA  MS4A1  gene expression. (c) Zoomed-in sub-region for detailed representation of orange box in panel b H&E image. (d) Zoomed-in sub-region for detailed representation of red box in panel (b) H&E image.            Multi-panel scientific figure showing the DeSpaST workflow and its application to breast cancer tissue. The workflow combines H&E histology, spatial transcriptomics, cell segmentation, cellular graph construction, and graph convolution to predict cell-level gene expression. Tissue maps compare H&E images, pathologist annotations, and ERBB2 and MS4A1 expression from DeSpaST, Visium, and TESLA, with zoomed regions highlighting tumor and immune-cell boundaries.         DeSpaST offers several practical advantages. First, it does not require scRNA-seq references, reducing experimental cost and avoiding dependence on matched dissociated-cell datasets. Second, it leverages morphology and local tissue architecture to improve spatial localization and denoising within spots, which is particularly valuable in heterogeneous tumors where boundaries and niches vary over short distances. Third, DeSpaST’s inferred cell-level expression supports downstream analyses that are difficult at spot resolution, such as cell-type mapping at cellular granularity, spatial domain characterization, and trajectory inference. In our experiments, these advantages manifest as improved agreement with orthogonal measurements (e.g. Xenium), clearer spatial patterns, and improved recovery of spatial domains, with robustness supported by ablations demonstrating that performance depends on both transcriptional input and morphology rather than visual cues alone. Together, these considerations motivate DeSpaST as a practical and interpretable approach for cell-level resolution inference from spot-based ST, while clarifying the conditions under which it is most reliable.    Result   Overview of the DeSpaST model  DeSpaST requires only two inputs: a histology image and ST data ( Fig. 1a ). Histology images offer the individual cell spatial organization and morphology characterization, while the ST data provide gene expression at the spot level. To explicitly extract the cell spatial and organization characterizations from the histology image, we first employed the HD-staining deep-learning algorithm [ 18 ,  19 ] to segment and classify the cell nucleus from the tissue image. Alternatively, other methods for cell or nuclei segmentation could also be applied at this step. We then extracted the morphology features for each cell to construct the cellular graphic structures (see  Fig. 1a  and  Method  section for details). DeSpaST builds the graphic convolution networks by performing the four following steps: (i) extract image patches based on the spot coordinates in the ST data; (ii) construct a directed cellular graphic structure for each patch using nearest neighbors based on the Euclidean distance from a cell to its neighbors; and (iii) derive features from the directed cellular graphic structures to incorporate the spatial and morphology information of the cells into the graph convolutional network. Each node in the graph represents a cell. Node features include cell size, shape, and other morphological features. Edges denote spatial and morphological relationships between cells. Edge features include cell spatial proximity, cell connectivity angle, and interaction edge categorization ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ) [ 4 ]. The model is then constructed using two convolutional layers and one fully connected layer ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). All cell nodes are updated through a message passing from all neighboring nodes in each convolutional layer, which incorporates both morphological and cell–cell spatial interaction features of neighboring cells. In this study, we demonstrate DeSpaST’s ability in accurately capturing cell-level gene expression to overcoming spatial resolution limitations in ST data, using breast, lung, and ovarian cancer datasets as examples. DeSpaST offers a new convenient tool for advancing biomedical research, with broad applicability to diverse spatial transcriptomics datasets.    DeSpaST effectively enhances gene expression resolution  To assess the efficacy of DeSpaST, we applied the model to a well-studied breast cancer 10× Visium dataset [ 20 ]. We then conducted a comparative analysis of DeSpaST’s performance against the TESLA model [ 15 ], which is a machine-learning framework designed to enhance gene expression to pixel-level resolution [ 15 ]. DeSpaST demonstrated notable advancements in elucidating gene expression patterns. To illustrate, we present two marker genes,  MS4A1  and  ERBB2 , as representative examples ( Fig. 1b ). The  MS4A1  gene encodes the surface molecule CD20, which serves as a widely recognized marker indicative of B-cell lineage [ 21 ].  ERBB2  encodes the human epidermal growth factor receptor-2 (HER2) protein [ 22 ], which is used as a tumor marker in breast cancer diagnosis [ 23 ,  24 ]. For each gene, the cell-level gene expression profile from DeSpaST, spot-level gene expression pattern from Visium ST data, and the pixel-level gene expression patterns from TESLA ( Fig. 1b ), iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3a  and  b ) were plotted separately. Compared to Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse, DeSpaST showed the gene expression profiles with highest clarity and precision for both genes, successfully enhancing the gene expression resolution. Notably, the gene expression patterns from DeSpaST correlated well with the pathologist-annotated regions. DeSpaST high  ERBB2  gene expression cells closely matched the pathologist-annotated tumor regions. Also, the DeSpaST high  MS4A1  expressed cells were well aligned with the annotated immune cell regions. In contrast, Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse did not achieve the same level of visual clarity as DeSpaST in these regions. The  MS4A1  gene expression profile is particularly noteworthy because it is nearly imperceptible in the Visium ST data and in the reconstructions produced by TESLA ( Fig. 1b , right), iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3b ), whereas DeSpaST accurately discerns the  MS4A1  gene expression pattern and immune cell regions.  Remarkably, DeSpaST’s cell-level gene expression predictions demonstrate its capability and reliability in distinguishing between different cell layers. In three specific areas ( Fig. 1c  and  d , and  Supplementary Fig. S4 ), pathologists meticulously annotated the invasive carcinoma and immune cell regions to delineate their boundaries in the H&E images. The gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST effectively differentiated between these immune cell and tumor cell regions. DeSpaST accurately captured the elevated expression of ERBB2 in tumor regions and the elevated expression of MS4A1 in immune cell regions. The distinct gene expression patterns of MS4A1 and ERBB2 predicted by DeSpaST ( Fig. 1c  and  d  ,  and  Supplementary Fig. S4b ) precisely delineated the tumor and immune boundaries. In contrast, Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse could not accurately delineate these cell layers and boundaries ( Supplementary Fig. S3a  and  b ); instead, they only provided ambiguous patterns, which indicates a lack of precision in defining the regions. Moreover, as shown in  Supplementary Fig. S4c , DeSpaST demonstrated exceptional potential in precise cell type annotation. Beyond the highly expressed ERBB2 tumor region, DeSpaST identified an additional layer outside the tumor region with abundant MS4A1 expression, which had not been previously annotated. Upon closer examination of the H&E image by the pathologist, the layer was found to be a lightly stained layer, containing fibrous connective tissues interspersed with inflammatory cells, crucial for restricting tumor expansion. This finding of interspersed immune cells is consistent with the MS4A1 gene expression pattern predicted by DeSpaST.    DeSpaST accurately predicts cellular-level gene expression  The above comparison between pathology annotation and DeSpaST highlights the resolution enhancement power of DeSpaST. To further evaluate the model’s performance, we conducted a direct and comprehensive comparison of cellular-level expression for individual genes. In addition to the Visium spot-level gene expression measurement, Janesick  et al . [ 25 ] also measured the cellular-level gene expression of hundreds of genes through the Xenium experiment. We applied DeSpaST to this breast cancer Visium dataset from Janesick  et al . [ 25 ], segmented and classified the cell nucleus from the H&E image ( Supplementary Fig. S5 ), and deconvolving spot-level ST signals into cell-level gene expression profiles. Despite the inherent limitations of adjacent-section comparisons (e.g. local distortion, cell displacement, and microenvironmental differences), DeSpaST showed strong concordance with Xenium in spatial distribution patterns. For example, for the breast cancer marker gene  CCND1  [ 26 ,  27 ] ( Fig. 2a ) and T-cell marker gene  CD69  [ 28 ,  29 ] ( Fig. 2b ), DeSpaST accurately predicted the gene expression patterns, in agreement with the observed patterns in the Xenium. Both Visium and TESLA failed to resolve these patterns adequately, especially in the complex tissue regions. Consider the top of the tissue section ( Fig. 2c  and  Supplementary Fig. S6a ) where intricate tumor and immune cell domains are present. Only DeSpaST successfully captured gene expression within intricate microenvironments ( Fig. 2d  and  e ), accurately reflecting the patterns observed in the Xenium experiment. Conversely, TESLA and Visium failed to capture these spatial variations in gene expression, resulting in unclear expression patterns. In the case of the  CD69  gene ( Fig. 2b ), the Visium ST data are noisy and lack a clear expression pattern. Although TESLA reduces some noise, it fails to capture the inherent gene expression patterns accurately. In contrast, DeSpaST effectively eliminates noise and accurately discerns the true gene expression pattern.    Figure 2   Evaluation of DeSpaST in cell-level gene expression prediction. With the gene pattern identified by DeSpaST, our next step involves a quantitative assessment of the performance enhancement achieved by the DeSpaST model. To facilitate this assessment, spot-level gene expression was reconstructed by taking the average expression of cells inside each spot. For quantitative comparison across methods, we reconstructed spot-level expression by averaging the predicted cellular expressions within each Visium spot and then computed gene-wise Pearson correlations against Xenium for DeSpaST, raw Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3 ). DeSpaST exhibits a stronger correlation to Xenium ( r  = 0.754 for  CCND1  gene and  r  = 0.665 for  CD69  gene) than both Visium ( r  = 0.477 for  CCND1  gene, and  r  = 0.239 for  CD69  gene) and TESLA ( r  = 0.720 for  CCND1  gene, and  r  = 0.424 for  CD69  gene) ( Fig. 2f  and  Supplementary Fig. S3c ). Similar enhancements in clarity and noise reduction in gene expression patterns were observed in other genes as well, such as the  ERBB2  and  MS4A1  genes ( Supplementary Fig. S7 ). DeSpaST demonstrated strong consistency with Xenium experiments for both of these genes, achieving a correlation of  r  = 0.850 for the  ERBB2  gene and  r  = 0.610 for the  MS4A1  gene ( Supplementary Fig. S7c  and  d ). In addition to the above genes, to assess transcriptome-wide generalizability, we computed spot-level Pearson correlations for all examined Xenium genes and summarize the overall trend using correlation density plots ( Fig. 2g ;  Supplementary Fig. S3c ): DeSpaST achieves higher overall agreement with Xenium (median  r  = 0.518) than Visium (median  r  = 0.198) and TESLA (median  r  = 0.479), and the top 20% highest-density region summary consistently favors DeSpaST, indicating systematic improvement beyond a small set of marker genes.  To address the concern that histology-guided models might rely on visual cues and to validate key graph-construction hyperparameters, we performed a comprehensive set of ablation and sensitivity analyses ( Supplementary Fig. S8 ). First, randomizing the input transcriptional counts (“Random count”) caused a substantial collapse in performance—gene-wise correlation with Xenium dropped (CD69:  r  = 0.188; CCND1:  r  = 0.379), the overall summary decreased (top 20% high-density mean correlation: 0.174), and downstream spatial domain agreement deteriorated (NMI: 0.033; ARI: 0.0196)—demonstrating that accurate transcriptional signals are essential and that morphology alone cannot recover meaningful spatial expression. Second, randomizing morphology features (“Random image info”) also reduced performance relative to the full model (e.g. CD69:  r  = 0.423 versus 0.665; top 20% high-density mean: 0.202 versus 0.582; NMI: 0.169 versus 0.194; ARI: 0.0910 versus 0.1167), indicating that morphology provides complementary information but is not solely responsible for DeSpaST’s gains. Finally, we evaluated the robustness of the k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) cell-graph parameter by varying        on the breast dataset: extreme values were suboptimal (e.g. top-20%-density mean correlation = 0.161 at        and 0.220 at       ), while intermediate values (      –12) consistently achieved higher performance (0.58–0.64) and stable domain-detection agreement, supporting our choice of        as a balance between locality and connectivity ( Supplementary Fig. S8 ). Together, these analyses show that DeSpaST integrates both transcriptional and morphological information and that its performance is stable across a biologically reasonable range of neighborhood sizes.  To further test whether the deconvoluted outputs preserve biologically meaningful spatial structure beyond individual marker genes, we evaluated each method using a downstream spatial domain detection task on the breast cancer 10× Visium dataset [ 20 ]. As shown in ( Supplementary Fig. S9 ), we used the manually annotated domains as ground-truth labels. For each tool, we took the predicted cell-by-gene expression matrix together with per-cell spatial coordinates as input, constructed (i) an expression kNN graph in PCA space and (ii) a spatial kNN graph in 2D coordinate space, fused them into a hybrid connectivity matrix, and inferred domains using Leiden community detection (parameters reported in Supplementary Information). We then quantified concordance with manual annotations using NMI and ARI ( Supplementary Fig. S9b ; higher is better). DeSpaST achieved the best agreement with manual labels (NMI = 0.194; ARI = 0.117), outperforming iStar (NMI = 0.182; ARI = 0.056), XFuse (NMI = 0.033; ARI = 0.011), and TESLA (NMI = 0.143; ARI = 0.031), indicating that DeSpaST’s deconvolution better preserves domain-level organization for downstream spatial analyses.  Supplementary Fig. S9c  further visualizes the inferred domains from each method, where DeSpaST produces domain boundaries that are qualitatively more consistent with the expert annotations.  The remarkable cell-level resolution achieved by DeSpaST creates new possibilities for examining cell–cell communications within a spatial context. For instance, within the cellular milieu surrounding the breast ducts ( Supplementary Fig. S10 ), we detected elevated expressions of breast cancer marker genes  CCND1  and  ERBB2  ( Supplementary Fig. S10a  and  c ). In contrast, immune cell marker genes  CD69  and  MS4A1  ( Supplementary Fig. S10b  and  d ) exhibited high expression in the outside layer adjacent to the tumor cells. The gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST align with the Xenium gene panel, while TESLA failed to predict them accurately. DeSpaST’s findings suggest possible interactions between immune and tumor cells, highlighting its potential for further studies on the tissue microenvironment and cell–cell communication. We plotted and compared the  MS4A1  and  ERBB2  gene expression patterns with the corresponding HER2 and CD20 protein immunofluorescence (IF) signals ( Fig. 3a  and  b ). Interestingly, the gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST closely align with protein expression profiles, while Visium and TESLA are not able to capture them. DeSpaST exhibits superior performance compared to TESLA and Visium with higher correlation ( r  = 0.622 for DeSpaST versus  r  = 0.420 for Visium and  r  = 0.401 for TESLA;  Fig. 3c ). DeSpaST also demonstrated a notably higher correlation of ERBB2 gene expression with HER2 protein expression ( r  = 0.839) when compared to Visium ( r  = 0.821) and TESLA ( r  = 0.660), as illustrated in  Fig. 3d . Although Visium and TESLA also showed good correlations with the HER2 IF signals, DeSpaST significantly outperformed them in predicting fine-grained details gene expression patterns ( Supplementary Fig. S11 ). Notably, only DeSpaST accurately captured the comprehensive pattern of ERBB2 gene expression, depicting the tumor’s shape around the breast duct in alignment with IF protein signals. In contrast, Visium and TESLA predicted a vague outline of ERBB2 expression, lacking finer details and failing to depict a clear pattern. Application of DeSpaST for cell type identification  Given the highly precise cell-level gene expression predicted by DeSpaST, we employed DeSpaST for downstream analysis. This involved leveraging the predicted cell-level gene expression to delineate the spatial distribution of various cell types. Unlike ST data, where one spot may contain multiple cells, DeSpaST’s cellular-level resolution offers a superior depiction of cell-type distribution. Utilizing DeSpaST’s gene expression predictions as input, we applied the cell-type identification algorithm ScType [ 32 ] to assign the cell type to each single cell. The resulting cell-type profiles were mapped back onto the spatial location and detected locations for tumor cells, lymphocytes, fibroblasts, and macrophages ( Supplementary Fig. S12a ). To validate the cell-type distribution by DeSpaST, we implemented the ScType algorithm with the Xenium data and plotted the cell-type distribution in  Supplementary Fig. S12b . The spatial distributions of annotated cell types from DeSpaST closely resemble the cell types obtained from Xenium, which further substantiate the accuracy of DeSpaST. To reveal the tumor’s immunological response, we specifically focus on tumor cells and immune cells ( Fig. 4a  and  b ). Both DeSpaST ( Fig. 4a ) and Xenium panel ( Fig. 4b ) delineated similar tumor and immune cell regions. Heterogeneous areas are found at the upper and middle portion of the tissue where tumor and immune cells closely interact, which indicates the recognition and attack of activated immune cells that impede tumor spread. In contrast, tumor regions at the lower portion of the slides appear less confined, forming dense and more aggressive tumor areas where there is a lack of immune cell control. Both Xenium and DeSpaST accurately classify these complex cell environments. While Xenium served as a valuable reference here, DeSpaST exhibits greater potential and offers the flexibility to include more marker genes for cell type classification analysis. Unlike Xenium's panel of 306 genes, DeSpaST can leverage the transcriptomic level gene expression data from ST data. This enables the inclusion of a wider range of cell-type markers, leading to more accurate classification.    Figure 4   Application of DeSpaST in spatial cell-level downstream analysis. Application of DeSpaST in uncovering pseudo temporal trajectories of tumor progression  Following the annotation of cancer cells, we calculated the pseudo-trajectories timeline of tumor development based on the inferred cell level gene expression predicted by DeSpaST. The partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) method was used to construct the topological graph and a cluster with high expression of cancer stem cell marker  ALDH1A 3 [ 33 ,  34 ] was selected as the root node ( Supplementary Fig. S13 ). Pseudotime values were estimated and mapped back to each cell's spatial location to infer the dynamic trajectories of tumor progression ( Fig. 4c ). Interestingly, the clusters of early pseudotime cancer cells and late pseudotime cancer cells occupy markedly distinct regions in the tissue section. These distributions align precisely with the DCIS (ductal carcinoma  in situ ) and invasive tumor regions annotated by expert pathologists ( Fig. 4d ). Tumor cells with early pseudotime exhibit a denser and more uniform composition characterized with reduced variability in size and shape, corresponding to DCIS regions ( Fig. 4d ). In contrast, late pseudotime tumor cells, located in the invasive tumor region, show increased invasivenexss and a more loosely organized structure. Discussion  In this paper, we presented DeSpaST, which is a graphic deconvolution model that integrates the cell morphology features from histology images with spatial transcriptomic data to predict the cellular resolution gene expression for cells across the tissue section. Unlike other methods that only enhance the ST resolution, DeSpaST stands out as the first model to directly infer cell-level gene expression from histology images and ST data. DeSpaST is innovative and beneficial in that it takes advantage of the histology images and explicitly models the spatial organization of cells. By constructing the cellular graphic structure, cell morphology and interaction information from histology images were successfully input to the GCN model as nodes and edges, respectively. GCN, with its capability to handle complex non-Euclidean structures, enables deconvolution at cell-level resolution by well aligning with the diverse and intricate cellular interaction topologies. We demonstrated the high accuracy, resolution, robustness, and efficacy of DeSpaST in this paper. This model can be easily applied to diverse types of tissues and ST data.  The cellular-level gene expression inferred from DeSpaST offers powerful support to many biomedical applications. In this study, we applied DeSpaST’s output to the spatial cell type annotation and inferred the pseudotime trajectories of tumor development. DeSpaST offers the cellular resolution for cell type identification compared to traditional spot-level cell type identification. DeSpaST clearly illustrates the cell types for individual cells, enabling the revelation of cell–cell interaction in the tumor microenvironment and providing valuable insights into tumor immunology studies. Pseudotime analysis further uncovers the pseudo-temporal trajectories of tumor progression, revealing distinct clusters of early- and late-stage cancer cells. The high precision of DeSpaST establishes a reliable foundation for subsequent spatial transcriptomics analyses, such as deriving differentially expressed genes and exploring cell–cell communication inference.  A key limitation of our evaluation is that the Xenium measurements used for validation are obtained from an adjacent FFPE section, rather than the exact same section profiled by Visium. Although adjacent-section validation is often necessary in practice because assays are destructive or mutually exclusive, it is inherently imperfect: consecutive sections can exhibit local tissue distortion during sectioning and mounting, cell displacement, partial-volume differences, and subtle microenvironmental heterogeneity (e.g. immune infiltration near boundaries). These factors can weaken strict quantitative comparability even when broad spatial trends remain visually similar. Therefore, the agreement we observe between DeSpaST predictions and Xenium should be interpreted primarily as qualitative and semi-quantitative evidence that DeSpaST recovers coherent spatial gene-expression patterns and microenvironmental structure, rather than as an absolute quantitative ground truth at single-cell resolution. To mitigate this limitation, we emphasize evaluations that do not require one-to-one cell correspondence across sections—such as region-level pattern concordance, marker-consistent localization, and spot-level correlations computed after aggregating predicted cells within each Visium spot—and we further assess whether predicted cell-level signals support consistent tissue organization using downstream spatial domain analyses.  Beyond the cross-section validation constraints discussed above, several additional limitations should be noted. First, DeSpaST’s accuracy depends on the upstream nucleus segmentation step; segmentation errors such as missed nuclei, over-segmentation, or misclassification propagate to the graph construction and deconvolution. Second, genes with very low or near-zero expression in the Visium data are inherently difficult to deconvolve, as there is minimal transcriptional signal to distribute among cells. Third, standardized simulation frameworks that jointly model realistic histology with spatially structured single-cell expression are not yet available, and matched single-cell spatial datasets with paired Visium and H&E inputs remain scarce, precluding direct ground-truth validation at single-cell resolution. Despite these limitations, DeSpaST demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple complementary evaluation criteria and tissue types.  In addition to uncovering cellular gene expression in ST data, DeSpaST holds the potential for deconvoluting cellular protein expression in spatial proteomics. Recently, numerous spatial proteomic methods have been developed to enable the direct detection of protein molecules with spatial variability. However, the resolution remains limited, typically operating at spot sizes around 20–100 μm [ 42–45 ]. The application of DeSpaST to improve the resolution of spatial proteomics encourages further exploration of spatially cellular protein expression.  DeSpaST is designed for broad applicability, leveraging histology images and ST data as input to uncover cellular-level expression. Its capabilities can be further extended by incorporating additional data sources. For example, if single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data are available from the same tissue or a similar sample, DeSpaST can integrate it as a cell type constraint, potentially improving the deconvolution accuracy. This is particularly valuable when dealing with very weak sequencing signals in ST data, as scRNA-seq offers higher sequencing depth. An additional enhancement for DeSpaST could involve its extension to 3D spatial transcriptomes. Recently, spatially resolved transcriptomic atlases in high-dimensional data have emerged to revolutionize the understanding of cell interaction and gene regulation within the organ. Organ-level 3D spatial transcriptomics [ 46–48 ] or proteomics [ 49 ] were reconstructed from serial 2D tissue sections. DeSpaST, with a potential 3D GCN version, could leverage these data’s complexity to learn 3D spatial cell features and deconvolute gene expression. This is particularly relevant as current 3D spatial transcriptomes often miss data between sections. DeSpaST can potentially address this gap and provide a more complete picture of the 3D spatial transcriptomic landscape.    Method   Datasets   Human breast cancer datasets 1  Two human breast cancer datasets were employed for constructing and validating the DeSpaST model. The first human breast cancer dataset consists of Visium ST data for DCIS and Invasive Carcinoma FFPE human breast cancer tissue. This dataset contains 2518 spots, with 5244 median genes per spot and a sequencing depth of 32 524 reads per spot.    Human breast cancer datasets 2  The second human breast cancer dataset is associated with a recently released Xenium  in situ  platform [ 25 ]. This research conducted a comprehensive analysis with three complementary technologies (Chromium, Visium, Xenium) on a single breast-cancer FFPE tissue. The Visium output ST data were used to deconvolute the cell-level gene expression using DeSpaST, which contains 4992 spots, with 5712 median genes per spot and 40 003 mean reads per spot. The Xenium panels were used as a reference standard to evaluate DeSpaST’s cell-level resolution prediction. Additionally, IF staining was performed after Xenium to assess the expression profiles of HER2 and CD20 proteins. The results from both the Xenium panel and the subsequent IF staining were then used to verify the effectiveness of DeSpaST.    Human ovarian cancer dataset  The human ovarian cancer dataset is obtained from 10× Genomics and contains 4674 spots, with 8792 median genes per spot.    Human lung cancer dataset  The human lung cancer dataset is obtained from 10× Genomics and contains 6195 spots, with 10 087 median genes per spot.     Spatial transcriptomics data preprocessing and image feature extraction  Spatial transcriptomics data were first preprocessed prior to analysis. Gene expression values in the spot barcode profile matrix were normalized to counts per million (CPM). To mitigate the impact of outliers, the normalized CPM values were scaled to the 95th percentile.  The cell morphology features were extracted from H&E images using HD-Staining (Histology-based Digital Staining of Pathology Images) [ 18 ], which is an automatic deep-learning model that simultaneously segments and classifies cell nuclei, as well as provides morphology information about each identified cell nucleus. The extracted morphological features encompassed the centroid position, cell area, convex area, eccentricity, extent, filled area, major axis length, minor axis length, orientation, perimeter, solidity, and probability. In addition, we further enriched DeSpaST by incorporating 1024-dimensional intermediate box features and 256-dimensional mask features derived from the HD-Staining model. These cell morphological features were incorporated into the construction of DeSpaST.    Cellular graphic structure construction  We initially divided whole-slide H&E images into 250 × 250-pixel patches centered on the Visium spots. In total, we generated 2518 patches for the 10× Visium human breast cancer dataset, 4992 patches for the Janesick  et al . [ 25 ] human breast cancer dataset, 4674 patches for the human ovarian cancer dataset, and 6195 patches for the human lung cancer dataset. For each patch, we first obtain each cell location by performing cell segmentation, then construct a directed graph structure by connecting the cells based on their spatial proximity. This graph structure was designed to incorporate at least eight nearest neighbors. Pairwise Euclidean distances between cell coordinates were computed to identify the nearest neighbors. For those patches with very low cell density (<8 cells), DeSpaST dynamically resized the patch to include at least eight neighboring cells. These directed graph structures captured the spatial relationship and connectivity among cells in the tissue.  Each graph structure consisted of two main components: nodes and edges. Nodes represent morphological features extracted through HD-Staining for individual cells. These node features have undergone global scaling as part of the preprocessing. Edges store information on edge categorization and edge spatial representation ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). Edge categorization is determined based on the types of cells connected by each edge, which provides insight into the type of interactions between the connected cells. Here, we included a total of 49 combinations of edge categorizations across seven cell types ( Supplementary Fig. S2a ). Edge spatial representation refers to the spatial aspects of cell interactions, including the Cell Connectivity Angle and Spatial Proximity. Cell Connectivity Angle indicates the connectivity between neighboring cells and the directionality of these connections. Spatial Proximity reflects the physical distance between cells. Both nodes and edges collectively constitute the cellular graphic structure, which synergistically contributes to the definition of complex cellular relationships.    Auto graph convolutional network for spatial transcriptomics deconvolution  Following the construction of the cellular graphic structure and thoughtfully derived essential node and edge features, we employed dynamic edge-conditioned convolution to manage graphs of varying size and connectivity. This process is mathematically represented in Equation ( 1 ). The embedding vector of the convolution filter is then used to deconvolve the spot-level gene expression into cell-level gene expression. Our model-specific architecture comprises of three layers: two ECC (Edge-Conditioned Convolution) [ 50 ,  51 ] GCN layers [ 52 ,  53 ] followed by a ReLU activation function [ 54 ], and one linear transformation layer. Each ECC layer incorporates both node and edge feature embeddings for propagating information across the graph ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Node features       contain the cell morphological features. Message passing and an aggregation step will update node        by incorporating the messages from all the neighbors        and messages from node        itself. The first GCN layer includes 1290 input node features and outputs 100 convolutional channels, and 100 output convolutional channels in the second GCN layer.  Output : Deconvolved gene expression for each cell  1: Initialize all weights for the model       .  2: Divide the input H&E image into patches; for each patch, classify and extract morphological features for each cell.  3:  for  each epoch  do   4:  while  not converged  do   5: Compute embedding vector        for each node        use Equation ( 1 ).  6: Compute MSE loss        from Equation ( 3 ).  7: Compute gradient of loss function        and update weight matrices       .  8:  end while   10: end for  11:  return  embedded deconvolved gene expression        for each cell  We implement DeSpaST in Pytorch and use Adadelta Optimizer with learning = 0.001, and momentum = 0.9.    Image registration and result comparison   Immunofluorescence image and Xenium panel registration to hematoxylin and eosin images  In order to register the IF image and Xenium panel to the Visium corresponding H&E images and facilitate the comparison to the protein/RNA expression experiment, we employed skimage.transform package for image transformation. To achieve a precise and efficient registration, we systematically tested various combinations of angles and scales between the IF and H&E images. To optimize computing efficiency, we initially conducted tests with 10% scaled-down images to obtain approximate scale and angle adjustments. Subsequently, we fine-tuned the registration using the original scale.    DeSpaST model validation  We validate DeSpaST through the assessment of RNA expression and protein expression by utilizing data from the Xenium panel and IF images, respectively. Using the spatial information from Visium spot locations, we reconstructed the spot-level expression for DeSpaST, TESLA, Xenium panel, and IF protein expression. The accuracies of Visium ST data, TESLA, and the DeSpaST model were evaluated using the Pearson correlation coefficient with the Xenium panel and IF image.     Cell type analysis  To assign cell types to each predicted single cell, we adopted a fully automated cell-type identification algorithm, ScType [ 32 ], which utilizes the Xenium-tested marker gene as the selected cell markers. The cellular level gene expression predicted by DeSpaST was used as input. The Seurat package was used to normalize the data with the default LogNormalize method. We then use the Seurat FindNeighbors function with parameter dims = 1:50 and FindClusters function with resolution = 0.9, which results in 23 clusters. ScType was also applied with Xenium Breast Cancer Cell Marker panel. Each cluster was assigned to the cell type with the highest score, and clusters assigned the same cell type were merged into larger clusters.    Pseudotime analysis  The gene expression of tumor cells predicted by DeSpaST was extracted for pseudotime analysis. We first reduced the gene expression dimension using principal component analysis (PCA). Then, cell clustering was performed using the Leiden algorithm, which is a fast approach to ensure that all cells are well connected for downstream optimal trajectory inference [ 55 ]. Partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) [ 56 ] is used to construct a topological graph based on the cell partitions. The cluster with high expression of  ALDH1A 3 [ 33 ,  34 ], a gene marker of cancer stem cells, was selected as the trajectory root node. The Diffusion Pseudotime (DPT) method [ 57 ] was then applied to estimate pseudotime values, which represented the tumor cell dynamics. All analyses were performed using the SCANPY [ 58 ] Python packages.    Spatial domain detection  To assess whether each deconvolution method preserves biologically meaningful spatial structure at the domain level, we performed downstream spatial domain detection using the predicted cell-by-gene expression matrix together with per-cell spatial coordinates as inputs. For each method, we first constructed two neighborhood graphs: (i) an expression kNN graph in a low-dimensional transcriptomic space, obtained by PCA on the predicted expression matrix and kNN graph construction using Scanpy, yielding an expression connectivity matrix       ; and (ii) a spatial kNN graph in the 2D coordinate space using Euclidean neighbors, yielding a symmetric binary adjacency matrix       . We then fused these graphs into a hybrid connectivity matrix via a linear combination,        where       balances spatial proximity and transcriptional similarity. Finally, we applied Leiden community detection on       to infer spatial domains for each tissue section, using identical processing across methods; all parameters are reported in the Supplementary Information. Domain assignments were benchmarked against manual domain annotations (when available) using Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) and the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI).    Key Points    DeSpaST introduces a dynamic edge-conditioned graph convolutional network for deconvolving spot-level ST data into true cell-level-resolution gene profiles.    DeSpaST integrates spatial and morphological features from histology images to model cell–cell organization and improve accuracy.    Extensively benchmarked across multiple cancer datasets, outperforming existing methods in resolution and precision.    DeSpaST enables diverse applications, including cell-type annotation, tumor trajectory analysis, and cell–cell communication discovery, demonstrating its potential to provide new insights in various biological contexts.
