Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) link a target-specific antibody to a cytotoxic payload and are now central to breast-cancer treatment [ 2 ]. Trastuzumab emtansine established the class in HER2-positive disease [ 3 ], extending median progression-free survival from 6.4 to 9.6 months and median overall survival from 25.1 to 30.9 months relative to lapatinib plus capecitabine. Trastuzumab deruxtecan and the TROP2-directed agents Sacituzumab govitecan and datopotamab deruxtecan have since broadened their use across breast cancer subtypes [ [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. In the long-term DESTINY-Breast04 analysis, investigator-assessed median progression-free survival was 8.8 versus 4.2 months (hazard ratio, 0.36), and median overall survival was 22.9 versus 16.8 months (hazard ratio, 0.69), with trastuzumab deruxtecan versus treatment of the physician's choice in HER2-low advanced breast cancer [ 4 ]. In the final ASCENT analysis, Sacituzumab govitecan improved median progression-free survival to 4.8 versus 1.7 months (hazard ratio 0.41) and median overall survival to 11.8 versus 6.9 months (hazard ratio 0.51) in metastatic triple-negative breast cancer [ 5 ]. HER3, NECTIN4 , folate receptor-α, B7-H3, MUC1 and CEACAM5 are among the additional targets in clinical development [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]; the molecular alterations of MUC1 and their therapeutic exploitation have been reviewed recently [ 11 ]. For an ADC, tissue-level abundance is not enough. The target must also be located on the relevant cells. Expression in stroma, vasculature or normal epithelium can contribute to target-dependent on-target/off-tumor toxicity, but ADC toxicity is multifactorial and also reflects payload cytotoxicity, platform-related properties, and host factors [ 12 ]. The clinical burden can nonetheless be substantial. In the updated DESTINY-Breast04 analysis, adjudicated drug-related interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis occurred in 12.1% of patients receiving trastuzumab deruxtecan, including 1.1% grade 5 events [ 4 ]. In the final ASCENT analysis, the most common grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events with Sacituzumab govitecan included neutropenia (52%) and diarrhea (12%) [ 5 ]. Conversely, target-negative tumor cells may escape direct binding, although a membrane-permeable payload can affect neighboring cells through a bystander effect [ 13 ]. Bulk assays and tissue-averaged immunohistochemistry do not resolve the cellular source of a target signal. The broader importance of tissue architecture extends beyond ADCs to other tumor-directed delivery platforms, including nanocarriers influenced by vascular permeability and retention, as well as stimuli-responsive nanoparticles under development for breast cancer [ 14 , 15 ]. Cell-resolved target assessment is already used in the chimeric antigen receptor T-cell field to anticipate on-target/off-tumor effects [ 16 ]. For ADCs, bulk surveys have catalogued target expression across tumors and normal tissues, including a 54-target pan-cancer analysis [ 17 ]. A post-mortem breast cancer series also compared metastases with matched normal organs [ 18 ]. In high-grade serous ovarian cancer, dissociated single-cell RNA sequencing identified clinical ADC targets that were most often restricted to cancer cells [ 19 ]. Spatial profiling has therefore been proposed as a means of interpreting target availability in tissue context [ 20 ]. Breast single-cell atlases have examined heterogeneity in ERBB2 and TACSTD2, but primarily within the malignant epithelial compartment [ 21 ]. Few studies have spatially identified multiple ADC targets across malignant and non-malignant compartments in breast cancer. Imaging-based transcriptomics can provide this information while preserving histological structure [ [22] , [23] , [24] , [25] ]. We therefore mapped 11 ADC targets in a publicly available whole-transcriptome breast cancer specimen, examined the recurrence of selected patterns in two public Xenium specimens, and compared the findings with TCGA-BRCA bulk transcriptomes. The study is descriptive. Its purpose is to identify which cells contribute to each target transcript and to show where tissue-level abundance may obscure that source. Materials and methods Single-cell spatial dataset We used the public CosMx Spatial Molecular Imager Human Whole Transcriptome FFPE breast dataset (Bruker Spatial Biology, "breast discovery" release, sample S0) [ 22 ]. The dataset contains one tumor specimen, which served as the discovery sample. Selected findings were examined in two additional public Xenium specimens (the cross-specimen Xenium analysis). We obtained the cell-by-gene matrix, cell metadata, and cell polygons from the public repository. The complete dataset contained approximately 645,000 cells. To make the analysis tractable using standard hardware, we drew a reproducible random subsample (seed = 1) and retained cells with at least 50 detected RNA molecules. This yielded 154,816 cells. Removing negative-control and system-control probes left 18,934 genes. Global coordinates were converted from pixels to micrometers using a scale of 0.12028 µm per pixel. We also split the retained cells into two random halves and compared cell-type mean target-expression matrices to assess sensitivity to subsampling. Clustering, annotation and differential expression Analyses were performed in R 4.5.2 with Seurat 5.5.1 [ 26 ]. Counts were log-normalized to counts per 10,000, then subjected to a natural-log transformation. We scaled the 2,000 most variable genes and used 30 principal components to construct a shared-nearest-neighbor graph. Louvain clustering was run at resolution 0.5, followed by UMAP embedding. Clusters were assigned to seven lineages using module scores for canonical markers and established breast cell-type signatures [ 27 ]. The lineages were tumor epithelial, fibroblast/stromal, myeloid, B/plasma, T, myoepithelial, and endothelial. One-versus-rest Wilcoxon rank-sum tests identified positive cell-type markers, with at least 10% detection, a minimum log2 fold-change of 0.25, and at most 500 cells per group. P values were adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg method. These cell-level tests treat cells from one specimen as independent observations. We therefore used them to describe within-sample marker specificity and placed greater weight on effect sizes than on nominal P values. ADC-target analysis We examined eleven clinically relevant ADC targets: ERBB2 (HER2), TACSTD2 (TROP2), ERBB3 (HER3), NECTIN4, FOLR1 (FRα), CEACAM5 (CEA), CD276 (B7-H3), MUC1, MET, EGFR and FOLH1 (PSMA). For each cell type, we calculated mean log-normalized expression and the number and fraction of cells with detectable expression. Per-cell expression was also mapped in tissue coordinates. Cross-platform single-target detection comparison To describe cross-platform differences in single-target detection, we compared ERBB2 and TACSTD2 between the whole-transcriptome CosMx dataset and a 313-gene Xenium breast panel [ 23 ]. For each dataset, we calculated the fraction of tumor cells with zero counts for the target gene. The assays were applied to different specimens and used different chemistries and panel sizes; this descriptive comparison was not designed to isolate a platform or panel-design effect. Receptor subtype, spillover control and spatial organization For each target, we report the number and fraction of expressing cells, along with the mean expression. This provides cellular support for findings in low-abundance microenvironments. To assess whether FOLH1 and CD276 enrichment could reflect transcript spillover across cell boundaries, we built a k-nearest-neighbor graph (k = 10) from cell centroids. We calculated the proportion of tumor-epithelial neighbors for each cell, then compared expression in the enriched lineage between cells with few (<25%) and many (>50%) tumor neighbors. The receptor phenotype was inferred from tumor-cell expression of ESR1, PGR, and ERBB2 , with GATA3 and MKI67 as context. This RNA-based classification is not equivalent to immunohistochemical receptor status. Cell-type neighborhood enrichment followed the approach implemented in Squidpy [ 28 ]. For each ordered cell-type pair, we compared the observed number of graph edges with a null distribution from 100 permutations of cell-type labels and expressed the result as a z-score. Bulk transcriptomic contextualization (TCGA-BRCA) TCGA-BRCA gene-level expression (log2(normalized count + 1)) and clinical data were obtained from the UCSC Xena TCGA hub [ 29 , 30 ]. Sample barcodes identified 1,097 primary tumors and 114 solid-tissue normals. In this dataset, NECTIN4 is recorded under its alias PVRL4 and was mapped accordingly. Tumor-versus-normal differences were tested for each target by the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment. Overall survival was derived from vital status and time to death or last follow-up. The full survival cohort contained 1,080 patients. For each target, we fitted a univariable Cox model using continuous expression and performed a median-split log-rank test. We interpreted these P values in the context of the 11 tested targets and did not search for additional endpoints and subgroups. Multivariable Cox models were fitted separately in the 808 patients with complete data for age, pathologic stage, and PAM50 intrinsic subtype. Cross-specimen validation on Xenium We analyzed two additional public Xenium breast cancer specimens: the Human Breast invasive ductal carcinoma sample and the breast cancer reference block [ 23 ]. The invasive ductal carcinoma specimen came from a different patient. Public metadata did not establish patient-level independence of the reference block. We used the vendor-supplied graph-based clusters and assigned cells to the same lineages by marker scores. Four ADC targets were represented in the Xenium panel: ERBB2, TACSTD2, MUC1, and EGFR . For each target, we compared detection fractions between tumor epithelial and non-tumor cells. Detection fraction was chosen because absolute expression is not directly comparable across platforms with different panel sizes and sequencing depths. Results A seven-lineage single-cell spatial map of the breast tumor Unsupervised clustering produced 15 clusters, which were assigned to seven cell types ( Fig. 1 ). Tumor epithelium was the largest compartment (95,803 cells; 61.9%). Fibroblast/stromal and myeloid cells each accounted for 10.3%, followed by B/plasma cells (6.9%), T cells (5.3%), myoepithelial cells (2.7%), and endothelial cells (2.6%). Quality-control distributions are shown in Supplementary Fig. S2. These populations occupied coherent tissue regions, with tumor epithelium forming contiguous fields and glandular structures ( Fig. 1 B). One-versus-rest testing identified 4,449 positive markers. The leading markers matched the assigned lineages, including PIP, SERHL2, and MLPH in the tumor epithelium; COL1A1, LUM, and POSTN in the stroma; and EGFL7, PLVAP, and FLT1 in the endothelium ( Fig. 2 ; Supplementary Table S4). The same correspondence was seen for myeloid ( APOE, LYZ, C1QC ), B/plasma ( IGKC, IGHA1, JCHAIN ), T ( GNLY, GZMA, ITGAE ) and myoepithelial cells ( ACTA2, MCAM, CSPG4 ). Fig. 1 Single-cell spatial map of the breast tumor. (A) Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) of 154,816 analyzed cells from one CosMx breast tumor specimen, colored by seven annotated cell types. (B) Spatial distribution of the same cells using tissue coordinates in micrometers. Each point represents a cell centroid. The same cell-type color key is used in both panels. Fig. 2 Cell-type marker expression in the discovery specimen. The five positive one-versus-rest markers with the largest average log2 fold change are shown for each of seven cell types. Dot color represents mean log-normalized expression across all cells in the indicated lineage, including zero-count cells. Dot size represents the fraction of cells with a nonzero gene count. The size-key values are fractions: 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75 correspond to 25%, 50% and 75%, respectively. Expression was normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and transformed using ln(1 + x). Marker-test results are provided in Supplementary Table S4. ADC targets show tumor-enriched and microenvironment-enriched patterns The eleven ADC targets followed two broad patterns ( Fig. 3 ). MUC1 (mean log-normalized expression 0.82), HER2/ ERBB2 (0.68), NECTIN4 (0.60), TROP2/ TACSTD2 (0.52) and HER3/ ERBB3 (0.39) were highest in tumor epithelium. Their mean expression in non-malignant compartments was 0.14 or lower. Spatial maps showed that HER2 and TROP2 expression were associated with the tumor-epithelial regions of the section ( Fig. 4 ). Fig. 3 ADC-target expression across cell types. Dot plot of 11 antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) targets in the CosMx discovery specimen. Dot color represents mean log-normalized expression across all cells in each lineage, including zero-count cells. Dot size represents the fraction of cells with a nonzero gene count; size-key values of 0.1-0.4 correspond to 10%-40%. Expression was normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and transformed using ln(1 + x). MUC1, HER2, NECTIN4, TROP2 and HER3 had their highest mean expression in tumor epithelium. B7-H3 was highest in endothelial and myoepithelial cells, and PSMA was highest in endothelium. Cell counts and detection fractions are provided in Supplementary Table S1. These measurements concern RNA expression. Fig. 4 Spatial expression of representative ADC targets. Per-cell expression of HER2 (ERBB2, upper left), TROP2 (TACSTD2, upper right), PSMA (FOLH1, lower left) and B7-H3 (CD276, lower right) in the CosMx discovery specimen. Each point represents a cell centroid. The four panels use the same tissue coordinates and a common expression color scale. Expression was normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and transformed using ln(1 + x). The maps show transcript localization and do not establish surface-protein abundance. Other targets were expressed preferentially outside the tumor compartment. B7-H3/ CD276 was highest in endothelial (0.35) and myoepithelial cells (0.31), followed by fibroblast/stromal and tumor cells (both 0.16). PSMA/ FOLH1 was concentrated in endothelium (0.47), whereas mean tumor-cell expression was 0.05. This distribution agrees with the reported localization of PSMA to tumor-associated neovasculature rather than breast carcinoma cells [ 31 ]. FOLR1 and CEACAM5 remained low across all cell types in this specimen (≤0.10). The microenvironmental findings were supported by the number of cells expressing (Supplementary Table S1). PSMA was detected in 20.0% of endothelial cells (817 of 4,076) and 3.2% of tumor cells. B7-H3 was detected in 16.0% of endothelial cells, 12.9% of myoepithelial cells, and 9.5% of tumor cells. Low PSMA expression in tumor cells argues against tumor-derived transcript spillover as the main explanation for endothelial enrichment. In the neighborhood analysis, endothelial cells with fewer than 25% tumor neighbors still had a mean PSMA expression of 0.39 (n = 2,282), compared with 0.05 in tumor cells. B7-H3 enrichment in stroma, endothelium and myoepithelium was also retained in cells located away from tumor epithelium (Supplementary Table S2). Single-target detection differed between platforms and specimens In the CosMx whole-transcriptome specimen, 60% of tumor cells had zero ERBB2 counts, and 68% had zero TACSTD2 counts. In the targeted 313-gene Xenium specimen, the corresponding fractions were 3.5% and 11%. Because the assays were applied to different tissue specimens and used different chemistries and panel sizes, these differences cannot be attributed solely to assay design. They nevertheless caution against interpreting a zero count as absence of target expression over spatial transcriptomic platforms. Tumor receptor phenotype and spatial organization Among tumor cells, ERBB2 was the most highly expressed receptor gene (mean 0.68; detected in 36.6% of cells). ESR1 (0.09; 5.8%) and PGR (0.04; 2.7%) were low. This RNA profile is compatible with, but not diagnostic of, a HER2-enriched or hormone-receptor-negative phenotype. The HER2 and TROP2 findings should therefore be interpreted in the context of these receptors. Neighborhood analysis showed strong self-association of the tumor epithelium (z = 507) and negative associations with all non-malignant cell types. The largest negative values were observed in myeloid cells (z = -308) and fibroblast/stromal cells (z = -294). Among non-malignant populations, fibroblasts co-localized most strongly with myeloid cells (z = 131), whereas endothelial cells co-localized most strongly with myoepithelial cells (z = 137; Supplementary Fig. S3). Subsampling had little effect. Two random halves of the retained cells produced nearly identical cell-type mean target-expression matrices (Pearson r = 0.998). HER2 and TROP2 tumor enrichment recurs in additional Xenium specimens Both Xenium specimens were public datasets distinct from the CosMx discovery sample, although only the invasive ductal carcinoma specimen was known to come from a different patient. We therefore assessed cross-specimen recurrence without treating the reference block as a separate patient-level replicate (Supplementary Fig. S4, Supplementary Table S3). Because panel content and sequencing depth differed, the comparison used detection fractions. Ranking cell types by mean expression gave the same ordering. Tumor epithelium had the highest HER2/ ERBB2 and TROP2/ TACSTD2 expression in all six specimen-by-target comparisons. In the invasive ductal carcinoma specimen, for example, TROP2 was detected in 84% of tumor cells and 26% of non-tumor cells. MUC1 showed the same pattern where it was included in the panel. EGFR differed. In both Xenium specimens, EGFR was detected as often as or more often in non-tumor cells, with the highest levels in myoepithelial cells. Bulk tumor-versus-normal expression In TCGA-BRCA (1,097 tumors and 114 normal tissues), six targets were higher in tumor tissue: CEACAM5 (log2 fold-change +4.1), MUC1 (+2.1), CD276 (+0.85), ERBB3 (+0.85), NECTIN4 (+0.75) and ERBB2 (+0.54). All adjusted P values were below 0.001 ( Fig. 5 ; Supplementary Table S5). TACSTD2 did not differ between groups (log2 fold-change -0.29; P = 0.06). Four targets were lower in tumors: FOLR1 (-3.8), EGFR (-3.5), MET (-2.4) and FOLH1 (-1.6). These bulk contrasts are influenced by tissue composition and do not identify the cell type expressing the gene. B7-H3 illustrates the distinction, as it was higher in bulk tumor tissue but arose mainly from endothelial, myoepithelial and stromal cells in the spatial data. Fig. 5 ADC-target expression in TCGA-BRCA tumors and normal tissues. Box plots show log2(normalized count + 1) expression of 11 ADC-target genes in primary tumors (n = 1,097; red) and solid-tissue normal samples (n = 114; blue). The center line is the median, boxes span the 25th-75th percentiles, and whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range. Points beyond the whiskers are outliers. The y-axis range differs between gene panels. Two-sided Wilcoxon comparisons and Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P values are reported in Supplementary Table S5. No ADC target shows a strong association with overall survival Among the 1,080 patients with survival data, no univariable association remained significant after correction for eleven targets. The lowest nominal P values in this full cohort were observed for NECTIN4 in the continuous Cox model (P = 0.040) and the median-split log-rank test (P = 0.053; Supplementary Fig. S1; Supplementary Table S6). The complete-covariate subset contained 808 patients. In this subset, CEACAM5 had a nominal univariable association (P = 0.019), which weakened after adjustment for age, pathologic stage, and PAM50 subtype (hazard ratio 1.22; P = 0.071; Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P = 0.478). No target was associated with overall survival after covariate adjustment (Supplementary Table S7). These analyses do not support a strong single-gene prognostic effect, although the unselected cohort and limited event count constrain the inference. Discussion At the RNA level, the eleven ADC targets separated into two expression patterns in the discovery specimen. HER2, TROP2, HER3, NECTIN4 and MUC1 were concentrated in tumor epithelium. Among these, MUC1 had the highest mean expression, consistent with its long-standing status as a tumor-associated antigen and with continuing efforts to exploit MUC1 alterations therapeutically [ 11 ]. B7-H3 and PSMA were more prominent in stromal or vascular compartments. Bulk and tissue-averaged assays cannot resolve this difference in cellular source. Recovery of the established PSMA neovascular pattern provides an internal check on the cell assignments. These data do not estimate the therapeutic index, which also depends on surface protein abundance, internalization, expression in vital normal tissues, and payload and linker chemistry. Localization alone does not indicate whether a compartment contains sufficient antigen to affect treatment. PSMA is a useful caution. We detected FOLH1 in 20% of endothelial cells, but quantitative immunohistochemistry found PSMA staining in only a small minority of breast-cancer neovessels [ 32 ]. Those authors questioned the viability of PSMA-directed theranostics in this disease. A cell type can therefore be the dominant source of a low-abundance transcript without presenting a clinically meaningful antigen burden. Our study locates the RNA signal but does not quantify surface protein or predict efficacy or toxicity. The bulk and spatial examinations answered different questions. TCGA-BRCA identified targets whose total expression differed between tumor and normal tissue. It could not show whether the signal came from malignant cells. B7-H3 was higher in bulk tumor tissue but mapped mainly to endothelium, myoepithelium, and stroma in the spatial specimen. This is not a contradiction. Tumor-versus-normal contrasts are influenced by tissue composition, so we do not interpret bulk upregulation as evidence of tumor-cell specificity. Prior work defines the limits of the study's novelty. Single-cell surveys have already been used to identify non-malignant expression of CAR-T targets [ 16 ]. ADC-target catalogues are available for pan-cancer and breast cancer tissues [ 17 , 18 ], and dissociated single-cell data have been used to assess ADC target restriction in ovarian cancer [ 19 ]. B7-H3 expression in tumor endothelium and fibroblasts has been reported [ 33 ], as has PSMA expression in breast cancer neovasculature [ 31 , 32 ]. Our contribution is narrower. We assign 11 ADC-target transcripts to cell types in intact breast tissue, including the myoepithelial compartment, and assess selected targets in 2 additional specimens using another platform. The recovery of the known B7-H3 and PSMA localizations supports the approach but does not constitute a new biological discovery. Tumor epithelium occupied spatially segregated regions, apart from stromal, immune, and vascular populations (Supplementary Fig. S3). Together with the neighborhood control, this pattern makes simple transcript spillover an unlikely explanation for the B7-H3 and PSMA findings. The discovery tumor had low ESR1 and PGR expression and comparatively high ERBB2 . HER2 and TROP2 localization should therefore be interpreted within the context of their respective receptors rather than generalized across all breast cancer subtypes. Cross-specimen support was strongest for HER2 and TROP2. Their enrichment in tumor epithelium recurred in both Xenium specimens and on a second imaging platform. The invasive ductal carcinoma specimen came from a different patient, but the public metadata did not establish patient-level independence for the reference block. The evidence therefore represents recurrence across three specimens and two platforms, not three independent patients. EGFR was highest in myoepithelial cells in both Xenium specimens, showing that tumor restriction cannot be assumed for every target. B7-H3 and PSMA were absent from the targeted panel, so their localization remains based on the discovery specimen. The survival analyses provide no evidence that any target is an independent prognostic marker. Nominal associations differed between the full cohort and the complete-covariate subset and did not survive correction for or adjustment for covariates. This null result should not be read as proof that the target expression has no prognostic relevance in any subgroup. The cohort was unselected, the number of events was limited, and we deliberately avoided exploratory analyses by subtype or alternative endpoints. Translating these transcript-level maps into clinical decisions will require protein-level measurement and direct correlation with ADC efficacy and toxicity. We regard this as the central next step, rather than a peripheral caveat. A practical sequence would begin with multiplexed immunofluorescence or imaging mass cytometry on matched tissue sections, using the lineage markers applied here to reproduce the cell assignments alongside antibodies directed against the ectodomains engaged by ADCs. Simultaneous RNA and protein co-detection on the same section would then allow the transcript-to-protein relationship to be assessed cell-by-cell rather than assumed. Compartment-resolved quantitative scoring, as applied to PSMA in breast-cancer neovasculature [ 32 ], could subsequently convert localization into an estimate of antigen burden within each compartment. Clinical correlation would require complementary study designs. For efficacy, pretreatment tumor blocks from patients subsequently treated with a defined ADC could be scored separately for tumor-cell and microenvironmental target protein expression and related to objective response and progression-free survival. Assessment of toxicity would require additional evidence from relevant normal tissues and organ-specific adverse events in ADC-treated cohorts, because protein expression within the tumor microenvironment alone cannot establish on-target/off-tumor toxicity. Only outcome-linked studies of this kind can determine whether compartment-specific expression patterns such as those reported here for B7-H3 and PSMA have measurable clinical consequences. The spatial framework may also be relevant beyond ADCs. Nanoparticle and other tumor-directed delivery systems are influenced by vascular permeability, stromal barriers, and the organization of the tumor microenvironment [ 14 , 15 ]. Although these mechanisms differ from antigen-dependent ADC targeting, they reinforce the broader value of resolving delivery-relevant compartments within intact tissue. Until protein-level and outcome-linked data become available, however, the present findings should be interpreted as a hypothesis-generating guide to where such validation should be directed, not as evidence of ADC efficacy or safety. Limitations The whole-transcriptome discovery analysis is based on one tumor. HER2 and TROP2 were examined in two additional public Xenium specimens, but only one was clearly documented as a different patient. B7-H3 and PSMA were not present in the targeted validation panel. Their low-abundance stromal and vascular patterns, therefore, require confirmation in larger, patient-level cohorts across breast cancer subtypes. Cell annotations were marker-based rather than reviewed against matched histopathology. Differential expression tests also treated cells from a single specimen as independent units, which can inflate statistical confidence. Effect sizes and marker identity are more informative here than nominal cell-level P values. Public metadata did not consistently provide specimen-level sex and gender information, and these variables were not analyzed. Whole-transcriptome imaging was sparse for individual genes, limiting per-cell quantification. The bulk and survival analyses were based on a single cohort, and no signal of survival remained after adjustment. Most importantly, every target measurement was messenger RNA. ADC binding depends on the availability of an accessible cell-surface protein, whose RNA abundance cannot be measured directly. We did not assess protein localization, internalization, drug response, or toxicity. The findings are therefore descriptive and hypothesis-generating. Conclusion Single-cell spatial transcriptomics separated ADC targets enriched in tumor epithelium from targets expressed in stromal and vascular cells. HER2 and TROP2 showed the most consistent tumor enrichment across the three profiled specimens, whereas EGFR did not. These RNA-level findings should inform the design of protein-level, multi-patient validation studies. They cannot substitute for direct measurement of surface antigen or ADC activity. Compartment-resolved protein confirmation, followed by correlation with ADC response and toxicity in treated cohorts, is the necessary next step before any of these observations is applied clinically. Ethics approval and informed consent This study used only publicly available, de-identified datasets and involved no direct participant contact or new data collection. Ethical approval and informed-consent procedures for the source studies were reported in the original dataset publications. No additional ethics approval or informed consent was required for this secondary analysis. Protocol for integrated multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling using Xenium and MACSima. Combining same-section spatial transcriptomics with high-plex protein imaging enables comprehensive characterization of the tissue microenvironment while preserving spatial information. Here, we present a protocol for multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling using Xenium transcriptomics and MACSima cyclic protein imaging. We describe steps for tissue preparation, hybridization, and RNA imaging, followed by slide recovery, antigen retrieval, and MACSima imaging cyclic staining (MICS). We provide Python scripts for data registration and integration to generate a single-cell multimodal map of the tissue microenvironment. Graphical abstract                     Highlights    •  Multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling on a single tissue section    •  Detailed Xenium and MACSima workflow protocol for single-section spatial multi-omics    •  Registration and integration of transcriptomic and proteomic data at single-cell level      Publisher’s note: Undertaking any experimental protocol requires adherence to local institutional guidelines for laboratory safety and ethics.    Combining same-section spatial transcriptomics with high-plex protein imaging enables comprehensive characterization of the tissue microenvironment while preserving spatial information. Here, we present a protocol for multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling using Xenium transcriptomics and MACSima cyclic protein imaging. We describe steps for tissue preparation, hybridization, and RNA imaging, followed by slide recovery, antigen retrieval, and MACSima imaging cyclic staining (MICS). We provide Python scripts for data registration and integration to generate a single-cell multimodal map of the tissue microenvironment.     status  released    display-pdf  yes    is-olf  no    is-manuscript  no    is-preprint  no    is-journal-matter  no    is-scanned  no    is-retracted  no       Collection date 2026 Dec 18.       Before you begin   Protocol overview  This protocol describes multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling on the same tissue section using Xenium (10x Genomics) and MACSima Imaging Cyclic Staining (MICS, Miltenyi Biotec). The workflow was established using human tonsil and tumor tissue sections; however, it can be adapted to other tissue types with appropriate optimization of RNA probe panels, antibody panels, and tissue processing conditions.    Innovation  This protocol introduces a novel workflow for multimodal spatial profiling by integrating Xenium spatial transcriptomics with highly multiplexed protein imaging using MICS on the same formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue microarray (TMA) section. Alternative multimodal workflows have demonstrated the combination of Xenium with other hyperplex protein imaging platforms, including PhenoCycler and COMET.  1   ,   2   Building upon these advances, this protocol provides the first detailed experimental and computational workflow for integrating Xenium with the current-generation MACSima platform, which supports significantly higher antibody plexity than comparable technologies. This workflow for sequential Xenium and MACSima analysis includes optimized requirements and procedures for sample processing, antigen retrieval, and iterative cyclic immunofluorescence that preserve tissue integrity and enable single-cell RNA and protein measurements on the same section. In addition to the experimental workflow, this protocol provides scripts for accurate registration of Xenium and MACSima imaging data, enabling direct correlation of transcriptomic and proteomic features within the same spatial framework. Importantly, both the laboratory workflow and computational approach can be adapted to other spatial multi-omics combinations, offering a flexible framework for integrating transcriptomic and proteomic data. Together, these advances address key technical challenges in spatial multi-omics and provide a reproducible and scalable approach for multimodal tissue analysis.    Institutional permissions  Experiments involving human-derived tissues require approval from the appropriate institutional ethics committee. Researchers must ensure that ethical approval is obtained and that informed consent is secured from all donors prior to sample collection. All specimens used in this study (see  key resources table ) were obtained with informed consent and handled in accordance with institutional regulations and approved protocols.    Tissue selection and preparation 
   1.  Obtain FFPE TMA samples with preserved morphology and RNA integrity.   
          CRITICAL:  Following proper handling, storage, preparation and sectioning of the FFPE tissues according to the demonstrated protocol  Xenium In Situ for FFPE – Tissue Preparation Handbook  (10x Genomics,  CG000578 ) is critical to ensure preservation of morphology and RNA integrity.  
   2.  Optimize sectioning conditions, such as rehydration time for the block and floating time of the sections in the water bath of the Section Transfer System (STS) before mounting on slides to prevent cutting artefacts.    3.  Assess tissue quality, morphology and RNA integrity of the blocks prior to mounting on Xenium slides by performing DAPI staining, H&E staining, and/or DV200 analysis.    4.  Place sections on Xenium slides and store them according to standard protocol (10× Genomics,  CG000578 ).   a.  If the tissue blocks are of optimal quality, section them at 4–6 μm thickness using a microtome and mount the sections on Xenium slides.    b.  Dry the slides appropriately as per standard protocol (10x Genomics,  CG000578 ).      
          Pause point:  Slides can be stored at room temperature (RT, 20°C–25°C) or at 4°C in tubes with desiccant sachets for up to 4 weeks prior to deparaffinization and Xenium workflow.  
   Xenium assay version compatibility 
    Note:   The workflow for sequential Xenium and MACSima is compatible with the v1 as well as the 5K Prime Xenium assay versions. It is also compatible with the Xenium In situ Multimodal Cell Segmentation which has now become standard in the Xenium workflows. Since the MACSima workflow uses directly conjugated antibodies, the antibodies in the Xenium multimodal cell segmentation kit do not pose a risk of cross-detection (10x Genomics,  CG000750 ).  
   Xenium probe panel design 
   5.  Select a pre-designed Xenium probe panel and/or design a custom Xenium probe panel (to be used as a standalone panel or as an add-on to the pre-designed panel) targeting genes of interest relevant to the biological question.    6.  Validate the custom probe panel performance in control samples, if available.   
    Note:   Perform add-on panel design in line with the guidelines provided in the  Technical Note: Xenium Add-on Panel Design  (10x Genomics,  CG000643 ). Transcript abundance and cell type specificity should be taken into consideration when designing a panel.  
    Note:   Reference to existing single-cell RNA-seq data, ideally from matched sample types, can guide panel design by enabling identification of cell type specific genes and transcript abundance.  
    Note:   The custom probe panel performance can be cross-validated post-Xenium run by comparing with existing single-cell RNA-seq and / or Xenium datasets for sensitivity in terms of number of transcripts detected and for specificity in terms of biologically relevant co-expression patterns of different genes.  3    
   Antibody panel design for MACSima 
   7.  Select antibodies targeting proteins of interest for multiplex imaging and check for compatibility of antibodies with the respective sample type (FFPE).    8.  Optimize antibody concentrations and staining conditions in a mock Xenium-MACSima experiment using control samples, if available, to test the compatibility of sequential Xenium and MACSima staining (see  problem 2  in  troubleshooting ).   
          CRITICAL:  Antibodies must be tested for compatibility within the Xenium-MACSima workflow (see  problem 2  in  troubleshooting ).  
          CRITICAL:  Ensure that tissue processing conditions, such as working in an RNase-free environment, sectioning thickness, and optimal slide recovery and antigen retrieval conditions post-Xenium are compatible with both Xenium RNA detection and downstream protein staining.  
          CRITICAL:  Check for tissue integrity after post-Xenium imaging slide recovery (steps 12 and 13 in the  step-by-step method details ) before continuing with the protein staining.  
          CRITICAL:  Optimize post-Xenium antigen retrieval conditions to achieve sufficient epitope accessibility for protein staining while preserving tissue integrity. Harsh antigen retrieval conditions can compromise tissue integrity and spatial registration between modalities.  
   Instrument and software preparation 
   9.  Prepare the Xenium Analyzer instrument and required reagents according to manufacturer guidelines (10x Genomics,  CG000584 ).    10.  Prepare the MACSima imaging system for cyclic staining and imaging. Install the MACS iQ View software on a data-analysis workstation.    11.  Install the scripts for the registration workflow, including required software dependencies ( Table 1 ).   a.  Clone the repository.  >git clone https://github.com/scOpenLab/MACSimaXenium.git    b.  Create the venv environment.  >python3 -m venv macsima_xenium    c.  Activate the venv environment.  >source macsima_xenium/bin/activate    d.  Install the Python package for the Xenium-MACSima analysis workflow from its repository in GitHub.  >pip install ./MACSimaXenium/    Note:   Ensure sufficient data storage and computational resources for handling large imaging datasets (see requirements listed in  materials and equipment ).        
   Table 1   Packages and resources required for data processing      Package or Resource  Version  IDENTIFIER  Reference      Python  ≥3.11   https://www.python.org/  RRID: SCR_008394  Programming language  Python Software Foundation    xenium_macsima_core_registration  1.0.0   https://github.com/scOpenLab/MACSimaXenium/   This protocol    harpy-analysis  ≥0.4.2   https://github.com/saeyslab/harpy   Rombaut et al.  4      Bioio  ≥3.3.0   https://github.com/bioio-devs/bioio   Brown et al.  5      bioio-ome-tiff  ≥1.4.0   https://github.com/bioio-devs/bioio-ome-tiff   Brown et al.  5      opencv-python-headless  ≥4.13.0.92   https://github.com/opencv/opencv-python   Alekhin et al.  6          Upstream data preparation (prerequisites)  The registration workflow in this protocol assumes that single-cell data and Xenium-MACSima region of interest (ROI) correspondences have been established beforehand. The following upstream processing steps are performed once per slide before the per-core registration loop and are summarized here for context. The code for these steps is experiment-specific and is not included in the shared repository; however, the analysis workflow follows standard practices using scanpy  7   and the Segment Anything Model (SAM).  8      12.  Build AnnData  9   feature matrix.   a.  Load each Xenium output folder by reading the transcript table (transcripts.parquet).    b.  Filter for quality value (QV) ≥ 20, remove control probes, and aggregate transcript counts per nucleus using nucleus boundary polygons (nucleus_boundaries.parquet).    c.  Store the resulting count matrix, centroid coordinates, and nucleus areas as an AnnData object.       13.  Segment TMA cores.   a.  Identify individual TMA cores using the Segment Anything Model (SAM1, ViT-H) applied to a 2D cell density histogram (binned centroids at approximately 50 μm per pixel). Each detected mask corresponds to one TMA core.    b.  Assign a position label to each cell according to which mask their centroid falls within and flag cells outside all masks with is_in_core = False.       14.  Perform quality filtering.   a.  Remove cells that are not assigned to a core and filter the remaining cells according to transcript counts and/or size.          Note:   A commonly used approach for cell-level quality filtering is to exclude cells with fewer than ten transcripts and genes expressed in less than five cells ( https://squidpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/notebooks/tutorials/tutorial_xenium.html ).  10   However, transcript counts per cell are dependent both on the tissue and gene panel  11   and thus the use of more or less stringent thresholds taking into account also the area of the cell might be required.  12   Finally, a visual inspection of the spatial distribution of the excluded cells can help to identify biases in the filtering by highlighting the presence of spatially organized clusters of excluded cells.  11       15.  Match the TMA cores between Xenium and MACSima data.   a.  Match the Xenium TMA core positions and MACSima ROI numbers manually by comparing a spatial scatter plot of Xenium cell positions (colored by core position) with the MACSima ROI overview image.    b.  Write this mapping as a CSV file with one column named “xenium” and the other named “macsima”.         Planning of multimodal data integration  This protocol describes the cross-modal alignment of Xenium spatial transcriptomics data (10x Genomics) with MACSima multiplexed cyclic immunofluorescence imaging data (Miltenyi Biotec) for TMA samples. Integration is performed per TMA core and produces multi-modal SpatialData  13   objects saved as Zarr  14   archives.           CRITICAL:  Accurate image registration is essential for reliable analysis of RNA and protein data at single-cell resolution.     Data requirements 
   16.  Provide Xenium and MACSima data sets, along with mappings that link Xenium cells to TMA cores and Xenium TMA cores to MACSima ROIs ( Table 2 ).   
          CRITICAL:  Maintain consistent orientation and handling of tissue sections and ROIs throughout the workflow.  
   Table 2   Input files for the Xenium and MACSima registration workflow      Files  Explanation      Xenium folder  Xenium output folder produced by the Xenium Onboard Analysis pipeline.  15      Annotated H5AD  AnnData Object  9   containing Xenium TMA core membership (position column) and MACSima slide_name identifier (e.g., TMAN02-1-1) for each Xenium cell.    MACSima folder  Path to the preprocessed MACSima folder generated after stitching and background subtraction with the MACS iQ View software.  16      Xenium-MACSima ROI matching CSV file  The Xenium TMA core positions and MACSima ROI numbers are mapped in a CSV file with one column named “xenium” and the other named “macsima”.     Step-by-step method details 
    Note:   The protocol was optimized for the Xenium Prime 5K workflow with Cell Segmentation Staining, using a Prime 5K Human pan Tissue and Pathways panel (10x Genomics, PN-1000724) and a custom 100-gene add-on panel. For alternative Xenium workflow formats, workflow parameters may require adaptation. Xenium processing should always be performed according to the corresponding manufacturer-recommended protocols. In addition, performance of downstream antibody staining following Xenium processing may vary depending on the selected Xenium assay configuration.  
  Preparation of FFPE TMA sections 
          Timing: 3 days when performing steps consecutively. Approximately 1.5 days are required for sectioning optimization, slide mounting, drying, and quality assessment. Another day is required for sectioning, mounting to Xenium slides, and drying. Half a day is required for deparaffinization, rehydration, and decrosslinking of sections.   
 This step describes the preparation of FFPE TMA samples for the Xenium Prime 5K workflow, including sectioning of the FFPE blocks, tissue mounting, deparaffinization, and decrosslinking of sections. Sample preparation is performed according to the demonstrated protocol  Xenium In Situ for FFPE – Tissue Preparation Handbook  (10× Genomics,  CG000578 ).           CRITICAL:  Sectioning conditions, such as rehydration time of the FFPE TMA block in ice-cold water, should be optimized depending on tissue type, degree of dehydration, and the age of the paraffin block. Similarly, the floating time of sections in the water bath prior to mounting on Xenium slides needs to be adjusted to prevent wrinkling, folding, or tearing of the sections.     1.  Assess tissue quality and RNA integrity.    Note:   Evaluate tissue quality and RNA integrity of the FFPE TMA samples prior to placement of sections onto Xenium slides by performing DAPI staining, H&E staining, and/or DV200 analysis.     a.  Mount serial sections on SuperFrost Plus slides and deparaffinize according to the standard protocol (10x Genomics,  CG000578 ).    b.  Perform DAPI and H&E staining as outlined in the demonstrated protocol (10x Genomics,  CG000578 , Appendix).    c.  Image the slide to assess nuclear integrity, tissue morphology, sectioning artefacts, and the presence of necrotic or degraded regions.    d.  For RNA quality assessment, collect approximately four 10 μm sections (for samples ≤ 6.5 × 6.5 mm) for RNA extraction and DV200 analysis.          CRITICAL:  Samples with DV200 values below 30 % are considered suboptimal and may result in reduced median transcript counts per cell in downstream Xenium analysis.         2.  Section the FFPE TMA block and dry the sections.          CRITICAL:  During sectioning, maintain RNase-free conditions by wiping the microtome with RNase Zap ™ solution and filling the water bath of the STS with nuclease-free water.     a.  Prepare the FFPE TMA block for sectioning by rehydrating it in ice-cold Milli-Q water for a previously optimized duration (typically 10–30 min, depending on tissue type and degree of dehydration).    b.  Trim the block until the area of interest is fully exposed. For previously sectioned TMA blocks, discard the first 5–10 sections to obtain uniformly hydrated and intact tissue sections prior to collection.    c.  Section FFPE TMA block at a thickness of 5 μm using a microtome. Let the sections slide via the STS into its water bath filled with nuclease-free water and maintained at 42°C–45°C.    d.  Incubate the sections in the water bath for a previously optimized duration (typically 10 s to 3 min for most FFPE tissues) to allow the section to fully flatten and to minimize wrinkles, folds, or tearing prior to mounting.          CRITICAL:  Excessive incubation times in the water bath may lead to tissue distortion or reduced adherence during downstream processing.      e.  From the water bath, mount the sections carefully onto the Xenium slides (10× Genomics, PN-1000465), within the designated sample area.          CRITICAL:  Avoid placing the sections covering the fiducials, specifically the top and bottom fiducials.            CRITICAL:  Monitor the section adhesion on Xenium slides throughout the workflow to ensure that sections remain intact and properly attached during all processing steps.      f.  Following section placement, incubate the slides at 42°C for 3 h to promote adhesion of the sections to the Xenium slide surface.    g.  After incubation, place the slides in 50 mL Falcon tubes containing desiccant and store them overnight (16–24 h) at RT (20°C–25°C) to allow complete drying of the tissue sections.          Pause point:  Following section mounting, Xenium slides can be stored at RT (20°C–25°C) or at 4°C in the presence of desiccant sachets for up to 4 weeks prior to deparaffinization and further processing with the Xenium workflow.         3.  Perform deparaffinization, rehydration, and decrosslinking of the sections.   a.  Incubate the slides at 60°C for 2 h, followed by cooling at RT (20°C–25°C) for 7 min prior to further processing.    b.  Sequentially incubate the slides in two Coplin jars containing xylene for 10 min each.    c.  Perform two washes in 100 % ethanol for 3 min each.    d.  Perform two washes in 96 % ethanol for 3 min each.    e.  Perform one wash in 70 % ethanol for 3 min.    f.  Perform a final rinse in nuclease-free water for 20 s.    Note:   Xylene and ethanol incubation steps should be performed in a fume hood.      g.  Assemble the slides into Xenium cassettes.    h.  Perform decrosslinking using the  Xenium Prime Sample Preparation Reagents  (10x Genomics, PN-1000720) (included in the  Xenium Prime Sample Preparation with Cell Segmentation with Slides  kit, 10x Genomics, PN-1000742).    i.  Immediately proceed with the Xenium in situ gene expression workflow.         Probe hybridization for Xenium Prime  in situ  gene expression

Day 2 comprises post-hybridization washes, ligation, amplification, and cell segmentation staining. Day 3 includes post-staining washes, autofluorescence quenching, and nuclear staining. Without cell segmentation staining, the workflow spans 2 days: day 1 includes priming and probe hybridization.  This section describes the preparation of deparaffinized and decrosslinked FFPE TMA sections for the Xenium workflow, enabling subsequent imaging and analysis using the Xenium Analyzer. The entire workflow is performed according to the  Xenium Prime In Situ Gene Expression with optional Cell Segmentation  user guide (10x Genomics,  CG000760 ) using the  Xenium Prime Sample Preparation with Cell Segmentation with Slides  reagents (10× Genomics, PN-1000742).    4.  Perform priming and probe hybridization.   a.  Hybridize priming oligos to decrosslinked RNA.    b.  Perform RNase treatment and a polishing reaction to release the RNA strand from the hybridized oligos, thereby enabling subsequent hybridization of Xenium probes to the target RNA (10× Genomics,  CG000760 ).    c.  Perform hybridization overnight (16–24 h) at 50°C in a thermocycler (Bio-Rad, C1000) using the Xenium Prime 5K probes ( Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue and Pathways Assay  kit, 10× Genomics, PN-1000671) together with an optional custom human add-on panel comprising up to 100 additional genes.       5.  Perform post-hybridization washes, ligation, and amplification.   a.  Perform post-hybridization washes to remove unbound probes, followed by ligation of hybridized probes, and enzymatic rolling circle amplification to generate amplified signal products for downstream imaging.       6.  Perform optional multimodal cell segmentation staining.   a.  To facilitate morphology-based cell segmentation, perform overnight (16–24 h) staining using the Xenium cell segmentation staining reagents, which label nuclei, cell boundaries, and intracellular RNA-rich regions according to the manufacturer’s instructions (10× Genomics,  CG000760 ).       7.  Perform autofluorescence quenching and nuclear staining.   a.  After amplification (and optional cell segmentation staining), perform autofluorescence quenching, brief drying at 37°C for 5 min and subsequent nuclear staining according to the manufacturer’s instructions.    b.  Upon completion of the workflow, store the slides in 0.05 % PBST until imaging and analysis using the Xenium Analyzer.                Pause point:  After completion of the Xenium sample preparation workflow and prior to loading onto the Xenium Analyzer, slides can be stored in 0.05 % PBST at 4°C in the dark for up to 1 week using a new Xenium cassette lid.      Note:   During the drying step following autofluorescence quenching, inspect the slides to ensure that the Xenium slide fiducials, particularly the top and bottom fiducials, remain free of tissue coverage. If fiducials are obstructed, carefully remove the tissue from these regions at the end of sample preparation, as covered fiducials may interfere with subsequent imaging and alignment on the Xenium Analyzer.      Note:   At the end of sample preparation, clean the underside of the Xenium slides using 70 % ethanol and lint-free wipes to remove residues and prevent fibers or debris from interfering with subsequent imaging.     Xenium  in situ  gene expression imaging 
          Timing: 2.5–5 days; half a day is needed for hands-on preparation, including buffer preparation and setup of the Xenium Analyzer. An additional 2–5 days are required for instrument run time, depending on the Xenium assay version (e.g., Xenium v.1, Xenium Prime 5K), whether cell segmentation staining is performed, and the size and number of ROIs.

CRITICAL:  In cases where a custom panel (add-on or standalone) is used, obtain the corresponding JSON file for the panel and upload it to the Xenium Analyzer prior to initiating the run.            CRITICAL:  Slides processed using different Xenium workflows cannot be run simultaneously in the same instrument run. However, slides processed with different probe panels within the same workflow can be run together during a single instrument run.      Note:   For the Xenium Prime workflow, ensure that the Xenium Analyzer software version is XA v3.0 or higher.     8.  Prepare buffers and set up the Xenium Analyzer.   a.  Prepare all required buffers and decoding reagents and set up the Xenium Analyzer for processing of slides generated using the Xenium workflow according to the  Xenium Analyzer User Guide  (10× Genomics,  CG000584 ). Use the  Xenium Prime 5K Decoding Reagents  (10× Genomics, PN-1000740),  Xenium Decoding Consumables v2  (10× Genomics, PN-1000726), and  Xenium Reagent Bottles  (10× Genomics, PN-1000730).          Note:   Transfer the  Xenium Prime Decoding Reagent Module B  (sealed in the mylar bag) from −20°C to 4°C at least one day before the run and allow it to thaw at 4°C for 16–72 h.      Note:   Prepare the Xenium Probe Removal buffer in a fume hood due to the hazardous nature of DMSO.     9.  Define ROIs.   a.  Following the overview scan, define one or more ROIs consisting of fields of view (FOVs) that encompass the tissue of interest while excluding blank areas, and initiate the run.          Note:   Up to eight ROIs can be defined per slide.      Note:   For TMAs, define a single ROI encompassing all FOVs containing TMA cores and excluding blank FOVs.     10.  Clean the instrument and store slides.   a.  After completion of the run, clean the instrument according to the standard protocol (10× Genomics,  CG000584 ).    b.  Replace the buffer on the slides with 1 mL 0.05 % PBST and store the slides at 4°C until further processing.       11.  Store and prepare post-Xenium slides for transport.   a.  Fill two 50 mL Falcon tubes with 0.05 % PBST up to the brim.    b.  Remove the Xenium slides from the Xenium cassettes and place each of them in a 50 mL Falcon tube filled with 0.05 % PBST. Ensure that the slides are completely submerged.    c.  Seal the lid of the Falcon tube with parafilm.    d.  Transport them at 4°C on cool packs.          Note:   For long term storage, transfer the slides into a 50 mL Falcon tube and replace the 0.05 % PBST weekly to prevent contamination or sample drying.      Note:   Alternatively, slides may be stored or transported in 50 mL Falcon tubes containing MACSima Running Buffer. In this case, exchange the buffer every four weeks.            Pause point:  Slides can be stored in MACSima Running Buffer at 4°C. In our experience, slides stored for up to nine months still yielded MACSima data meeting established QC criteria; longer storage periods have not been systematically evaluated.  This step describes the preparation of FFPE TMA sections for MICS after the Xenium run and includes quencher removal, antigen retrieval, DAPI pre-staining, and dust particle removal. Following Xenium imaging, perform quencher removal as recommended in  Xenium In Situ Gene Expression – Post-Xenium Analyzer H&E Staining  (10x Genomics,  CG000613 ) to reduce residual Xenium-associated background signals and improve compatibility with downstream cyclic immunofluorescence imaging using MACSima.    12.  Remove the quencher (see  problem 1  in  troubleshooting ).   a.  In a fume hood, prepare quencher removal solution by weighing 17.4 mg sodium hydrosulfite and transfer it to a conical tube containing 10 mL Milli-Q water.    b.  Cap the tube tightly and vortex for 10 s until the reagent is fully dissolved.    c.  Keep the solution at RT (20°C–25°C) until use.          CRITICAL:  Prepare quencher removal solution immediately before each use to ensure optimal performance, as its effectiveness decreases after 10 min.      Note:   Because sodium hydrosulfite is hazardous, prepare the solution in a fume hood.      Note:   Vortexing may be performed outside the fume hood if the tube is tightly capped.      Note:   Do not use alternative chemicals for quencher removal.      d.  Add 10 mL quencher removal solution into the slide mailer.    e.  Prepare three slide mailers with 10 mL Milli-Q water each.    f.  Gently immerse Xenium slide into the slide mailer with quencher removal solution and incubate for 10 min at RT (20°C–25°C).    g.  Immerse slide in each Milli-Q water containing slide mailer for 1 min, then move to the next one.    h.  Transfer the Xenium slide into a 50 mL Falcon tube filled with MACSima Running buffer until further use.    Note:   Alternatively, transfer Xenium slide into a MACSwell One Small imaging frame ( Figure 1 A, right) and add 1.5 mL quencher removal solution. After 10 min incubation at RT (20°C–25°C), wash slide with 1.5 mL Milli-Q water three times, waiting for 1 min each time.      Note:   Residual purple staining after Xenium processing indicates the presence of autofluorescence quencher and should disappear following successful quencher removal ( Figure 1 B).         13.  Perform heat-induced epitope retrieval (HIER).   a.  Prepare the 10× stock solution of TEC antigen retrieval buffer at pH 9.0.    Note:   The 10x stock solution can be stored at 4°C for up to 3 months.      b.  Immediately before use, dilute the 10x stock to 1x working solution.    c.  Adjust the pH to 9.0.    d.  Preheat the 1× working solution to 95°C in a pressure cooker.    e.  Place the Xenium slide in a slide mailer and immerse it in the preheated TEC buffer. Incubate for 20 min at 95°C.          CRITICAL:  Ensure the slide is fully submerged and does not touch the pressure cooker container.            CRITICAL:  Avoid using open-bottom slide mailers, as air bubbles could directly contact the tissue section and cause partial lifting or detachment from the slide surface.      Note:   Depending on the antibody panel, alternative antigen retrieval buffers may be required (see  problem 2  in  troubleshooting ).      f.  After incubation, remove the pressure cooker container and transfer it to a pre-cooled water bath (ice-cold) for cooling.    g.  When the buffer has reached RT (20°C–25°C), carefully remove the slide from the buffer.    h.  Dry the edges with a lint-free wipe to remove excess liquid.    i.  Mount the slide onto a MACSwell One Small imaging frame.    Note:   The MACSwell One Small imaging frame accommodates the Xenium imaging area optimally and enables complete coverage of the imaged region ( Figure 1 A).      j.  Add 550 μL MACSima Running Buffer.       14.  Pre-stain the sample with DAPI and remove dust particles.   a.  Incubate the Xenium slide with DAPI staining solution at a 1:5 dilution using MACSima Running Buffer (final concentration 1 μg/mL) in the dark for 10 min at RT (20°C–25°C).          CRITICAL:  Protect the slide from light during DAPI incubation to prevent photobleaching.      Note:   Ensure the staining solution fully covers the section.      b.  Wash the slides three times with 550 μL MACSima Running Buffer to remove excess dye.    c.  Check the TMA section under bright transmitted light to ensure there are no dust particles or debris in the experimental area.    d.  Remove any visible dust or debris, as these can interfere with imaging quality.    e.  Cover the slide with a final experimental volume of 550 μL MACSima Running Buffer and seal with pierceable aluminum foil.    Note:   Clean the underside of the Xenium slides using 2-propanol and lint-free wipes to remove residues and prevent fibers or debris from interfering with subsequent imaging.            Pause point:  Store slides in running buffer at 4°C for ≤1 week.  This section describes staining of FFPE TMA sections using fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies and automated cyclic imaging using the MACSima platform.  2   ,   12   The workflow enables high-dimensional spatial characterization of protein expression following Xenium imaging and includes experimental setup, reagent and procedure configuration, reagent preparation, ROI selection, autofocus definition on each ROI and automated cyclic image acquisition. Basic information of the control software is based on the  MACS® iQ View Software Control Module 1.0 User manual  (Miltenyi Biotec).    15.  Register the sample and configure the sample setup.   a.  Open the Sample Setup tab and create a new sample entry.    b.  Enter all required metadata for each sample, including sample type, species, and fixation method. Additional experimental information is recommended where available.    c.  Assign samples to the appropriate imaging wells according to the selected MACSwell imaging frame configuration.          Optional:   Create duplicate sample entries or sample groups for organizational purposes.      Note:   Sample groups are intended for organization only and do not affect imaging or analysis settings.      Optional:   For multiple tissue sections located within the same well (e.g., TMAs), samples can be defined as a complex sample.     16.  Configure the sample and reagent rack.   a.  Generate a new rack configuration within the Sample Setup tab.    b.  Select the appropriate rack type corresponding to the MACSwell imaging frame and reagent plate format used in the experiment.    c.  Assign the sample to the correct well position within the rack layout by dragging it to the correct well.          Note:   Not every well requires a sample assignment.     17.  Register antibodies and define the reagent panel.   a.  Under the Reagent Definition tab, register pre-validated Miltenyi Biotec antibodies using the integrated reagent registration system or manually enter reagent information.    Note:   Pre-validation data for the antibodies is provided to confirm compatibility with acetone-, PFA-fixed, or FFPE tissues; however, they have not been tested for compatibility after Xenium.      b.  Add non-Miltenyi antibodies by specifying antibody type, species reactivity, antigen target, fixation compatibility, and fluorochrome assignment.    c.  Create reagent panels by combining antibodies from the reagent inventory into predefined staining panels.    d.  Review fluorochrome assignments and reagent compatibility prior to experiment setup.          CRITICAL:  Use fluorochromes compatible with cyclic imaging workflows (e.g., FITC, PE, APC) and directly conjugated primary antibodies to avoid issues when using the Xenium multimodal cell segmentation kit.            CRITICAL:  Include DAPI staining in regular intervals (e.g., every 3–4 imaging cycles) to facilitate reliable image registration and alignment across staining cycles for the MACSima images.      Note:   Evaluate antibody compatibility, for example by performing a mock Xenium experiment followed by a MACSima run (see  problem 2  in  troubleshooting ). A representative example of antibody panel validation and resulting multiplex protein staining on human tonsil tissue is shown in  Figure 2 , illustrating the expected staining quality and marker performance achievable with this workflow.      Note:   Antibody compatibility should be assessed based on specificity, signal-to-background ratio, reproducibility, and preservation of the expected staining pattern after Xenium processing. Compatible antibodies show the expected cellular and subcellular localization, clear separation of positive signals from background, and staining consistent with previous MACSima or immunohistochemistry validation and reference databases (see  problem 2  in  troubleshooting ). Representative examples of antibodies that fulfilled ( Figures 3 C–3E, 3G, and 3H) or failed to meet ( Figures 3 B and 3F) these criteria are shown in  Figure 3 .      Note:   Selected examples of antibody performance for the panel used in this study, following the Xenium Prime 5K workflow with an additional custom panel of 100 transcripts, are shown in  Figure 4 . Antibody compatibility and staining quality may vary depending on tissue type, Xenium assay design, and experimental conditions and should therefore be validated for each application.      Alternatives:   While pre-validated multiplex panels help streamline optimization, their compatibility with the Xenium-MACSima workflow must be confirmed experimentally.         18.  Set up the cyclic imaging procedure.   a.  Open the Procedure Creation tab and create a new procedure from an existing template or generate a new procedure.    b.  Add reagent panels and/or individual antibodies to the procedure.    c.  Adjust staining and imaging parameters as needed, including dilution factor, incubation time, exposure settings, bleaching conditions, and wash parameters.    d.  Recalculate imaging cycles after all reagents and parameters have been defined or assign the antibodies to the individual cycles manually.    Note:   When manually assigning antibodies to imaging cycles, consider the following guidelines:     i.  Avoid placing multiple markers targeting the same cell type in the same cycle.    ii.  Preferably place low-abundance, transiently expressed, activation-dependent markers, cytokines, and chemokines in earlier cycles, as their detection can be more challenging.    iii.  Place abundant, constitutively expressed, or structural proteins in later cycles, as they provide more robust signals.    iv.  Evaluate receptors and ligands individually based on antigen abundance, subcellular localization, and expected staining performance.    v.  Avoid FITC for broadly expressed or critical phenotyping markers because of its relatively low photostability and potential signal loss during image acquisition.    vi.  For alternative fluorochromes (e.g., Alexa Fluor dyes), empirically determine the bleaching intensity required for efficient signal removal or perform at least two bleaching cycles before staining with the subsequent conjugated antibody in that channel.    vii.  Avoid combining strongly expressed FITC signals with weak PE signals in the same cycle to minimize spectral overlap and signal interference.          CRITICAL:  Validate any modifications to exposure times, bleaching settings, or wash parameters empirically prior to large-scale experiments.            19.  Create and configure the experiment.   a.  In the Experiment Planning tab, create a new experiment.    Note:   When duplicating an experiment, ROIs from earlier runs can be reloaded and reused.      b.  Enter experiment metadata and assign the corresponding sample racks.    c.  Assign cyclic staining procedures to all occupied wells containing sections.    Optional:   Define the expected number and size of ROIs to obtain runtime and dataset size estimates.      d.  Export the pipetting scheme for antibody preparation and documentation purposes from the Reagent rack Info tab.       20.  Prepare the antibody plate.   a.  Dispense antibodies into a compatible deepwell reagent plate, distributing them into the designated wells according to the generated pipetting scheme.    Note:   Briefly centrifuge antibody tubes prior to pipetting and aspirate antibodies carefully from the top of the solution to avoid transferring antibody aggregates or clumps.      b.  Cover the prepared reagent plate with adhesive, pierceable aluminum foil to protect fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies from light exposure.       21.  Load the instrument and initiate the experiment.   a.  In the Experiment Planning tab, initiate the experiment by clicking the Run button or by right-clicking the experiment and selecting Run Experiment.    b.  Scan or manually register the reagent racks.    c.  Load sample racks onto the imaging stage according to the software instructions. Insert the MACSwell with the frosted labeling area of the slide facing the front of the device.    d.  Load the reagent rack into the instrument.    Optional:   During reagent loading, include the MACSima Stain Support Kit (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-127-574) when using REAlease® antibodies or predefined commercial antibody panels according to the manufacturer’s recommendations.      e.  Verify waste bottle status and ensure sufficient storage solution, running buffer, and system buffer volumes prior to starting the experiment.    f.  Start the experiment and allow the system to perform the preview scan.          CRITICAL:  Monitor buffer levels and waste bottle capacity daily during long imaging runs to avoid interruptions.         22.  Define ROIs and autofocus settings (see  problem 3  in  troubleshooting ).   a.  Define ROIs and autofocus settings following completion of the preview scan.    b.  Inspect the preview image and adjust brightness, contrast, and gamma settings as needed.    c.  Define ROIs using polygon, rectangle, or circular selection tools.    d.  Ensure ROIs encompass all regions to be analyzed while excluding empty imaging areas.          CRITICAL:  Avoid selecting large empty imaging areas within the ROIs, as image stitching and alignment rely on sufficient DAPI signal across the imaged region.      Note:   Large ROIs may be more prone to autofocus instability. Inspection of autofocus profiles and acquired images is recommended before proceeding with downstream analysis ( Figure 5 ).      e.  Configure autofocus settings for each ROI and refine parameters where necessary.   i.  Set the autofocus parameters, including Method, Exposure Time, Offset Range, and Z-Offset, to ensure optimal focus adjustment for each ROI.       f.  Accept autofocus settings and continue the experiment.    Note:   For TMAs, define a single ROI for each core and exclude blank regions.      Note:   Imaging duration depends on the antibody panel size and the number and size of selected ROIs. Long imaging experiments may require several days to complete.            CRITICAL:  Accurate ROI definition and autofocus settings are essential for optimal image quality across all imaging cycles.         23.  Complete the experiment and retrieve data.   a.  After completion of the imaging run, unload the instrument and retrieve the imaging data.    b.  Remove sample and reagent racks according to the software-guided unloading procedure.          CRITICAL:  Create a backup of raw and processed imaging data prior to deleting experiments from the instrument workstation.      c.  Continue downstream image analysis using MACS iQ View on external computational systems.       24.  Preprocess the data.   a.  Perform data preprocessing using the MACS iQ View’s Preprocessing Pipeline, selecting the appropriate processing settings.  16   ,   18     i.  Load the “RawData” folder into the “Preprocessing” tool in MACS iQ View by selecting “Open Raw Directory”.    Note:   If multiple imaging runs were performed on the same slide, append the cycles accordingly.      ii.  Verify that the dataset is assigned to the correct objective (“Nikon 20× Plan Fluor ELWD”) and load the appropriate calibration file for the experiment and verify.    iii.  Configure exposure settings to “Automatic” with 100 % scaling and enable the “Crop to DAPI” option during preprocessing setup.    iv.  Save the preprocessed data to a new folder.    Note:   The preprocessing tool may fail to save images into the preprocessing output folder if the image name exceeds the allowed character limit (256 characters).      Note:   During image processing, the raw data undergoes the following essential correction steps: Removal of saturated pixels, correction of hot and cold pixels, flatfield correction to normalize illumination, pixel remapping, registration, image stitching, and subtraction of the pre-stain image/background signal to assemble full regions of interest. Match ROIs to TMA Positions ( Figures 6 A and 6B).   a.  Load cell metadata from the H5AD file.    b.  Filter to the target slide and in-core cells.    c.  Define the mapping between Xenium TMA positions and MACSima ROI indices according to the mappings in the input CSV file ( Table 2 ).    d.  Visualize the mapping and save diagnostic plots.
