     Note:   The cell-type annotations and obs_name_orig identifiers are generated during upstream processing (see  before you begin ). The obs_name_orig field links each cell to its original Xenium cell boundary polygon.     26.  Load Xenium core mappings.   a.  Load the H5AD file, filter to the target slide and position, and retain only cells flagged as is_in_core.       27.  Load Xenium Spatial Data.   a.  Load cell/nucleus boundaries, cell labels, transcripts, expression matrix, and the morphology focus images from the Xenium output folder.       28.  Perform the per-core Registration Loop ( Figures 6 C and 6D).   a.  For each position-ROI pair, execute Steps 29–37 below. Pairs where the output Zarr folder already exists are automatically skipped.       29.  Align Observation Tables.   a.  Join annotated metadata with the Xenium cell table by cell_id/obs_name_orig. Filter to the highlighted position and set obsm['spatial'] from centroid coordinates (cell_centroid_x, cell_centroid_y).       30.  Load the MACSima images.   a.  Load the DAPI channel for the first cycle as well as all other non-DAPI and non-background channels.       31.  Compute Core Bounding Box.   a.  Derive the ROI bounding box in pixel coordinates from the spatial extent of the aligned cell table.       32.  Transform Cell/Nucleus Boundary Polygons and crop the Xenium dataset.   a.  Scale each polygon by the transform_factor (micrometers to pixels).    b.  Translate it by subtracting the bounding box origin multiplied by scale_factor, placing the boundaries in the same coordinate space as the full-resolution images.       33.  Perform a Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT)-Based Image Registration.  19     a.  Perform downscaling by scale_factor, using dask_image.ndinterp.affine_transform().  20      b.  Apply Contrast-Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE)  21   with skimage.exposure.equalize_adapthist()  22   with default parameters: clip_limit = 0.01, kernel_size = 1/8 of image dimensions.    c.  Convert pixel values to uint8.    Note:   The downscaling by scale_factor = 3 reduces runtime and suppresses high-frequency photon noise during feature detection. If registration fails or produces poor results, try scale_factor = 2 for higher-resolution feature detection or adjust CLAHE parameters.  21        d.  Detect SIFT key points and match descriptors with Fast Library for Approximate Nearest Neighbors (FLANN)  23   (Parameters: KD-tree, 5 trees, 50 checks).    e.  Apply Lowe’s ratio test  19   with threshold 0.5 to retain high-confidence matches.    f.  Compute a 2D affine transformation from the surviving inlier matches using spatialdata.transformations.get_transformation_between_landmarks().    g.  Scale the translation components by scale_factor to obtain the full-resolution affine transformation matrix.    h.  Apply the full-resolution affine transformation to the entire MACSima image using dask_image.ndinterp.affine_transform().       34.  Assemble a multi-modal SpatialData Object containing the following data:   a.  macsima: aligned MACSima images.    b.  morphology_focus: Xenium morphology focus images (all channels).    c.  cell_boundaries: Xenium cell segmentation polygons.    d.  nucleus_boundaries: Xenium nucleus segmentation polygons.    e.  transcripts: cell expression table and spatially filtered transcripts.    f.  cell_labels: Xenium cell segmentation labels.       35.  Write the assembled object to: <output_folder>/Pos_<position>_ROI_<roi>.zarr.       Note:   All loaded MACSima channels are read and transformed using dask_image.ndinterp.affine_transform() and stored as an Image2DModel layer in the SpatialData object.      Note:   The Zarr store can be explored interactively with napari  24   using the napari-spatialdata  25   plugin.     36.  Quantify the per-cell protein signal.   a.  Aggregate protein signal per cell. For each MACSima image layer, call harpy.tb.allocate_intensity() using the cell labels image as the spatial mask.          Note:   The mean pixel intensities within each cell mask are appended to the gene expression table and saved as rna_protein_table.     37.  Visualize the registration quality.   a.  Generate a 2×2 summary figure and save it as POS_<position>_registration_summary.png. The Figure follows the layout described in  Table 3  and representative resulting images are included in  Figure 7 .                CRITICAL:  Visually inspect the overlay to check the registration quality. Cell boundaries should fall on top of nuclear structures and the red and green channels of the RGB overlay should be highly overlapping for good quality registration. A poorly registered core will show systematic lateral or rotational offsets between the channels. In addition to visual inspection,  26   registration quality could also be evaluated quantitatively with several image-based metrics. For instance, the normalized mutual information  27   between the Xenium DAPI channel and the registered and the unregistered MACSima DAPI channel images can be calculated and compared. When processing a large number of slides, these metrics could facilitate the identification of potentially misaligned cores for further evaluation by virtual inspection or manual adjustment.      Note:   Processing all MACSima channels for a full TMA slide (approximately 30–40 channels per core, 40 cores) requires ∼50 GB RAM and takes 60–90 min per core.     Table 3   Layout of the registration summary plot generated for each core      Panel  Content      Top-left  Xenium morphology focus DAPI (red)    Top-right  MACSima DAPI (green)    Bottom-left  Registered MACSima DAPI with cell boundaries overlay (red)    Bottom-right  RGB overlay: red = Xenium DAPI, green = MACSima DAPI        Figure 7   Quality control of Xenium-MACSima spatial data registration and SpatialData assembly  Quality-control visualization of the multimodal registration workflow.  (A) Xenium morphology focus DAPI channel.  (B) Non-aligned MACSima DAPI image.  (C) Overlay of Xenium morphology focus DAPI image (green, position 1) and aligned MACSima DAPI (purple, position 40), where white regions indicate strong overlap between images.  (D) Aligned MACSima DAPI image (blue) with Xenium cell boundaries overlaid in red. Together, these panels demonstrate registration quality across the full field of view.                      Expected outcomes  Successful implementation of this protocol results in the generation of a multimodal spatial dataset containing both transcriptomic and proteomic information from the same FFPE TMA section. The wet-lab workflow provides practical guidance for the critical experimental steps required for successful Xenium and MICS procedures, including tissue preparation, Xenium processing, post-Xenium slide recovery, antigen retrieval, antibody staining, and multiplexed imaging. Important considerations and troubleshooting insights are provided throughout to help users optimize tissue integrity, RNA and protein signal quality, and overall assay performance. Following Xenium spatial transcriptomics and subsequent MICS, users obtain high-resolution spatial maps of RNA transcripts and protein markers while preserving tissue morphology and spatial context. The experimental workflow enables detection of thousands of RNA targets using the Xenium platform together with highly multiplexed protein profiling using MICS. The workflow is expected to enable comprehensive multimodal characterization of individual cells by combining Xenium transcriptomic information with highly multiplexed and customizable protein profiling. The increased antibody plexity and flexibility of MACSima compared with the protein-detection capabilities of Xenium and other hyperplex protein imaging platforms, such as PhenoCycler and COMET, enable broader phenotypic and functional characterization, particularly in complex immune and tumor microenvironments. Following image registration and protein channel intensity quantification, transcriptomic and proteomic measurements are linked at single-cell resolution, generating a combined RNA-protein expression matrix for each cell together with its spatial coordinates within the tissue. The resulting dataset can be used to identify and characterize cellular phenotypes, investigate cell states, study cell-cell interactions, and explore tissue organization by integrating complementary transcriptomic and proteomic information. In addition, the image registration and data integration framework provided in this protocol can be adapted to combine Xenium data with other multiplex imaging modalities.  Users should expect preservation of tissue integrity throughout the workflow, successful recovery of Xenium-processed slides for downstream protein imaging, and generation of registered multimodal datasets suitable for downstream spatial and single-cell analyses. Depending on tissue quality, RNA integrity, antibody performance, and imaging conditions, signal intensity and the number of detected transcripts or proteins may vary between samples.  After step 35 (SpatialData assembly), the output Zarr store contains aligned images from both modalities, transformed cell and nucleus segmentation polygons ( Figure 7 D), the gene expression count matrix with cell-type annotations, and spatially filtered transcript coordinates. The data can be visualized interactively with napari using the napari-spatialdata plugin, where all layers overlay correctly in a shared coordinate space.  After step 36 (protein quantification,  Figure 6 D), each cell in registration.aligned_data[”rna_protein_table”].X contains numeric columns for each MACSima antibody. A cross-modal concordance between RNA-based cell-type annotations and protein measurements can serve as an additional quality metric for the overall registration and quantification workflow. This concordance could be visually explored by plotting heatmaps showing the expression of corresponding RNA and protein markers for each of the identified cells using standard tools such as scanpy.  7   The correlation coefficients between transcript counts and mean protein expression per cell for pairs of corresponding markers can also be used for a quantitative evaluation of the concordance between RNA and protein measurements.  2    After step 37 (registration quality assessment), the color overlay should show white overlap at nuclear positions, with minimal red-only or green-only fringes ( Figure 7 C).    Quantification and statistical analysis  The per-cell protein quantification (step 36,  Figure 6 D) yields absolute fluorescence intensity values (mean of aligned pixel values within each cell mask). These values are instrument- and acquisition-specific and should be used for within-experiment comparisons. Cross-experiment normalization (e.g., percentile normalization or z-score per channel) may be necessary when integrating multiple MACSima runs. It is important to note that errors in per-cell protein quantification could substantially affect downstream analysis. Per-cell protein quantification depends on accurate image registration and cell segmentation, as fluorescence intensity is calculated from the pixels within each cell mask. The sensitivity to segmentation errors may vary according to subcellular localization: nuclear markers are generally less affected by small changes in cell boundaries, whereas membrane-associated markers may be more sensitive to segmentation inaccuracies, particularly at cell-cell interfaces. Cytoplasmic markers typically show intermediate sensitivity. Applications requiring improved or alternative segmentation, advanced segmentation approaches can be evaluated and compared with the default segmentation approach to assess their suitability for the respective tissue and marker composition. Therefore, segmentation quality and image alignment should be carefully assessed before interpreting per-cell fluorescence intensities.  The combined RNA and protein measurements are stored in a single AnnData table within the SpatialData Zarr store. Downstream analyses, including joint RNA and protein cell-type classification, ligand-receptor interaction inference, and spatial neighborhood analysis, can be performed using standard tools (e.g., scanpy,  7   squidpy,  28   LIANA  29  ) applied to the exported AnnData table.    Limitations  Antibody performance may vary between tissue types. For example, we observed tissue-dependent variation in staining performance in the data generated in the scope of this workflow. Therefore, as described in  before you begin  (step 7) and in  problem 2  in  troubleshooting , antibody performance should be validated in the tissue type of interest e.g., by performing a mock Xenium-MACSima.  The SIFT-based registration relies on sufficient structural similarity between the Xenium DAPI morphology focus image and the MACSima DAPI staining. If tissue morphology is substantially altered between the two acquisitions (e.g., due to tissue loss, folding, or deformation during antigen retrieval), registration may fail or produce locally poor alignment. In such cases, non-rigid (deformable) registration methods may be required but are not implemented in this workflow (see  problem 6  in  troubleshooting ).  The per-cell protein quantification uses the Xenium cell segmentation labels projected onto the MACSima images. Any residual registration error directly propagates into protein allocation. Cells at the boundary of registration artifacts or at the tissue edge may receive inaccurate protein measurements.  The current computational workflow performs image registration of MACSima images to the Xenium coordinate system. As with any image transformation and resampling procedure, image registration involves interpolation of pixel values. Therefore, minor changes in pixel intensities may occur in the registered images. In our experience, these effects were not observed to materially impact the intended downstream analyses, including RNA-protein based cell annotation and spatial characterization of tissue microenvironments.  The scripts process each TMA core independently. Cross-core normalization of protein signal intensities is not performed automatically and must be applied by the user if comparing protein levels across cores or slides, due to the technical variation within staining intensities. There are several normalization methods (e.g., Y score, ComBat, MxNorm or mean division) that can fail to consider skewed patterns that arise from this type of data. Thus, we recommend using a more reliable non-parametric normalization methods that can be employed in both pixel and feature level, such as UniForm.  30      Troubleshooting   Problem 1: Insufficient quencher removal after Xenium-processing (related to step 12 in the protocol)  Occasionally, incomplete removal of the Xenium autofluorescence quencher using quencher removal solution (10 mM sodium hydrosulfite) may be observed, indicated by persistent lilac discoloration of the tissue section ( Figure 1 ).    Potential solution 
   •  Verify that the sodium hydrosulfite solution was freshly prepared at a final concentration of 10 mM prior to use.    •  If quencher removal was insufficient, repeat this step with freshly prepared quencher removal solution and use it immediately after preparation.   
   Problem 2: Low/insufficient antigen staining intensity (related to before you begin step 8 and step 13 in the protocol)  Xenium-processed slides may exhibit reduced or absent staining for previously established antigen markers during MICS imaging. Compatibility of an antibody clone with standard MACSima workflows does not necessarily guarantee successful staining performance on post-Xenium tissue sections.    Potential solution 
   •  Confirm proper antibody storage conditions and expiration dates, and assess antibody performance using appropriate control tissues.    •  Optimize HIER by extending the incubation time up to 60 min, ensuring that slides remain fully submerged throughout the retrieval process, and testing alternative antigen retrieval buffers (e.g., pH 6).    •  Evaluate alternative antibody clones or, where applicable, fluorescently label validated unlabeled primary immunohistochemistry antibodies to enable compatibility with MICS.    •  We suggest performing a mock Xenium run on a consecutive section to test and optimize antibody clones and establish panels that are suitable for post-Xenium MICS experiments mimicking v1 or 5k panel conditions. Note that the mock experiment should be considered a pre-screening approach rather than a substitute for validation following the complete Xenium workflow.   ○  For the mock Xenium run, mount a serial section (from the same block as the section used for the Xenium-MACSima experiment) onto a blank Xenium slide.   -  Perform sectioning of the block and initial sample preparation comprising deparaffinization, rehydration, and decrosslinking as described in steps 1–3.    -  Perform the subsequent steps, including hybridization, post-hybridization washes, ligation, and amplification, using only the buffer components from previously used  Xenium Slides and Sample Prep Reagents  (10x Genomics, PN-1000460), but omit the enzymes.    -  Perform hybridization overnight (16–24 h) at 50°C in a thermocycler as described in step 4, using the hybridization mix without a probe panel.    -  Perform autofluorescence quenching and nuclei staining as described in step 7.    -  Following sample preparation, setup the samples on the Xenium Analyzer according to the  Xenium Analyzer User Guide  (10x Genomics,  CG000584 ) as described in step 8. Prepare all the buffers as mentioned in the above user guide. Decoding reagents are replaced with plates containing 1x PBS. Start the run and define ROIs as mentioned in step 9.    -  After the mock Xenium run is complete, replace the buffer on the slides with 0.05 % PBST and store at 4°C until quencher removal and subsequent MICS imaging (step 12 onwards).       ○  Alternatively, a mock Xenium run can also be performed in an off-the-Xenium-Analyzer setting. In this case, mount the serial section onto a SuperFrost Plus slide. The sample preparation workflow from deparaffinization to nuclei staining is exactly as mentioned above. Following sample preparation, incubate slides in Probe Removal Buffer (30 min at RT, 20°C–25°C) followed by Wash Buffer (30 min at RT, 20°C–25°C), at least 4 cycles each, to mimic buffer exposure during the Xenium Analyzer processing. Buffers are prepared as per the  Xenium Analyzer User Guide  (10x Genomics,  CG000584 ).       •  An antibody should be considered compatible when it fulfills the following criteria (see  Figure 3 ):   ○  Specific staining pattern: Signal is restricted to the expected cell population and subcellular localization.    ○  High signal-to-background ratio: Positive cells are clearly distinguishable from surrounding tissue with minimal nonspecific background.    ○  Reproducible performance: Comparable staining is observed across technical replicates or appropriate control tissues.    ○  Preserved staining after Xenium processing: The staining pattern is consistent with the expected biology, previous MACSima or immunohistochemistry validation, and comparable to reference databases.       •  The resulting images ( Figure 3 ) allow users to identify antibodies that fulfilled ( Figures 3 C, 3D, 3E, 3G, and 3H) or failed ( Figures 3 B and 3F) these criteria.   
   Problem 3: Autofocus failure with large ROIs during MICS (related to step 22 in the protocol)  Selecting tissue sections that cover the entire Xenium imageable area as a single, large ROI during ROI definition on the MACSima instrument occasionally resulted in autofocus instability during imaging. Such issues manifested as blurry FOVs or blurry images in the output folders ( Figure 5 ). In our experience, ROIs larger than approximately 100 FOVs were more prone to the aforementioned focusing issues.    Potential solution 
   •  Divide large imaging areas into smaller ROIs to improve autofocus performance and overall image quality.    •  Select the image contrast-based focusing approach instead of constant height-based focusing for your MICS experiment.    •  Cover the MACSwell frame with adhesive, pierceable aluminum foil to prevent evaporation and drying of the sample during extended imaging cycles, as insufficient liquid coverage may lead to autofocus and imaging issues.    •  If the tissue to be imaged is larger than the above-mentioned limitation, consider splitting it into several (non-overlapping) ROIs.    •  For TMAs, every core should be imaged as a separate ROI.    •  We suggest using the slides from a mock Xenium run to test suitable ROI sizes and decide on the best autofocusing method.   
   Problem 4: SIFT registration fails or produces identity affine matrix  A failed or bad quality registration could be due to the identification of too few matching keypoints between the Xenium and MACSima DAPI images.    Potential solution  Verify that the correct DAPI file is used (cycle-0 stained DAPI with “_S_” flag, not the baseline “_B_“ image). Try reducing scale_factor from 3 to 2 for higher-resolution feature detection. If images have very low contrast, adjust the CLAHE parameters in preprocess_reg().  21   Confirm that the Xenium morphology focus images contain the expected core region by visually inspecting the cropped image.    Problem 5: Xenium positions do not match MACSima ROI position  If some Xenium positions do not match the MACSima ROI positions, these cores were probably not captured during MACSima scanning (e.g., edge cores or tissue damage).    Potential solution  Do not include these positions in the roi_map_file CSV file, so that they are skipped in the full-slide processing script (“match_rois_cores_fullslide.py”).    Problem 6: Variable registration offset across the tissue  The presence of a misalignment between the Xenium DAPI image and the registered MACSima image that is not constant in magnitude and direction across the image shows that a global affine transformation is insufficient to register the images correctly. A visual inspection of the overlaid Xenium and registered MACSima DAPI image allows for the easy identification of this issue by showing a non-uniform alignment quality across the image. This heterogeneous misalignment is more common for larger ROIs and typically arises from tissue deformation or folding between acquisitions, lens distortion in either imaging system, different tissue mounting geometry, or non-linear shrinkage or expansion of the section.    Potential solution  A non-rigid (deformable) transformation is required.     Note:   Non-rigid (deformable) transformation is not addressed in this protocol, as only a single transformation type was tested. This represents a current limitation; users are advised to adapt the methodology as needed for their specific application. Recommended alternatives are RAMI2D  31   or ST-align.  32       Additional computational problems and diagnostic tips  Other possible computational problems could lead to TMA cores being skipped or output folders not being written due to lack of disk-space ( Table 4 ). For troubleshooting the user can refer to the error message to identify the cause of the problem and correct their workflow or report it as an issue on the GitHub repository associated with this protocol ( https://github.com/scOpenLab/MACSimaXenium ).    Table 4   Additional potential issues with the computational workflow and troubleshooting tips      Issue  Step  Quick fix      Out of memory  Any stage  Increase scale_factor, use HPC    KeyError on cell_id or obs_name_orig  Xenium Cropping  Ensure that H5AD obs column names match the required values    Zarr write fails  Xenium Cropping  Ensure there is sufficient disk space and that the script user has write permissions for the output path    Core skipped unexpectedly  Xenium Cropping  Check if an output.zarr folder already exists at the specified output path and delete to reprocess the core         Resource availability   Lead contact  Requests for further information, resources, or clarification should be directed to the lead contacts, Sophia Scheuermann ( sophia.scheuermann@kitz-heidelberg.de ). X-SPEAR: An Extensible Framework for Spatial Panel Evaluation and Refinement Introduction  Targeted in situ transcriptomics platforms such as 10x Genomics Xenium measure hundreds to thousands of genes at subcellular resolution in intact tissue, so that cell types, subtypes and states can be identified in their spatial context ( Janesick et al., 2023 ). They require the user to choose the gene panel before the experiment. The panel is usually chosen from an annotated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) or single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) reference, and the choice determines which cell identities the experiment can resolve. A probe that hybridises to unintended transcripts can also produce misleading spatial signal, so the designed probes need checking.  Several computational methods select markers or probe sets for this purpose: differential-expression rankings such as the Wilcoxon rank-sum test ( Wilcoxon, 1945 ); specificity scores such as COSine similarity-based marker Gene identification (COSG) ( Dai et al., 2022 ); minimal marker combinations such as Necessary and Sufficient Forest (NS-Forest) ( Aevermann et al., 2021 ); and probe-set optimisation such as Spapros ( Kuemmerle et al., 2024 ). Two problems remain. First, single-gene markers are often insufficient for rare populations, closely related subtypes and transient states, and methods that find gene combinations usually reduce each cell type to one combination, which fails if any of its genes is poorly detected. Second, a gene’s detection in a targeted spatial assay differs from its detection in the single-cell reference. Across the ovarian cancer panel studied here, the median gene is detected in Xenium in only about half as many cells as in the matched reference, and the loss varies strongly from gene to gene. A marker that looks excellent in the reference may be nearly invisible in situ. The methods we compare choose genes from the reference as measured and do not model this loss.  Here we present eXtensible Spatial Panel Evaluation And Refinement (X-SPEAR), a framework with two modules. The first is Decision-rule Aggregation for Rare-cell Typing (DART), which learns short Boolean gene rules and selects several gene-disjoint rules for each cell type. Before learning, DART thins the reference to each gene’s measured single-cell-to-Xenium detection rate, so that rules relying on poorly detected genes score poorly and are not chosen. The detection rates come from a  Xenium prior : a previous experiment in which a single-cell reference and a Xenium run were both measured, usually on a different tissue, because a designer never has Xenium data from the target sample before ordering its panel. The second module checks the probes of any panel, whichever method chose it, for predicted off-target transcripts that are expressed in other cell types. The current version targets cell-type marker selection for Xenium. The “X” denotes extensibility, toward other targeted platforms and other selection objectives.  We first ask which Xenium priors help DART, using every combination of prior and target among five paired single-cell and Xenium datasets. We then benchmark DART against the Wilcoxon test, COSG, NS-Forest and Spapros on three targets (ovarian cancer, mouse brain and cervical cancer), with a deployment rule throughout: nothing measured on the target’s Xenium informs the panel, and its labels are used only for scoring. With a Xenium prior from a different tissue, DART outperformed all four methods at matched panel size on every target. Its rules agree with the downstream classifier and name interpretable marker programs. On 45 mouse retinal ganglion cell (RGC) subtypes, held out within a single-cell atlas, DART matched the best methods and led COSG and NS-Forest at every subtype abundance.    2  Results   2.1  X-SPEAR designs a detection-aware panel and checks its probes  X-SPEAR takes an annotated single-cell reference of the tissue to be profiled, together with a Xenium prior, and returns a Xenium gene panel with evidence for classification performance and probe-level off-target risk ( Fig. 1 ). It is a Python package that can be used as a library, from the command line or as a pipeline of twelve stages (below). Panel design with DART proceeds in three steps ( Fig. 2 ).  The first step is detection-aware thinning. For each gene, a keep probability      p   keep       is the ratio of its detection rate (the fraction of cells with a nonzero count) in the Xenium prior’s Xenium run to its detection rate in that experiment’s single-cell reference ( Methods ). Each nonzero count of the single-cell reference is kept with probability      p   keep       and zeroed otherwise, so that the thinned reference reproduces each gene’s expected in situ detection. The prior’s cells need no labels, and the target’s Xenium is never used.  The second step is rule learning. Three learners propose candidate Boolean rules for each cell type: thresholded conjunctions such as     G  e  n  e  A  >   t  1   ∧  G  e  n  e  B  ≤   t  2     , which require one gene to be high and another to be low. The Asymmetric Tree Panel Finder (ATPF), developed here, grows decision trees whose splits isolate one target cell type rather than separating all classes. R ule F it  ( Friedman and Popescu, 2008 ), a rule-ensemble method, is applied to random-forest and gradient-boosted ensembles; it extracts rules from the trees and keeps those with nonzero      L  1     -penalised coefficients.  The third step is orthogonal selection. Candidates are ranked by      F  1      minus a penalty per additional gene, and up to     K     rules are kept per cell type, sharing at most      O   max       genes. The default is gene-disjoint rules        O   max    =  0      . The panel is the union of the selected rules’ genes.  The off-target module reads the probe report that the Xenium Panel Designer returns for a submitted panel, which lists each probe’s predicted off-target genes. For each marker it draws a dotplot of the marker beside its off-target genes across the reference’s cell types. A probe whose off-target genes are expressed in cell types that the marker does not mark would add false signal there and should be replaced; the dotplot shows which probes these are. Because the check needs only the probe report and the reference, it applies to a panel from any selection method ( Section 2.12 ).  X-SPEAR’s pipeline runs these steps as twelve numbered stages, each configured by its own file and each optional ( Fig. 3 ). Stages 00–04 load and prepare the single-cell reference: ingest, quality control, a cap on the cells per cell type, normalisation and, if wanted, an embedding. Stage 06 thins a copy of the reference to the Xenium prior’s detection rates, and stage 07 selects the panel, with DART (as four substages: rule learning, rule scoring, ranking and orthogonal selection) or with one of the other selectors compared here. Stage 10 exports the panel together with the reference bundle that the Xenium Panel Designer takes, and stage 11 checks the probe report it returns. Where a labelled Xenium run of the target exists, stages 05, 08 and 09 load it, label its cells with a classifier trained on the reference and score the labels, as the evaluations in this study do. Every selector writes the same panel file, which is all the later stages read, so the classification, export and off-target stages serve a panel from any method. The interfaces and each stage are described in the  Methods  ( Section 4.1 ).    2.2  Datasets  We used five paired datasets, each with a single-cell reference and a Xenium run, and one single-cell atlas ( Table 1 ). Three pairs serve as  targets , which need cell-type labels on the Xenium cells to score a panel: ovarian cancer, cervical cancer and mouse brain. All five pairs serve as Xenium priors. Ovarian and cervical cancer are the reference cases: formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue profiled with the 10x Genomics Chromium Flex assay (Flex) and Xenium Prime 5K on the same tissue block, with 10x’s cell-type annotation of the Xenium cells. Mouse brain adds a fresh-frozen (FF) target of another species. The mouse retina pair supplies a same-species prior for mouse brain; it has no cell-type labels, so it cannot be a target. The breast cancer pair is used only as a prior: its Flex reference and its Xenium run come from different tumours, so it is not suitable as a target. The mouse RGC atlas, with 45 annotated subtypes, has no Xenium counterpart with subtype labels, so it is used for a held-out single-cell benchmark of fine subtypes.  Several other datasets were considered and set aside. A skin melanoma pair was removed because its single-cell reference turned out to be from mouse lemur while its Xenium run was human, so its detection rates measured a species mismatch. A dermatomyositis skin pair had a nearly flat detection profile from a shallow reference and was not validated. A second ovarian cancer Xenium dataset was measured with an earlier 5K panel version lacking about 30% of the genes, and in situ whole-transcriptome Atera data show no detection loss to correct, so neither tests detection-aware design. A human spleen pair was set aside because the source of its Xenium run could not be documented.    2.3  Detection loss is large, gene-specific and reproducible across experiments  A Xenium prior is only useful if a gene’s detection loss measured in one experiment predicts its loss in another. On the ovarian cancer Xenium, the median gene is detected in 52% as many cells as in the matched single-cell reference (4,259 genes detected in at least 0.1% of reference cells), and the loss varies widely between genes ( Fig. 4a ). The loss is reproducible. Per-gene      p   keep       in ovarian and cervical cancer, two different tissues profiled on the same Xenium panel, correlate at Spearman     ρ  =  0.88     over 3,056 shared genes. That is more strongly than the genes’ single-cell detection breadth correlates between the two tissues (    ρ  =  0.62    ), so      p   keep       captures a property of the gene and its probes rather than shared biology ( Fig. 4b ).    2.4  Designing a panel without the target’s Xenium  Every panel in this study is designed and evaluated in the same way ( Fig. 5 ). Three datasets are involved. The  single-cell reference  is annotated single-cell data of the target tissue; the panel is chosen from its genes. The  Xenium prior  supplies per-gene detection rates from a previous experiment that measured both a single-cell reference and a Xenium run; only its detection rates are used. The  target Xenium  is the Xenium run of the target tissue. Its Xenium cells were split into two spatial halves by a checkerboard, and only the held-out half was scored. Nothing from the target Xenium informs the panel. To score a panel, a classifier is trained on the single-cell reference restricted to the panel’s genes, it predicts the cell type of every held-out target Xenium cell, and the predictions are compared with the target’s labels by macro      F  1     , the unweighted mean of the per-cell-type      F  1      scores.    2.5  A Xenium prior helps when it matches the target’s chemistry and species  We first asked which Xenium priors help DART. For each target we designed DART panels with every available prior, and with none, and compared them at the target’s default panel size ( Fig. 6 ;  Methods ). The target’s own Xenium is shown as an upper bound that no designer has before ordering.  The prior that helped most, other than the target’s own, always matched the target’s chemistry and species. For the two human FFPE tumours it was the other tumour, profiled with the same Flex reference and Xenium chemistry: cervical cancer raised ovarian cancer from 0.470 macro-     F  1      without a prior to 0.563, against 0.600 with the target’s own Xenium, and ovarian cancer raised cervical cancer from 0.517 to 0.612 (own 0.666). The breast pair, of the same chemistry but with its reference and Xenium run from different tumours, helped less (0.520 and 0.538). For the fresh-frozen mouse brain, the fresh-frozen mouse retina prior helped (0.643 to 0.673; own 0.700), whereas every human FFPE prior lowered accuracy, by 0.05 to 0.13. Conversely, the two fresh-frozen mouse priors helped ovarian cancer little (+0.011 and +0.025) and lowered cervical cancer (−0.016 and −0.033). A prior from the other species reaches only the genes whose human and mouse symbols agree, about half of the target’s genes ( Methods ). The best results therefore need a prior of the same chemistry and species as the planned experiment, which can come from a different tissue.    2.6  Benchmark against existing marker-selection methods  We then compared DART with four existing methods: the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, COSG, NS-Forest and Spapros. Each target used a Xenium prior from a different tissue, chosen by how closely its samples match the target’s and not by any score on the target: for ovarian and cervical cancer, each other (FFPE tissue with a Flex reference and Xenium Prime 5K on the same block), and for mouse brain, the mouse retina pair, the only other mouse pair, which like the target is fresh-frozen tissue with a single-nucleus reference and the mouse 5K panel ( Fig. 7 ). The other methods select genes from the single-cell reference as measured, as they are normally used. Because panel size drives accuracy, DART was run with     K  =  1–10     rules per cell type and the Wilcoxon test and COSG with 1–12 genes per cell type, and methods were compared at matched realised panel size by interpolating along each accuracy curve. NS-Forest’s panel barely changes with its budget (21–24 genes on ovarian cancer and one identical panel on each of the other targets), and Spapros was run at its default size, so neither gives an accuracy curve and DART was compared with them at their own panel sizes.    2.7  DART outperforms existing marker-selection methods  At matched panel size, DART outperformed the Wilcoxon test, COSG, NS-Forest and Spapros on every target ( Fig. 8 ;  Table 2 ). On ovarian cancer, the mean advantage over the Wilcoxon test was +0.064 macro-     F  1     , ranging from +0.036 to +0.118 across panel sizes, and DART reached the Wilcoxon test’s best accuracy (0.581 with 144 genes) with 83 genes. On mouse brain the advantage was +0.105, and DART needed 41 genes to match the Wilcoxon test’s best, against its 132. On cervical cancer it was +0.044, with 28 genes against 58. Across the three targets the margins were +0.038 to +0.079 over COSG, +0.099 to +0.175 over NS-Forest and +0.044 to +0.082 over Spapros. When DART’s thinning and rule learning were repeated at four seeds, every margin stayed positive (the smallest was +0.039, over Spapros on ovarian cancer), and the seed-to-seed standard deviation of a margin was 0.005–0.017 ( Methods ).  Two qualifications apply to COSG. First, on mouse brain DART’s lead over COSG is concentrated in small panels: it is +0.041 to +0.217 below about 55 genes, but from about 65 genes upward the two are level (−0.018 to +0.017), and COSG’s best point (0.708 with 120 genes) is slightly above DART’s best (0.703). On cervical, COSG’s best point (0.656 with 72 genes) lies beyond the largest panel on DART’s curve (50 genes). Second, COSG’s accuracy depends on how the reference is normalised; normalising over the full transcriptome rather than the shared gene universe would raise COSG by about 0.015 on ovarian and 0.036 on cervical ( Supplementary S2 ).   Fig. 8a  ranks one panel per method near DART’s default size on each target. DART ranked first on every target and by mean macro-     F  1      (0.610), ahead of Spapros (0.565), COSG (0.558), the Wilcoxon test (0.509) and NS-Forest (0.389). At each method’s own panel size, DART led Spapros by 0.060, COSG by 0.052, the Wilcoxon test by 0.099 and NS-Forest by 0.150 on average over the three targets.  The methods also differ in their compute ( Fig. 8a ;  Supplementary Fig. S3 ). DART splits its rule learning into independent tasks, one per cell type and learner, and runs them on parallel worker processes. It used the most CPU time, 1.2–8.9 core-hours per target against 0.3–1.1 for Spapros and at most 1.8 for the marker selectors, but with eight workers it finished in 12–82 minutes, six to seven times faster than on one core, and its largest process needed at most 6.3 GB of memory. Spapros took 11–28 minutes and needed 16–25 GB, and the Wilcoxon test and COSG finished in under three minutes.    2.8  Per-cell-type accuracy on the target Xenium  The differences in macro-     F  1      come from particular cell types ( Fig. 9 ). On ovarian cancer, DART’s panel gave the highest      F  1      of the five methods for 6 of the 14 cell types and Spapros’s larger panel for 5; DART scored above the Wilcoxon test on 11 types and above NS-Forest on 12. Its largest gain was on T and natural killer (NK) cells (0.50, against 0.14–0.27 for the other methods). It fell furthest behind the best method, by 0.14–0.17, on two tumour states, proliferative and VEGFA-positive tumour cells, which the Wilcoxon test and Spapros separated better. On mouse brain, DART gave the highest      F  1      for 6 of 12 cell types and scored above the Wilcoxon test on 11, most of all on neurons (0.86 against 0.24). The two rarest mouse brain types, macrophages (48 held-out cells) and T cells (36), were poorly classified by every method (     F  1      at most 0.38). On cervical cancer, with six broad cell types, DART’s advantage came from macrophages (0.64, against 0.09–0.30), and it was weakest on squamous carcinoma (0.28, against 0.29–0.43).    2.9  Number of rules per cell type and rule overlap  Two settings control a DART panel:     K    , the number of rules kept per cell type, and      O   max      , the number of genes that two rules of the same cell type may share ( Fig. 10 ). Each additional rule adds genes, so     K     also sets the panel size. macro-     F  1      rose with     K     on every target, steeply from     K  =  1     to     K  =  3     and more slowly afterwards. On ovarian cancer it rose from 0.455 with one rule per type (18 genes) to 0.555 at the default     K  =  4     (58 genes) and 0.623 at     K  =  10     (128 genes); on mouse brain from 0.574 to 0.680 and 0.703; and on cervical cancer from 0.499 to 0.595, reaching 0.643 at     K  =  9     before falling to 0.629 at     K  =  10    . The effect of letting rules share one gene        O   max    =  1       depended on the target. On ovarian cancer it lowered macro-     F  1      at every     K     above 1, by 0.085 at     K  =  4    . On mouse brain the two settings differed by at most 0.024, with no consistent sign. On cervical cancer sharing was better from     K  =  4     upward, by 0.014 at     K  =  4     and 0.043 at     K  =  10    .    2.10  DART’s rules are interpretable and agree with the classifier  Each DART panel comes with explicit rules, such as a gene above a threshold, alone or combined with others. These rules name recognisable marker programs ( Table 3 ). For the interferon-high inflammatory tumour cells of the ovarian cancer reference, DART’s four gene-disjoint rules use  MX1  (in a conjunction that also requires  ESR1  high and  NAMPT  and  CD200  low),  IFIT1 ,  IFIT3  and  DDX58 , all interferon-stimulated genes. The rules for ciliated epithelial cells use cilia genes ( CFAP100 ,  CDHR4 ,  TEKT1 ,  DNAH9 ), those for proliferative tumour cells use cell-cycle genes ( CIP2A ,  RRM2 ,  TYMS ,  TPX2 ), and those for T and natural killer cells use  TRAC ,  CD8A ,  CXCR4  and  IL7R . A ranked gene list carries no threshold and does not say which genes act together.  Panels are deployed with a classifier that never sees the rules, yet the classifier’s coefficients recover them ( Table 4 ). A “    g  e  n  e  >  t    ” condition in a cell type’s rule carries a positive coefficient for that type in 98–100% of cases on the three Xenium targets and in 96.5% across the 45 RGC subtypes. Rule genes carry 2.0–3.0 times the weight of the panel’s other genes, and a cell type’s largest coefficient belongs to one of its rule genes for every cell type of the three targets and for 92% of the RGC subtype panels. The rules are therefore an accurate, human-readable account of why the classifier calls a cell type.    2.11  Fine retinal ganglion cell subtypes  The Xenium targets have 6–14 broad cell types, which a single marker usually separates; on them most DART rules use one gene. RGCs, the projection neurons of the retina, comprise more than 40 transcriptionally related subtypes ( Tran et al., 2019 ;  Sanes and Masland, 2015 ), many without a unique marker. No Xenium dataset has RGC subtype labels, so we evaluated the 45 subtypes of a published atlas by five-fold out-of-fold prediction within the single-cell data ( Methods ): each panel is designed on four folds and scored on the held-out fold. Here 75% of DART’s rules are multi-gene conjunctions, with a mean of 2.4 genes per rule (    K  =  4     panels of the five folds), against 7–15% on the three Xenium targets.  DART, the Wilcoxon test and Spapros reached the same accuracy at matched size, about 0.955 to 0.96 macro-     F  1      from 150 genes upward ( Fig. 11a ): DART scored 0.959 with 184 genes and 0.960 with 223, the Wilcoxon test 0.957 with 191 and 0.958 with 224, and Spapros 0.956 with 175. COSG was 0.04–0.06 lower at matched size and reached 0.945 only with 393 genes, and NS-Forest’s single panel (71 genes) scored 0.879. DART led COSG (+0.028 to +0.037) and NS-Forest (+0.052 to +0.076) in every third of subtype abundance, from the rarest to the commonest, whereas against the Wilcoxon test and Spapros the per-subtype differences stayed within ±0.007 at every abundance ( Fig. 11b ). No single probe was load-bearing, consistent with each subtype being covered by several gene-disjoint rules: among the 230 single-gene knockouts of one fold’s     K  =  4     panel, the largest drop in macro-     F  1      was 0.003.    2.12  Checking a panel’s probes for off-target expression  The off-target check applies to a panel from any method once its probes are designed.  Fig. 12  shows its output for a 176-gene human retina panel designed in a separate study, using the probe report returned by the Xenium Panel Designer and a single-nucleus atlas of the human retina ( Li et al., 2026 ). The probe for the cone marker  CRX  has one predicted off-target,  RPS6KL1 , which is expressed weakly and evenly across the retinal cell classes, so it cannot mimic the cone pattern and the probe can be kept. Three of the probes for the amacrine-cell marker  PAX6  have predicted off-targets. Of those measured in the atlas,  ALX1  is barely expressed, but  PAX2 ,  PAX5  and  PAX8  are strongly expressed in astrocytes, where  PAX6  itself is absent. Those probes could report amacrine-like signal in astrocytes, so they are flagged for replacement.     3  Discussion  X-SPEAR turns an annotated single-cell reference into a Xenium panel without any data from the target sample. It makes three contributions:
    Detection-aware design from a Xenium prior.  The gap between a gene’s detection in a single-cell reference and in Xenium is large, gene-specific and reproducible across tissues. Thinning the reference to a previous experiment’s detection rates anticipates that gap before ordering. The prior should match the planned experiment’s chemistry and species, and it can come from another tissue; a mismatched prior can lower accuracy.     DART.  With a Xenium prior from a different tissue, DART outperforms the Wilcoxon test, COSG, NS-Forest and Spapros at matched panel size on every target we tested, and reaches the Wilcoxon test’s best accuracy with 42–69% fewer genes. Its rules name interpretable marker programs and agree with the classifier that uses the panel. On fine RGC subtypes it matches the best methods, leads COSG and NS-Forest at every subtype abundance, and no single probe is load-bearing.     A method-independent off-target check.  Dotplots of each marker beside its predicted off-target genes show which probes would add signal in the wrong cell types, for a panel chosen by any method.     Two limitations matter most. First, the benefit depends on a suitable Xenium prior: for the best results, the prior should come from the same assay chemistry and the same species as the target. Second, the evaluation labels of the Xenium targets derive from reference-based annotation: 10x’s for ovarian and cervical cancer and our own label transfer for mouse brain. The comparisons are therefore within the reference’s annotation scheme, although an independent annotation of the ovarian section agreed with the evaluation labels on 82.8% of cells at the level of five lineages ( Supplementary S3 ).  The thinning, selection and off-target modules are separable. Other targeted platforms can be supported once a detection profile and a probe-design output exist for them, and the same architecture can host objectives beyond cell-type identification, such as panels that preserve differential expression across conditions or spatial niches.    4  Methods   4.1.  The X-SPEAR software   Interfaces.  X-SPEAR is a Python package (Code availability statement) with three interfaces. As a library,  design_panel  takes an annotated single-cell reference, a dataset configuration and, optionally, a Xenium prior, and returns the panel’s genes, the selected rules (each with its cell type, thresholds, precision and recall) and the full pool of candidate rules.  Panel.reselect  selects again from that pool at another     K     or      O   max       without relearning; this study used it for the RGC panels with     K  =  1–3    .  classify  labels a target’s cells with a panel, and  metrics.evaluate  scores the labels. A dataset configuration, one JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) file, names the reference’s cell-type column, the cell types to leave out, and the renames and exclusions that map the target’s labels onto the reference’s. On the command line,  xspear design, xspear classify  and  xspear evaluate  wrap these calls.  xspear prior  lists and exports the Xenium priors shipped with the package,  xspear profile  depth-normalises priors and  xspear kcurve  plots accuracy against     K     ( Supplementary S6 ).  xspear init  writes annotated configuration files for the pipeline, and  xspear run  runs it, in full or for chosen stages.    Pipeline. The stages of the pipeline ( Fig. 3 ) pass files to each other. Every selector writes the panel’s gene list, which is all that stages 08–11 read, and DART also writes its rules. Each stage records its outcome, with the package version and commit, in a run manifest, and a stage does not start if an earlier one failed. Stage 00 loads counts (an AnnData h5ad file or a Matrix Market (MTX) matrix) and can attach Ensembl gene identifiers from a gene transfer format (GTF) file or mygene.info (needed for the export bundle), merge per-cell metadata and assign a group label such as the sample of origin. Stage 01 computes quality metrics and keeps cells with 500–8,000 detected genes and genes detected in at least three cells; it can also filter on mitochondrial fraction and call doublets with Scrublet ( Wolock et al., 2019 ). Stage 02 caps the cells per cell type (3,000, seeded). Stage 03 normalises counts per 10,000, or per median library size, applies     log  (  1  +  x  )     and can flag highly variable genes. Stage 04, off by default, computes principal components, a neighbour graph, a uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) ( McInnes et al., 2018 ) and Harmony integration ( Korsunsky et al., 2019 ). Stage 05 loads the target Xenium and its labels, which are used only for scoring. Stage 06 resolves a Xenium prior and thins a copy of the reference to it ( Supplementary S6 ); every data-driven selector of stage 07 uses the thinned copy, and the classifier of stage 08 uses the original. Stage 07 runs DART as four substages, 07a rule learning, 07b rule scoring, 07c ranking and 07d orthogonal selection ( Sections 4.3  and  4.4 ; defaults     K  =  4    ,      O   max    =  0     and 1,000 estimators per ensemble, as in this study). It can instead run the Wilcoxon test, COSG or NS-Forest (10 genes per cell type by default), read a curated marker list, run Spapros or its reference probe sets (principal components, differential expression, highly variable genes and random genes), or adopt an existing panel. Stage 10 writes the panel and, for the Xenium Panel Designer, a reference bundle of counts, gene and cell tables and cell types. Stage 11, off by default, is the off-target check ( Section 4.9 ). This study ran stage 00 to load the references of the three Xenium targets and called the functions behind stages 06, 07 and 11 from its analysis scripts; the capping, splitting and scoring described below are in the paper repository.  Classification and evaluation.  Stage 08 trains a classifier on the reference restricted to the panel and labels the target’s cells. The default is a one-versus-rest logistic regression (    C  =  1    , at most 1,000 iterations, unweighted), as in this study’s scoring; a random forest (500 trees, depth 8) and balanced class weights are options. Reference and target are first normalised over the genes they share, as in this study’s scoring, and so does the library’s  classify ; normalising over the panel’s genes alone, which is what a Xenium run measuring only the panel provides, is an option. Cells can also be labelled by voting with DART’s rules instead of a classifier ( Supplementary S5 ). Stage 09 reports macro-     F  1      and weighted      F  1      over the reference’s cell types, per-type precision, recall and      F  1     , the confusion matrix and the fraction of cells assigned a type. An alternative evaluation built on Spapros’ forest classifier is described in  Supplementary S7 .    Environments.  The analyses ran in Python 3.11.15 with numpy 2.4.6, pandas 2.3.3, SciPy 1.17.1, scikit-learn 1.9.0 ( Pedregosa et al., 2011 ), scanpy 1.10.3 ( Wolf et al., 2018 ), anndata 0.12.19, imodels 3.0.0 ( Singh et al., 2021 ), Cython 3.3.0 (for the compiled ATPF criterion), COSG 1.2.0 and NS-Forest 4.1. Spapros 0.1.6 cannot run on numpy 2 or pandas 3, so X-SPEAR runs it in a second environment (numpy 1.26.4, pandas 2.3.3) as a subprocess that returns only the panel file. The package’s installer builds both environments, pinned to lock files of exactly these versions.     4.2.  Datasets and preprocessing   Table 1  lists every dataset. For each target the candidate gene pool is the set of genes measured in both the single-cell reference and the Xenium panel: 4,766 (ovarian cancer), 4,548 (cervical cancer) and 4,791 (mouse brain). Expression is     log  (  1  +  x  )     of counts per 10,000 (CP10k), computed over this shared universe for both modalities before subsetting to a panel. For the benchmark, the reference was capped at 40,000 cells by stratified sampling, keeping small cell types whole, and the selectors were run on a stratified 80% of the capped reference.  The target Xenium cells were divided into design and evaluation halves by a spatial checkerboard, and only the evaluation half was scored: about 183,000 cells for ovarian cancer, 181,000 for cervical cancer and 32,000 for mouse brain. The design half was not used.   Evaluation labels.  For ovarian and cervical cancer, the labels are 10x Genomics’ cell-type annotation, mapped to the reference vocabulary. For cervical cancer, 10x left 56% of cells unassigned, and those cells were excluded. For mouse brain, the labels come from our label transfer, a scaled multinomial logistic regression trained on the reference over the shared genes. The original transfer normalised the reference over its full transcriptome but the Xenium over its panel; rebuilding it with consistent normalisation changed the labels of 18.3% of evaluation cells, and mouse brain results use the rebuilt labels except where noted ( Supplementary S3 ). Labels are used only to score.     4.3  Rule generation   ATPF.  ATPF grows scikit-learn ( Pedregosa et al., 2011 ) decision trees with a custom precision– recall impurity,     I  (  n  )  =  1  −  P  ×  R    , where    P    is precision and    R    recall. This criterion targets isolation of one cell type rather than global class separation. Root-to-node paths are extracted as candidate rules.    R ule F it . evidence_text:
A Melanoma Brain Metastasis CTC Signature and CTC:B-cell Clusters Associate with Secondary Liver Metastasis: A Melanoma Brain-Liver Metastasis Axis.

Abstract

Melanoma brain metastasis is linked to dismal prognosis and low overall survival and is detected in up to 80% of patients at autopsy. Circulating tumor cells (CTC) are the smallest functional units of cancer and precursors of fatal metastasis. We previously used an unbiased multilevel approach to discover a unique ribosomal protein large/small subunit (RPL/RPS) CTC gene signature associated with melanoma brain metastasis. In this study, we hypothesized that CTC-driven melanoma brain metastasis secondary metastasis (“metastasis of metastasis” per clinical scenarios) has targeted organ specificity for the liver. We injected parallel cohorts of immunodeficient and newly developed humanized NBSGW (huNBSGW) mice with cells from CTC-derived melanoma brain metastasis to identify secondary metastatic patterns. We found the presence of a melanoma brain–liver metastasis axis in huNBSGW mice. Furthermore, RNA sequencing analysis of tissues showed a significant upregulation of the RPL/RPS CTC gene signature linked to metastatic spread to the liver. Additional RNA sequencing of CTCs from huNBSGW blood revealed extensive CTC clustering with human B cells in these mice. CTC:B-cell clusters were also upregulated in the blood of patients with primary melanoma and maintained either in CTC-driven melanoma brain metastasis or melanoma brain metastasis CTC–derived cells promoting liver metastasis. CTC-generated tumor tissues were interrogated at single-cell gene and protein expression levels (10x Genomics Xenium and HALO spatial biology platforms, respectively). Collectively, our findings suggest that heterotypic CTC:B-cell interactions can be critical at multiple stages of metastasis.

Significance

This study provides important insights into the relevance of prometastatic CTC:B-cell clusters in melanoma progression, extends the importance of the CTC RPL/RPS gene signature beyond primary metastasis/melanoma brain metastasis driving targeted organ specificity for liver metastasis ("metastasis of metastasis"), and identifies new targets for clinical melanoma metastasis therapies.

title: A unified framework for identification of cell-type-specific spatially variable genes in spatial transcriptomic studies.
xenium_reason: Text indicates reuse of public Xenium data
evidence_text: A unified framework for identification of cell-type-specific spatially variable genes in spatial transcriptomic studies. Characterizing cell-type-specific spatially variable genes (SVGs) within tissue context is essential for exploring the landscape of complex biological systems in spatial transcriptomic (ST) studies. In this paper, we present a unified framework, the Mixture of Mixed Models (MMM), designed to directly model RNA count data and identify cell-type-specific SVGs while accounting for cell type composition and correcting for platform effects. Through a comprehensive simulation study and the analyses of eight publicly available ST datasets from various tissues and technologies with different resolutions, we demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of MMM in identifying cell-type-specific SVGs. Notably, our integrative analysis with genome-wide association studies reveals that the cell-type-specific SVGs identified by MMM in a mouse brain study exhibit significant heritability enrichment in brain-related phenotypes. This finding suggests that cell-type-specific SVGs play a vital role in elucidating the mechanisms underlying complex traits and diseases. When applying MMM to analyze a high-resolution Xenium human breast cancer dataset by accounting for the uncertainties in cell segmentation, we find that certain cell-type-specific SVGs may contribute to cell-cell communications, thereby regulating the tissue microenvironment. Furthermore, we show the versatility of MMM by applying it to the 3D tissue models constructed from multiple ST slices, highlighting its utility in analyzing the 3D ST data.

Scaling up spatial transcriptomics for large-sized tissues: uncovering cellular-level tissue architecture beyond conventional platforms with iSCALE. Recent advances in spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies have transformed our ability to profile gene expression while preserving crucial spatial context within tissues. However, existing ST platforms are constrained by high costs, long turnaround times, low resolution, limited gene coverage and inherently small tissue capture areas, which hinder their broad applications. Here we present iSCALE, a method that reconstructs large-scale, super-resolution gene expression landscapes and automatically annotates cellular-level tissue architecture in samples exceeding capture areas of current ST platforms. The performance of iSCALE was assessed by comprehensive evaluations involving benchmarking experiments, immunohistochemistry staining and manual annotations by pathologists. When applied to multiple sclerosis human brain samples, iSCALE uncovered lesion-associated cellular characteristics undetectable by conventional ST experiments. Our results demonstrate the utility of iSCALE in analyzing large tissues by enabling unbiased annotation, resolving cell type composition, mapping cellular microenvironments and revealing spatial features beyond the reach of standard ST analysis or routine histopathological assessment. Main  Understanding spatial gene expression distributions across tissues is essential for answering crucial biological questions and uncovering cellular functions, disease mechanisms and tissue development. ST technologies have transformed our ability to profile gene expression across tissues while retaining crucial spatial context  1 – 3  . However, major barriers to the widespread adoption of commercial ST platforms in biomedical research include high costs, long turnaround times, low resolution, limited gene coverage and inherently small tissue capture areas offered by current ST platforms. Sequencing-based ST platforms, such as Visium  4  , can sequence the whole transcriptome but lack single-cell resolution and come with a limited standard tissue capture area of 6.5 mm × 6.5 mm. Although Visium offers an extended version with a larger capture area of 11 mm × 11 mm, it is more expensive than the standard version. Additionally, many tissue samples still surpass this size limitation, restricting spatial profiling to a small portion of a biopsy or organ and often missing key biological regions. The recently released Visium HD  5   offers subcellular resolution but at considerably higher cost than Visium, and its tissue capture area is only 6.5 mm × 6.5 mm. Imaging-based ST platforms such as MERSCOPE  6  , CosMx  7   and Xenium  8   provide subcellular resolution and can handle moderately larger tissues, but the number of genes is limited, and image scanning time is typically extensive. These limitations make commercial ST platforms impractical for large-scale investigations, particularly when studying sizable tissues common in human studies. A recent approach, ‘visiumStitched’  9  , attempts to extend the spatial profiling window by manually stitching a few Visium captures; however, it requires manual alignment and supports only low-resolution analysis of directly measured regions.  On the other hand, hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained histology images, routinely used by clinical pathology laboratories, are considerably more cost-effective than ST. Additionally, the physical size of a standard whole-slide H&E image can be as large as 25 mm × 75 mm, greatly exceeding the capture area of all ST platforms. Previous studies showed correlations between gene expression profiles and histological image characteristics  10 – 15  , suggesting the feasibility of inferring spatial gene expression from these histology images  16 – 20  . Because obtaining histology images from large-sized tissues is easily achievable, this opens the possibility of virtually predicting gene expression directly from histology, overcoming the tissue size limitations of conventional ST platforms.  Here we introduce iSCALE (inferring Spatially resolved Cellular Architectures in Large-sized tissue Environments), a novel machine learning framework designed to predict gene expression for large-sized tissues with cellular-level resolution. By leveraging the gene expression–histological feature relationship, learned from a small set of training ST captures, iSCALE enables comprehensive gene expression prediction and tissue annotation across entire large tissue sections, including regions without direct gene expression measurements. Unlike existing resolution enhancement methods such as iStar  16   and RedeHist  19  , which rely on a single ST capture for prediction, iSCALE aligns and combines information from distinct ST sections and leverages large-sized H&E images to infer gene expression across extensive tissue areas. This is achieved by mapping individual sections onto the full tissue image and integrating information across multiple ST captures to enable spatially continuous gene expression prediction. This flexible framework allows iSCALE to provide a more comprehensive and scalable approach for spatial gene expression analysis compared to current state-of-the-art methods. Our results demonstrate that iSCALE can provide critical insights into disease by generating high-resolution spatial gene expression maps for large tissue sections.    Results   Overview of iSCALE  An overview of the iSCALE workflow is shown in Fig.  1 . Our goal is to predict gene expression in an H&E image generated from a large-sized tissue section, referred to as the ‘mother image’. The pipeline begins by selecting regions from the same tissue block, potentially spanning adjacent sections, with regions fitting standard ST platform capture areas (Extended Data Fig.  1 ). This process generates a small set of training ST captures, referred to as ‘daughter captures’. iSCALE then implements spatial clustering analysis on the daughter ST data to guide the alignment of the daughter captures onto the mother image through a human-in-the-loop, semiautomatic process (Extended Data Fig.  2a–c ). Next, iSCALE harmoniously integrates the gene expression and spatial information across the aligned daughter captures. To construct a gene expression prediction model, iSCALE extracts both global and local tissue structure information from the mother image. Subsequently, a feedforward neural network is employed to learn the relationship between histological image features and gene expression transferred from the aligned daughter captures. The resulting model predicts gene expression for each 8-µm × 8-µm superpixel—corresponding to approximately the size of a single cell—across the entire mother image. Leveraging these predictions, iSCALE further annotates each superpixel in the mother image with cell types and identifies enriched cell types in each tissue region, providing a detailed characterization of tissue architecture at cellular resolution.    Fig. 1   Overview of iSCALE workflow.  iSCALE enables ST analysis in large-sized tissues using a multi-capture study design. A high-resolution mother H&E image is obtained from a large tissue slice while multiple standard-sized daughter ST captures containing both gene expression and spatial information are collected from adjacent slices. iSCALE aligns and integrates the daughter captures based on gene expression, corrects for batch effects and smooths across spatial neighborhoods. Histological features are hierarchically extracted from regions of the mother image and combined with integrated ST data to predict super-resolution gene expression across the entire large tissue section. These predictions are then used for automatic cell type annotation and tissue segmentation. iSCALE also supports out-of-sample predictions for additional tissue sections using only H&E images. px, pixel.                     Extended Data Fig. 1   Conceptual overview of study design approaches for spatial transcriptomics in large tissues.   a , Ideal grid-based layout design: The tissue is divided into a grid, and each section (daughter capture) is profiled using an ST platform (for example 10x Visium). This layout allows for systematic and contiguous spatial coverage of the tissue.  b , Real-world adjacent tissue slice design: Daughter captures are obtained from adjacent sections of the same tissue block. Due to technical and experimental challenges of tissue processing, these captures often only partially overlap in the X-Y plane, and gaps may arise, leaving regions of the mother tissue unmeasured. Benchmark evaluations on a large gastric cancer sample  To evaluate the effectiveness of iSCALE, we conducted a benchmarking experiment using a ground truth single-cell gene expression dataset derived from a large gastric cancer tissue section profiled with 10x Xenium (10.5281/zenodo.15164980)  21  . The section contains 377 genes and spans the full Xenium slide (12 mm × 24 mm), making it ideal for benchmarking. In this experiment, we simulated a scenario where gene expression data were available only from a set of daughter captures, each with size of 3.2 mm × 3.2 mm, mimicking the conditions typically observed in real large tissue studies. Within each daughter capture, we simulated pseudo-Visium data, following the spot size and layout of the Visium platform (Fig.  2a ). First, to assess the accuracy of iSCALE’s semiautomatic alignment algorithm, we aligned daughter captures using the proposed algorithm described in the  Methods  section and achieved 99% alignment accuracy (Extended Data Fig.  2d ). Next, the iSCALE model was trained using the integrated gene expression data from five daughter captures, assuming their true alignment on the mother image. For comparison, we also predicted gene expression using iStar  16   and RedeHist  19  . Because both iStar and RedeHist can process only one daughter capture at a time to build their prediction models, we applied these algorithms for each daughter capture. As RedeHist requires a reference single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) dataset, we used a gastric tumor scRNA-seq dataset from Cheng et al.  22  . Figure  2b  shows the tissue segmentation results obtained from iSCALE, iStar and RedeHist. iSCALE’s segmentation closely resembles the pathologist’s manual annotation and successfully identified key tissue structures, including tumor, tumor-infiltrated stroma, mucosa, submucosa, muscle and tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS). In contrast, iStar and RedeHist segmentations varied noticeably across the five models, depending on the daughter capture used for training. For instance, iStar struggled to distinguish between tumor and mucosa when using daughter captures D1 and D5 as the training data. RedeHist performed even more poorly, failing to identify tissue structures regardless of which daughter capture was used as the training data. This is likely due to its inability to correctly detect a large portion of the nuclei (Supplementary Fig.  1 ), a critical component of its algorithm. To further demonstrate the advantage of iSCALE, we focused on the upper-left region of the tissue containing signet ring cells (Fig.  2c ), which are associated with aggressive gastric cancer and poor prognosis and play a critical role in guiding treatment  23  . iSCALE accurately identified the boundary between the poorly cohesive carcinoma region with signet ring cells and the adjacent gastric mucosa, with its inferred boundary closely aligning with the pathologist’s manual annotation. However, both iStar and RedeHist failed to detect this boundary when using daughter capture D1, which covers that boundary for model training (Fig.  2c  and Supplementary Fig.  2 ). As another demonstration, we examined the TLSs in this sample. Detecting TLSs in cancer is crucial because they are associated with improved immune responses, enhanced antitumor activity and better patient prognosis, making them key indicators of the tumor microenvironment’s immune dynamics  24 – 26  . As shown in Fig.  2d , cluster 11 (peach color) identified by iSCALE closely aligns with the manually annotated TLSs. In contrast, iStar tends to detect false-positive TLSs, whereas RedeHist exhibited substantially lower detection accuracy (Supplementary Fig.  3 ). Notably, the daughter capture models that performed well in certain regions often performed poorly for other critical regions, demonstrating considerable variability among predictions. These results underscore the importance of integrating multiple daughter captures to accurately detect fine-grained tissue structures, such as TLSs.  The availability of the ground truth single-cell gene expression data in this benchmarking experiment enables a quantitative evaluation of iSCALE’s gene expression prediction accuracy. Although iSCALE was designed for Visium (spot-level) ST data, its prediction model can be readily adapted to use Xenium (cellular-level) ST data for training. In the following evaluations, we compared two versions of iSCALE: iSCALE-Seq, which used pseudo-Visium data for training, and iSCALE-Img, which used Xenium data for training. To evaluate the prediction performance, we focused on the top 100 highly variable genes (HVGs). We computed the following metrics: root mean squared error (RMSE), structural similarity index measure (SSIM) and Pearson correlation. As shown in Fig.  3a,b , iSCALE-Seq outperformed iStar across all evaluation metrics, achieving performance similar to iSCALE-Img, despite being trained on spot-level resolution ST data. RedeHist was excluded from this comparison due to its unsatisfactory performance (Supplementary Fig.  4 ). Although the Pearson correlation coefficients for iSCALE-Img and iSCALE-Seq were generally low at the superpixel level (8 µm × 8 µm), the correlations improved as the superpixel size increased. Approximately 50% of the genes achieved correlation coefficients greater than 0.45 at a spatial resolution of 32 µm × 32 µm for iSCALE-Seq. Moreover, we observed that low correlation values at the superpixel level, such as  r  = 0.27 for  ACTA2 , still resulted in spatial distributions that almost perfectly resembled the ground truth predictions (Fig.  3c ). Additionally, the top 100 spatially variable genes, identified by Moran’s  I , revealed even stronger performance by iSCALE (Extended Data Fig.  3a ). Results across all genes in the dataset (Extended Data Fig.  3b ) confirm iSCALE’s robustness and consistent superior performance compared to iStar. Applications to large human multiple sclerosis brain sample  Encouraged by the promising performance of iSCALE in benchmark evaluations, we next applied the method to data generated from a postmortem human brain of a patient with multiple sclerosis (MS). MS is a chronic inflammatory disorder that affects the central nervous system by mistakenly attacking the myelin sheath of nerve fibers, leading to inflammation and damage, which disrupts electrical impulse transmission along nerves  29 – 31  . Our focus is on cellular alterations in MS, specifically changes in abundance, distribution and activity of different cell types within and near MS lesions. Identifying distinct cellular profiles around MS lesions can offer insights into the disease’s pathology, the immune response it provokes and potential therapeutic targets.  To characterize cell attributes associated with MS lesions, we analyzed a tissue block (Sample 1) containing an active core and complete white matter chronic active lesion from a patient with MS (10.5281/zenodo.15151354)  32  . Because the size of the mother tissue section (approximately 22 mm × 19 mm = 418 mm 2 ) greatly exceeded the standard ST capture area (Extended Data Fig.  6 ), we obtained 11 smaller daughter captures from the same tissue block following the large-tissue multi-capture study design in Fig.  1 . These captures underwent gene expression analysis using the standard 10x Visium protocol with tissue capture area of 6.5 mm × 6.5 mm (Supplementary Table  1 ). Using the iSCALE alignment process described in the  Methods  section, we aligned these daughter captures onto the mother image (Fig.  5a , Extended Data Fig.  7  and Supplementary Fig.  5 ). Traditional ST analysis, which relies solely on observed spot-level gene expression from directly measured daughter captures, would be inadequate due to its low-resolution, spot-level segmentation and limited coverage of critical regions, such as the lesion rim and core. In contrast, iSCALE integrates gene expression information from 11 daughter captures across different regions to train a super-resolution gene expression prediction model for the entire large tissue section. For this analysis, iSCALE predicted the expression of the top 3,000 HVGs, along with 145 additional key cell type markers selected based on in-house single-nucleus RNA sequencing data generated from the same brain. As shown in Supplementary Fig.  6 , the iSCALE pipeline successfully removed gene expression batch effects across all daughter captures. In total, iSCALE predicted super-resolution gene expression for the entire mother image, consisting of 2,013,871 superpixels, after downsampling for computational purposes. These super-resolution gene expression data allowed iSCALE to segment the tissue and identify regions closely matching pathologist manual annotation (Fig.  5a ). iSCALE successfully detected the white matter chronic lesion core (purple cluster), the rim with increased microglial activation (red cluster), normal-appearing white matter (orange cluster) and normal-appearing gray matter (blue and green clusters) continuously across the whole mother image.
