Background Ampulla of Vater (AoV) carcinoma is a malignancy arising from the ampulla of Vater, the anatomical convergence of the common bile duct, pancreatic duct, and duodenum. This unique anatomical location gives rise to both histological and molecular heterogeneity, reflecting contributions from intestinal and pancreatobiliary lineages. AoV carcinoma is often categorized into intestinal and pancreatobiliary subtypes, which exhibit distinct prognostic and therapeutic characteristics [ 1 , 2 ]. However, this binary classification does not fully account for the molecular diversity and variable clinical behavior observed among patients [ 3 ]. Previous genomic studies have provided important insights into the molecular landscape of AoV carcinoma. Notably, Yachida et al. [ 4 ] identified frequent mutations in the ELF3 gene, implicating it as a potential driver of tumorigenesis. Similarly, Gingras et al. [ 5 ] reported recurrent ELF3 inactivation and widespread dysregulation of the WNT signaling pathway. While these studies advanced our understanding of AoV carcinogenesis, they were based on whole-exome sequencing and bulk transcriptome profiling, which lack the resolution to capture cell type-specific transcriptional programs and the complexity of tumor-microenvironment interactions. As a result, the biological basis of epithelial heterogeneity and the functional contributions of non-malignant cell populations remain poorly understood. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) offers a powerful approach to address these limitations by enabling high-resolution, cell-type-resolved transcriptomic profiling [ 6 ]. This technology facilitates the identification of cellular subpopulations, and intercellular communication networks that are not accessible through bulk sequencing methods. Despite its potential, scRNA-seq has not yet been applied to AoV carcinoma, leaving fundamental gaps in our understanding of its cellular and transcriptional architecture. Therefore, our study is essential to move beyond bulk-level genomic insights and establish a high-resolution, cell-type-resolved atlas of AoV carcinoma. In this study, we present the first single-cell transcriptomic analysis of AoV carcinoma. Using scRNA-seq on primary tumor specimens, we identify distinct epithelial subtypes characterized by unique oncogenic and reveal their associations with the immune landscape and clinical outcomes. This work establishes a foundational single-cell atlas of AoV carcinoma and provides new insights into its cellular diversity with potential translational implications. Methods Study patients This study included 70 patients histologically diagnosed with AoV adenocarcinoma between September 2005 and March 2023 at Samsung Medical Center (SMC), of whom eight underwent single-cell RNA sequencing and 62 underwent bulk RNA sequencing. Patient demographics and clinical characteristics, including age, gender, tumor stage according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 8th edition, tumor differentiation, adjuvant chemotherapy administration, and survival data, were retrospectively collected. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board at SMC (IRB No. SMC-2022–06-076) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. All participants provided written informed consent for the future research use of their pathology specimens. Single-cell RNA sequencing Fresh tumor and adjacent normal tissue specimens were obtained from patients with AoV carcinoma before treatment through Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) for scRNA sequencing. Acquired tissues are collected in MACS® Tissue Storage Solution (Miltenyi Biotec., Auburn, CA, USA) on ice and processed to the single cell dissociation immediately. Biopsy tissues are placed on a petri dish with a small volume of enzyme mixture solution (Tumor Dissociation Kit, Miltenyi Biotec.) and minced into small pieces under 1–2 mm with surgical blades. Minced pieces are transferred to gentleMACS TM C-tube containing enzyme mixture solution. By choosing an appropriate program of gentleMACS TM Dissociator, tissue pieces are further dissociated three times with two interval incubations for 30 minutes at 37 °C under continuous rotation using the MACSmix TM Tube Rotator. Resuspended samples are applied to a cell strainer (70 μm) and washed with 10 ml of DMEM/F12 media with 1% FBS. After a centrifugation at 400xg for 5 minutes, cells were resuspended in an appropriate volume of media and counted with trypan blue staining or acridine orange/propidium iodide staining. Optionally, erythrocytes are removed by red blood cell lysis solution for 10 min before counting. We initiated the cell preparation process by employing the LUNA-FL™ Automated Fluorescence Cell Counter (logos biosystems). Detailed guidelines for cell preparation were sourced from the 10x Genomics Single Cell Protocols Cell Preparation Guide and the Guidelines for Optimal Sample Preparation flowchart. Libraries were meticulously constructed using the Chromium controller in accordance with the 10x Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3’ v3.1 protocol (10x Genomics). In brief, cell suspensions were diluted in nuclease-free water, aiming to achieve a targeted cell count of 10,000. The diluted cell suspension was mixed with a master mix and subsequently loaded onto a Chromium Next GEM chip, along with Single Cell 3’ V3.1 gel beads and partitioning oil. Within the droplets formed in the chip, RNA transcripts from individual cells underwent unique barcoding and reverse transcription. Pooled cDNA molecules then underwent sequential processes, including end repair, addition of a single ‘A’ base, and adapter ligation. Subsequently, the resulting products were subjected to purification and enrichment through polymerase chain reaction (PCR), ultimately yielding the final cDNA library. To ensure library quality and quantify the purified libraries, we adhered to the qPCR Quantification Protocol Guide (KAPA). Furthermore, library qualification was performed using the Agilent Technologies 4200 TapeStation from Agilent Technologies. The sequenced libraries were processed using the HiSeqX platform from Illumina to obtain the requisite data for our study. Data preprocessing and quality control Raw sequencing data were processed using CellRanger (v7.0.1; 10x Genomics) [ 7 ], with alignment to the GRCh38 reference genome via STAR. CellBender (v 0.2.2) [ 8 ] was applied to each sample to eliminate background RNA contamination. Doublets were detected using Scrublet (v 0.2.3) [ 9 ], with thresholds determined according to simulation-derived scores. we excluded low-quality cells with fewer than 500 detected genes and a mitochondrial gene proportion exceeding 20%. Seurat (v4.3.0) [ 10 ] was used for downstream processing, including normalization, variable gene selection, scaling (regressing out total UMI counts, mitochondrial gene proportion, and cell cycle scores), principal component analysis, and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) projection. Clustering was performed using the FindNeighbors and FindClusters functions, with dimensionality assessed via JackStraw and ElbowPlot methods. Cell type annotation was conducted using SingleR (v2.0.0) [ 11 ] and further validated through the expression of canonical lineage markers. Major cell types were identified using EPCAM (epithelial cells), COL1A1 (fibroblasts), VWF (endothelial cells), CD3D (T cells), CD14 (myeloid cells), and CD79A (B cells). For more granular annotation of immune and stromal subsets, we utilized the following marker sets: CD4 for helper T cells, CD8 for cytotoxic T cells, FOXP3 for regulatory T cells (Tregs), and NCAM1 and NCR1 for NK cells. Myeloid sub-populations were defined by C1QC (macrophages), LYZ and S100A9 (monocytes), CD1C (dendritic cells), and CPA3 and KIT (mast cells). B cell lineages were further distinguished using CD79A and MS4A1 (B cells), CD38 and CD27 (plasma cells). Subclustering analyses were performed on major immune and stromal compartments following additional doublet removal [ 12 ]. Identification of epithelial subtypes using cNMF To identify transcriptional programs within epithelial cells, we applied consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF) (v0.2) [ 13 ] to the normalized gene expression matrix. The number of components (k) was varied from 2 to 15, and the optimal solution was selected based on silhouette scores and Frobenius reconstruction error. Copy number variation inference To infer copy number alterations at the single-cell level, CopyKAT (v1.1.0) [ 14 ] was applied with default parameters. T cells were used as a reference for normal diploid profiles. CNV scores were computed for individual epithelial cells and summarized across samples to evaluate subtype-specific genomic instability. Transcription factor regulatory network inference Regulatory network analysis was performed using the pySCENIC (v0.12.1) [ 15 ] pipeline. Regulon activity scores were computed from raw UMI matrices to identify transcription factor-target gene modules, and average activity scores were calculated per subtype for downstream comparative analyses. Modular score and stemness estimation The CytoTRACE algorithm (v0.3.3) [ 16 ] was used to infer the differentiation potential of malignant epithelial cells. CytoTRACE computes transcriptional diversity and expression correlation to derive stemness scores, ranging from 0 (fully differentiated) to 1 (highly undifferentiated). This approach enables the identification of less differentiated, stem-like cell states at single-cell resolution. To evaluate functional characteristics of epithelial subtypes, including stemness potential, we calculated gene module scores using AddModuleScore function in the Seurat package. This approach determines the average expression of a specific gene program at the single-cell level, which is then normalized by subtracting the aggregated expression of control feature sets. To ensure a robust baseline, all analyzed features are binned based on their average expression levels, and control features are randomly selected from each bin. This process effectively accounts for technical noise and the influence of overall gene expression profiles. The stemness gene set was constructed using previously reported stemness-associated markers [ 17 ]. Functional enrichment analysis Differentially expressed genes were selected based on adjusted p -values and fold changes. Functional enrichment analysis was performed using EnrichR (v3.2) [ 18 ], employing the hypergeometric test with default parameters to identify overrepresented pathways and biological processes. We employed the hypergeometric test with default parameters to identify overrepresented pathways and biological processes from the MSigDB Hallmark gene set collection. Cell-cell communication analysis Ligand-receptor interaction analysis was conducted using CellPhoneDB (v5.0.0) [ 19 ] to identify potential intercellular communication events between cell types. Significant interactions were inferred via permutation testing using default parameters. Pseudotime trajectory analysis To infer the developmental hierarchy of epithelial subtypes, we performed pseudotime trajectory analysis using the Monocle2 R package (v2.30.0) [ 20 ]. To minimize potential biological variations across patients, we utilized the integrated data generated via the FindIntegrationAnchors and IntegrateData functions from the Seurat package. For trajectory ordering, we selected the top 30 differentially expressed genes from each epithelial cluster. Dimensionality reduction was performed using the DDRTree algorithm. Bulk RNA sequencing and processing For bulk RNA sequencing, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor tissues from an independent cohort of surgically resected 62 AoV carcinoma patients were analyzed. Transcript-level quantification was achieved using RSEM (v1.3.0) [ 21 ], aligned to the GRCh38 genome with GENCODE v33 annotation. Gene-level expression matrices were derived for integrative analyses with single-cell data. Proportions of each subtype were estimated in bulk RNA-seq samples using MuSiC (v1.0.0) [ 22 ]. Xenium in situ hybridization and spatial analysis Surgically resected FFPE tissue samples from AoV tumor patients were profiled using Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue and Pathways Panel (10x Genomics). FFPE tissue sections (5 µm) were prepared on Xenium slides using Xenium Prime Sample Preparation Reagents. RNA quality was assessed by calculating the percentage of RNA fragments > 200 nucleotides (DV200) extracted from tissue sections, and H&E staining were also used to assess tissue morphology and region of interests by a specialized pathologist before performing the Xenium in situ hybridization. Slides were deparaffinized, rehydrated and decrosslinked, followed by hybridization with Xenium 5K Priming Oligos and probes targeting messenger RNA. Probes were ligated, amplified and washed, with subsequent antibody staining for cell segmentation. Autofluorescence quenching and nuclei staining were performed and slides they were stored in phosphate-buffered saline with tween-20 (PBS-T) at 4 °C. The Xenium Analyzer (version 3.1) was used for imaging, decoding, segmentation and cell assignment, following the manufacturer’s protocols. During the initial quality control and filtering step, cells with a transcript count below 100 were classified as low-quality and excluded from all downstream analyses. For cell type classification, we utilized our own scRNA-seq dataset as the reference. Cell assignment was performed using the FindTransferAnchors and TransferData functions within the Seurat package, employing default parameters. Cells with a prediction score below 0.5 were classified as unknown and excluded from further downstream analyses. Survival analysis The clinical relevance of epithelial subtypes was evaluated using survival analysis. Kaplan-Meier curves were generated using the survival and survminer R packages (v0.5.2). Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression models were implemented using the coxph function to assess associations with overall survival and disease-free survival. Statistical analysis All statistical analyses were performed in R. Pair-wise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were utilized to analyze the proportional differences between groups within each cell type/subset. Significance is displayed as *, p  < 0.05; **, p  < 0.01; and ***, p  < 0.001. For comparisons among multiple groups, the Kruskal-Wallis test was used to determine global significance, followed by Dunn’s test for pairwise post-hoc comparisons with adjustments for multiple testing. Statistical significance for multiple comparisons is presented as adjusted p -values (Padj), indicated as follows: *, Padj < 0.05;, Padj < 0.01; and ***, Padj < 0.001. Pearson correlation was employed to calculate the correlation between the proportions of each pair of cell subsets, and Spearman correlation was used for the co-ecosystem analysis. Results Patient characteristics This study included 70 patients (scRNA-seq: n  = 8 and bulk RNA-seq: n  = 62) with AoV carcinoma. Median age was 61.5 years (range, 36–83 years) and 33 were male (47.1%). Tumor stage (AJCC 8th edition) was I-III in the majority of patients (67/70, 95.7%), with only one patient classified as stage 0 and two as stage IV. During a median follow-up of 9.7 years (interquartile range, 6.4–12.7 years), 27 deaths (38.6%) occurred (Table S1 ). Single-cell transcriptomic profiling reveals diverse cellular composition in AoV carcinoma To investigate the cellular architecture of AoV carcinoma, we performed scRNA-seq on tumors ( n  = 8) and matched adjacent normal tissues ( n  = 4) (Fig. 1 a). After quality filtering, a total of 34,672 cells were analyzed and grouped into 18 clusters, which were subsequently classified into six major cell types based on cell type marker gene expression (Fig. 1 b–c). UMAP visualization revealed that while immune cells were broadly shared across patients, epithelial cell clusters displayed strong patient-specific transcriptional profiles, consistent with the absence of batch effects and reflecting inter-patient variation driven by tumor-specific copy number alterations [ 23 , 24 ] (Fig. 1 d). We further examined the distribution of cell types across individual samples, revealing substantial inter-patient heterogeneity in cellular composition (Fig. 1 e). Some tumors were highly enriched in epithelial or myeloid populations, whereas others showed greater T cell infiltration. These findings highlight the cellular complexity of AoV carcinoma and underscore the diversity of tumor-immune microenvironments across patients. Fig. 1 Single-cell transcriptomic profiling of ampulla of Vater (AoV) carcinoma tissues. ( a ) Schematic overview of the study design. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was performed on 8 AoV tumor samples and 4 matched normal tissues. Bulk RNA-seq data from 62 AoV samples were also generated. ( b ) Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) visualization of major cell types identified in scRNA-seq data. Cells are colored by their annotated cell type: B cell, endothelial cell, epithelial cell, fibroblast, myeloid, and T cell. ( c ) Feature plots showing expression of representative marker genes for each major cell type: EPCAM (epithelial), COL1A1 (fibroblast), VWF (endothelial), CD3D (T cell), CD14 (myeloid), and CD79A (B cell). Expression levels are indicated by color intensity. ( d ) UMAP plot of scRNA-seq data color-coded by individual patient. ( e ) Estimated cell-type proportions in scRNA-seq data across tumor ( T ) and matched normal ( N ) samples for each patient, based on annotation from ( b ). Bar plots display relative proportions of each major cell type Epithelial subtyping reveals distinct transcriptional programs and inter-patient heterogeneity To investigate epithelial heterogeneity in AoV carcinoma, we performed subclustering of epithelial cells. This analysis revealed strong patient-specific clustering patterns (Fig. 2 a), indicating pronounced transcriptional differences between tumors. We then applied consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF) to the epithelial transcriptomes, identifying four robust molecular subtypes (NMF-1 to NMF-4) (Fig. S1 a-b). Although each subtype included epithelial cells from multiple patients, their relative proportions varied markedly across samples (Fig. 2 b). This suggests that, while certain transcriptional programs are shared among tumors, their dominance is highly patient-specific, reflecting substantial inter-patient heterogeneity. Fig. 2 Identification and characterization of transcriptional subtypes in AoV carcinoma. ( a ) UMAP visualization of epithelial cells from AoV tissues ( n  = 8), color-coded by patient sample. ( b ) Proportional composition of four transcriptional subtypes (NMF-1 to NMF-4) in each AoV tumor, identified by consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF) clustering of epithelial transcriptomes. ( c ) Violin plots showing expression levels of well-known marker genes associated with AoV subtypes: CDX2 and KRT20 (intestinal subtype), MUC1 and KRT7 (pancreatobiliary subtype). ( d ) Functional enrichment analysis of each transcriptional subtype, visualized as a bubble plot. The pathways were identified using the MSigDB hallmark gene set collection. The size of each dot represents the statistical significance (-log 10 adjusted p -value), and the color denotes the corresponding transcriptional subtype We further examined the expression of established AoV subtype marker genes across the four subtypes (Fig. 2 c). Intestinal markers ( CDX2 and KRT20 ) were strongly expressed in NMF-1 and NMF-3, whereas pancreatobiliary markers ( KRT7 and MUC1 ) were predominantly enriched in NMF-2. These findings support the biological relevance of the identified subtypes and their alignment with previously described histological features [ 2 , 25 ]. Functional enrichment analysis revealed distinct transcriptional programs characterizing each subtype (Fig. 2 d and Table S2 ): NMF-1 was enriched for Wnt/β-catenin signaling (designated Int-Wnt), NMF-2 for KRAS signaling (PB-KRAS), NMF-3 for hypoxia-related pathways (Int-Hypoxia), and NMF-4 for cell cycle-associated signatures (Cycling). We categorize these four programs as three lineage-driven, differentiated subtypes and one progenitor/functional subtype (NMF-4, Cycling). To further characterize the regulatory landscape underlying epithelial heterogeneity, we performed regulon activity analysis across epithelial cells. This analysis revealed that multiple transcription factor regulons were differentially activated in a subtype-specific manner (Fig. S1 c). MSX1 activity was predominantly elevated in the Int-Wnt subtype compared to the PB-KRAS and Cycling subtypes. HNF1B activity reached its highest levels in the PB-KRAS subtype, showing a significant increase over the Cycling subtype and a strong upward trend compared to the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtypes. SIRT6 activity was notably enriched in the Int-Hypoxia subtype, while CDX1 was most active in the Cycling subtype, significantly surpassing the levels in the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia groups (Fig. S1 d). The MSX1 is a known WNT/β-catenin responsive transcription factor implicated in promoting intestinal tumorigenesis [ 26 ]. Similarly, the enrichment of HNF1B in the PB-KRAS subtype is relevant, as its overexpression has been shown to enhance the expression of liver progenitor cell markers and stemness in liver cancer cells [ 27 ]. Finally, the activation of the SIRT6 regulon in the Int-Hypoxia subtype is consistent with its known role in enhancing the stability of HIF-1α, a process linked to epithelial-mesenchymal transition under hypoxic conditions [ 28 ]. These regulon profiles were concordant with the transcriptional programs defined by cNMF, further supporting the molecular distinction among AoV epithelial subtypes. Collectively, these results demonstrate that epithelial cells in AoV carcinoma exhibit diverse transcriptional states driven by lineage-specific and oncogenic programs, with subtype composition varying substantially between tumors. PB-KRAS subtype exhibit distinct genomic instability and stem-like properties To interrogate the degree of genomic instability underlying each epithelial subtype, we first analyzed copy number variation (CNV) profiles inferred from single-cell transcriptomes. Notably, CNV patterns were strongly patient-specific, indicating inter-patient variability in genomic alterations (Fig. 3 a). At the single-cell level, CNV scores were markedly elevated in tumor epithelial cells compared to non-epithelial controls, with the PB-KRAS subtype exhibiting the highest levels of genomic aberrations (Fig. S2 a). To validate these findings at the sample level, we averaged CNV scores across epithelial cells within each sample and compared them across subtypes. This analysis confirmed that the PB-KRAS subtype exhibits the highest CNV burden among all epithelial subtypes (Kruskal-Wallis, p  = 0.00013; Fig. 3 b). These results indicate that genomic instability is unevenly distributed among AoV epithelial subtypes and is particularly pronounced in PB-KRAS subtype. For pairwise post-hoc comparisons, Dunn’s test was used to adjust for multiple comparisons. *Padj < 0.05, ** Padj < 0.01, *** Padj < 0.001; n.s., not significant Given that high genomic instability is frequently associated with aggressive phenotypes and enhanced self-renewal capacity [ 29 ], we next investigated the functional and developmental hierarchy of these subtypes. Based on its highest CNV burden, we specifically focused on evaluating the stem-like properties of the PB-KRAS subtype. We first focused on the Cycling subtype. Given its cell cycle-associated transcriptional program and the enrichment of progenitor-associated regulons, such as CDX1 (Fig. S1 d), we hypothesized that it represents a less differentiated, progenitor-like state. To infer the developmental potential across all subtypes, we employed CytoTRACE [ 16 ], a computational tool that infers developmental potential using transcriptional entropy. As expected, the Cycling subtype exhibited high CytoTRACE scores (Fig. 3 c and Fig. S2 b), supporting its identity as a less differentiated, progenitor-like state. Surprisingly, the PB-KRAS subtype, which otherwise presents as a differentiated lineage, exhibited the highest CytoTRACE scores (Fig. 3 c and Fig. S2 b), suggesting unexpected stem-like features. This combination—a seemingly differentiated state with high developmental potential—defines a non-canonical stemness phenotype. This suggests that, unlike the canonical progenitor-like Cycling subtype, the PB-KRAS subtype represents a distinct, highly aggressive stem-like epithelial state that deviates from the typical differentiation pathway. To further examine this possibility, we calculated stemness scores based on a curated stem cell gene signature [ 17 ]. The PB-KRAS subtype exhibited elevated stemness scores that were comparable to those of Cycling cells, while remaining notably higher than the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtypes (Kruskal-Wallis, p  = 0.00043; Fig. 3 d and Fig. S2 c). To provide dynamic evidence of this developmental hierarchy, we performed pseudotime trajectory analysis using Monocle2 [ 20 ]. The resulting trajectory delineated a clear lineage progression originating from the Cycling subtype, passing through the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtype, and ultimately culminating in the PB-KRAS subtype at the terminal end (Fig. 3 e). Notably, despite its terminal position on the pseudotime axis—which typically denotes a fully differentiated state—the PB-KRAS subtype harbored exceptionally high developmental potential, consistent with its elevated CytoTRACE (Fig. 3 f) and stemness scores (Fig. 3 g). This paradoxical terminal stemness suggests that PB-KRAS cells do not merely follow a conventional differentiation path but may undergo a coordinated transcriptional reprogramming or de-differentiation process, re-acquiring progenitor-like properties at an advanced stage of lineage development. We next sought to determine the potential molecular drivers of this phenotype, focusing on KRAS , the defining feature of the PB-KRAS subtype. Expression of KRAS was significantly upregulated in PB-KRAS subtype compared to the Int-Wnt subtypes (Fig. 3 h and Fig. S2 d), whereas CNV at the KRAS locus showed no significant difference among the subtypes (Fig. 3 i). Consistent with this, correlation analysis at the sample level revealed a moderate positive correlation between CNV score and stemness score ( r  = 0.5, p  = 0.014, Fig. S2 e). Furthermore, the expression of KRAS showed a strong positive correlation with both stemness score ( r  = 0.6, p  = 0.002, Fig. S2 f) and CNV score ( r  = 0.59, p  = 0.002, Fig. S2 g). These findings collectively highlight the robust association of both genomic instability and KRAS expression with the enhanced stem-like properties of the PB-KRAS subtype. Since KRAS knockdown in pancreatic cancer cells is known to reduce stemness characteristics [ 30 ], these observations suggest that the transcriptional upregulation of KRAS , rather than genomic alterations, is the likely contributor to the stemness signature of the PB-KRAS subtype. Epithelial subtypes confer distinct prognostic significance and clinical relevance in AoV carcinoma To evaluate the clinical significance of the four epithelial subtypes (Int-Wnt, PB-KRAS, Int-Hypoxia, and Cycling), we first deconvoluted their proportions in bulk RNA-seq profiles from 62 AoV carcinoma samples using the single-cell-derived subtype signatures. Among these, the Int-Wnt subtype was the most abundant, followed by Int-Hypoxia and PB-KRAS, whereas the Cycling subtype was relatively rare across samples (Fig. 4 a and Table S3 ). Regarding tumor stage, the Int-Hypoxia subtype was found to be more prevalent in Stage I tumors compared to Stage II (Padj = 0.045; Fig. S3 d). Next, we examined the prognostic impact of each subtype on OS. Proportions of Int-Wnt subtype was positively correlated with OS ( r  = 0.4, p  = 0.001) (Fig. 4 b), while PB-KRAS subtype abundance was negatively correlated with survival ( r  = −0.34, p  = 0.007) (Fig. 4 c). To determine whether AoV subtypes independently contribute to prognosis, we performed multivariate Cox regression analyses incorporating clinical covariates. Notably, PB-KRAS subtype was significantly associated with worse OS (hazard ratio; HR = 116.6, 95% confidence interval; CI = 5.4–2496.6, p  = 0.002) and DFS (HR = 101.1, 95% CI = 3.3–3132.4, p  = 0.008), independent of other factors (Fig. 4 e–f), while Int-Wnt subtype was significantly associated with improved prognosis (DFS: HR = 0.1, 95% CI = 0.004–0.7, p  = 0.028) (Fig. 4 f). Consistently, univariate Cox regression analyses supported the prognostic significance of PB-KRAS subtype for both OS and DFS (Fig. S3 e-f). Together, these findings highlight that the composition of epithelial subtypes, particularly PB-KRAS and Int-Wnt subtype, has significant prognostic and clinical relevance in AoV carcinoma. The PB-KRAS subtype is associated with a most distinctly aggressive phenotype and a higher likelihood of recurrence. At the single-cell level, the proportion of Tc- GZMK cells was strongly correlated with the abundance of PB-KRAS subtype within each tumor ( r  = 0.98, p  < 0.001; Fig. 5 c). These Tc- GZMK cells represent a pre-dysfunctional state of CD8 + T cells [ 31 ], characterized by the robust expression of effector molecules such as GZMK and the absence of terminal exhaustion markers like HAVCR2 , while exhibiting moderate levels of early activation markers such as LAG3 (Fig. S4 a). This association was further validated in bulk RNA-seq data, where higher PB-KRAS subtype proportions were positively correlated with Tc- GZMK proportions across patients ( r  = 0.26, p  = 0.037; Fig. 5 d). These results suggest a potential interaction between PB-KRAS subtype and Tc- GZMK cells. We also examined whether their abundance was associated with clinical outcomes. Patients with high Tc- GZMK cell proportions exhibited significantly worse OS compared to those with lower levels (Fig. 5 e). We next explored potential epithelial-immune crosstalk using ligand-receptor interaction analysis. PB-KRAS subtype exhibited enriched interactions with Tc- GZMK cells through multiple ligand-receptor axes, including TGFB2 , SPP1 , and FGF2 , which are well-known mediators of immunosuppressive signaling (Fig. S4 b). These factors are associated with T cell exhaustion, suppression of cytotoxic responses, and immune evasion, suggesting that PB-KRAS subtype may contribute to shaping a dysfunctional yet Tc- GZMK -rich immune microenvironment. Spatial profiling reveals an immunosuppressive microenvironment in PB-KRAS subtype regions To investigate the spatial relationships between cellular subtypes and the tumor microenvironment, we performed Xenium in situ analysis on two representative AoV carcinoma samples, categorized as intestinal type and pancreatobiliary type based on the consensus judgment of experienced pathologists examining the tumor sections (Fig. 5 f). We first used single-cell RNA sequencing to estimate the major cell types and then mapped their spatial distribution across the tissue (Fig. 5 g). To investigate subtype-specific spatial patterns, we next identified and distinguished specific regions within the tumors, focusing on the AoV-ST1 sample, which are characterized by high proportions of Int-Hypoxia, and the AoV-ST2 sample, which are characterized by high proportions of the PB-KRAS subtype (Fig. 5 h). Importantly, the classification of regions derived from scRNA-seq mapping into Int-Hypoxia high (AoV-ST1) and PB-KRAS high (AoV-ST2) categories showed strong agreement with the initial pathological classification. Visualization of the spatial maps revealed a striking co-localization between the PB-KRAS subtype and Tc-GZMK cells (indicated by triangle-shaped dots), with a denser infiltration observed in the PB-KRAS high sample (Fig. 5 h). Quantitative analysis confirmed this observation: the PB-KRAS high sample exhibited a markedly higher proportion of PB-KRAS cells (among all epithelial cells) and a corresponding elevation in the proportion of Tc- GZMK cells (among all T cells) compared to the Int-Hypoxia high sample (Fig. 5 i). To further validate the spatial association between these populations, we performed a nearest neighbor distance analysis using the Xenium spatial coordinates. Our results revealed that Tc- GZMK cells were located significantly closer to PB-KRAS cells, with a mean minimum distance of 114.3 µm, whereas the distance to Int-hypoxia cells was nearly three-fold higher at 321.4 µm (Fig. 5 j). To visually confirm the presence of the Tc- GZMK population, we performed multiplex immunofluorescence using MACSima Imaging System ( n  = 3 per each group; see supplementary methods). Although this population was relatively sparse, pancreatobiliary subtype enriched samples showed higher infiltration of Tc- GZMK cells, whereas intestinal subtype dominant tumors displayed sparse Tc- GZMK infiltration (Fig. S5 a-b). Quantification confirmed that the proportion of Tc- GZMK cells was significantly higher in Pancreatobiliary subtype compared to intestinal subtype tumors ( p  = 0.0375; Fig. S5 c). These initial findings collectively suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype is associated with a distinctive and highly infiltrated tumor microenvironment. PB-KRAS subtype associates with an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment To gain deeper insights into the immune microenvironment of AoV carcinoma, we conducted detailed subclustering analyses specifically focusing on myeloid and B lineage cells. This allowed us to resolve cellular heterogeneity within these immune compartments. Myeloid cells were classified into distinct subpopulations including macrophages, monocytes, dendritic cells (DCs), and mast cells based on canonical lineage markers and differentially expressed genes (Fig. 6 a), with neutrophils excluded from this analysis because they were predominantly derived from a single sample (Fig. S6 a-b). Similarly, B lineage cells were divided into naive B cells and multiple subsets of plasma cells, each characterized by unique transcriptomic signatures (Fig. 6 b). These refined annotations enabled a more precise characterization of cell-type-specific contributions to the tumor microenvironment. Notably, the PB-KRAS subtype exhibited strong positive correlations with macrophage- SPP1 and Tc- GZMK clusters (Fig. 6 c). SPP1 -expressing macrophages have previously been associated with immunosuppressive and pro-tumorigenic functions [ 32 , 33 ]. In addition to the T cell infiltration, the spatial distribution of pro-tumorigenic myeloid cells also exhibited a marked preference for the PB-KRAS-rich environment. The nearest neighbor distance analysis demonstrated that macrophage- SPP1 were predominantly localized in close proximity to the PB-KRAS subtype, with a mean distance of 352.6 µm, compared to a significantly larger distance of 903.0 µm from the Int-hypoxia subtype (Fig. 5 j). To investigate the molecular mechanisms that may underlie this observation, we conducted a formal cell-cell communication analysis between epithelial subtypes and myeloid subclusters. This analysis identified several significant signaling axes, including PTN-ALK, FGF2–FGFR1, and FGF19–FGFR1, which were specifically enriched in the interaction between the PB-KRAS subtype and SPP1 + macrophages (Fig. S6 c). Notably, FGF2 is a well-established mediator known to promote the polarization of tumor-associated macrophages toward a pro-tumorigenic, M2-like state within the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment [ 34 ]. These findings provide molecular evidence that the PB-KRAS subtype actively modulates the functional phenotype of the myeloid compartment, offering a mechanistic basis that extends beyond mere numerical correlation. These findings suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype may develop within, or contribute to, a uniquely immunologically conditioned microenvironment enriched in tumor-promoting macrophages and pre-dysfunctional CD8 + T cells. This immune landscape may underlie the aggressive behavior and recurrence-prone nature of this epithelial subtype. Further mechanistic studies are warranted to clarify the functional significance of these immune–epithelial interactions and evaluate their potential as therapeutic targets. Discussion This study presents the first single-cell transcriptomic analysis of AoV carcinoma, offering a high-resolution landscape of its epithelial and immune cell composition. Previous genomic investigations, primarily based on whole-exome sequencing, have significantly advanced our understanding of AoV carcinoma by identifying recurrent alterations such as ELF3 mutations and WNT pathway dysregulation [ 4 , 5 ]. However, these bulk approaches lack the granularity required to resolve cell type-specific programs and microenvironmental interactions. Our single-cell approach addresses these limitations and provides novel insights into epithelial heterogeneity, differentiation states, and tumor-immune crosstalk in AoV carcinoma. Among the four molecular subtypes identified, our data demonstrate that the intestinal subtype itself is not homogeneous but comprises at least two molecularly distinct programs: one characterized by active WNT/β-catenin signaling (Int-Wnt) and another driven by hypoxia-associated pathways (Int-Hypoxia). The Int-Wnt subtype was defined by robust expression of WNT target genes and selective activation of the MSX1 regulon. MSX1 is known to function downstream of WNT/β-catenin signaling, playing a key role in promoting intestinal tumorigenesis. Its loss suppresses ectopic crypt formation in Apc-deficient models, suggesting that MSX1 is a critical mediator of WNT-driven epithelial transformation [ 26 ]. These features suggest that the Int-Wnt subtype retains a proliferative, WNT-responsive phenotype reminiscent of early intestinal neoplasia. In contrast, the Int-Hypoxia subtype displayed prominent enrichment of hypoxia-related gene sets and strong activation of the SIRT6 regulon. This suggests a mechanism involving SIRT6-enhanced stability of HIF-1α, which is known to promote the expression of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-related transcription factors like SNAIL and TWIST [ 28 ]. The resultant overexpression of SNAIL and TWIST leads to suppression of E-cadherin and induction of Vimentin, hallmark events of EMT [ 28 ]. This molecular cascade facilitates increased cellular plasticity and motility, thereby promoting invasive behavior. EMT has been associated with enhanced metastatic potential and poor recurrence-free survival in several cancers, including papillary thyroid carcinoma, and may similarly portend aggressive clinical behavior in the Int-Hypoxia subtype of AoV carcinoma. By uncovering both a WNT-driven and a hypoxia-induced EMT program within the intestinal group, our analysis emphasizes the subtype’s underlying complexity and suggests that these distinctions may carry prognostic or therapeutic significance. The PB-KRAS subtype emerged as a particularly notable finding in our comprehensive epithelial subtyping. This subtype is defined by elevated KRAS expression and a transcriptional program robustly enriched for KRAS signaling. The PB-KRAS subtype exhibited a pronounced degree of genomic instability, carrying the highest CNV burden among all identified epithelial subtypes. Reflecting these substantial genomic aberrations, which are often associated with aggressive and self-renewal-enhancing phenotypes, we were guided to investigate its developmental hierarchy and specifically focused on evaluating its stem-like properties. Strikingly, the PB-KRAS subtype paradoxically exhibited high developmental potential and stemness scores, comparable to the canonical progenitor-like Cycling subtype. This unique combination of an apparent differentiated PB lineage state possessing high developmental potential defines a non-canonical stem-like epithelial state. Unlike the Cycling subtype, which represents a classical progenitor state, PB-KRAS cells achieve stemness through oncogenic signaling. Specifically, we found that the stemness signature was driven by the transcriptional upregulation of KRAS expression, independent of differential CNV at the KRAS locus. This suggests that elevated KRAS expression forces an aberrant, de-differentiated potential within a seemingly mature lineage. This is consistent with prior findings implicating KRAS signaling in the maintenance of stem-like features in pancreatic cancer cells [ 30 ]. Supporting this stem-like phenotype, HNF1B regulon activity was also selectively enriched in the PB-KRAS subtype. As HNF1B overexpression has been shown to enhance the expression of liver progenitor cell markers and stemness in liver cancer cells [ 27 ], this activation suggests a conserved role in supporting KRAS-associated epithelial states. Clinically, the PB-KRAS subtype was associated with significantly worse OS and DFS, as well as a higher incidence of recurrence. These findings collectively suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype program, defined by unique genomic instability and a KRAS-driven non-canonical stemness, represents the most clinically aggressive AoV subtype identified in this study, associated with poor outcomes and inherent therapeutic resistance. In addition to epithelial heterogeneity, our analysis revealed striking differences in the immune landscape across subtypes. PB-KRAS subtype were enriched for a distinct immune microenvironment characterized by abundant GZMK + CD8 + T cells (Tc-GZMK cells) and SPP1 + macrophages. GZMK enriched cytotoxic T cells, recently described as pre-dysfunctional T cells, represent an intermediate state preceding terminal T cell exhaustion [ 31 ]. Their accumulation within the PB-KRAS tumor microenvironment, coupled with spatial proximity to tumor epithelium and signaling through immunosuppressive ligand-receptor pairs (such as TGFB2 , FGF2 , and SPP1 ), strongly suggests active immune remodeling by tumor cells. These specific axes are known mediators of immunosuppressive signaling. For instance, TGF-β is known to suppress CD8 + T cell cytotoxicity by repressing a distinct program of cytotoxic gene responses, thereby limiting the antitumor immune response [ 35 ]. Similarly, FGF2 has been implicated in promoting T-cell exhaustion by regulating the expression of SPRY1 in esophageal tumor-infiltrating T cells, further impairing T cell function [ 36 ]. SPP1 directly suppresses CD8 + T cell proliferation and interferon-γ production, contributing to immune evasion by the tumor [ 37 ]. The co-enrichment of SPP1 + macrophages, previously implicated in promoting immune evasion and supporting tumor progression, further supports the presence of an immunosuppressive TME in PB-KRAS subtype. Importantly, high abundance of Tc-GZMK cells was associated with poor clinical outcomes, reinforcing the relevance of the immune milieu in disease progression. Taken together, our findings suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype defines a biologically aggressive, stem-like epithelial population that may either arise within or actively sculpt an immunosuppressive TME enriched for dysfunctional immune cell states. This epithelial-immune crosstalk may contribute to tumor recurrence and resistance to therapy. In contrast, the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtypes are characterized by alternative oncogenic programs and immune environments, with divergent prognostic implications. A key limitation of this study is that the observed association between the PB-KRAS subtype and the immunosuppressive TME is based on correlational multi-omics analysis rather than direct functional validation. It is well established that activating KRAS mutations can actively modulate the immune microenvironment by promoting pro-tumorigenic macrophage polarization, inhibiting T-cell cytotoxicity, and accelerating T-cell exhaustion. Moreover, KRAS-mediated metabolic reprogramming may create a feedback loop where metabolite accumulation induces further genomic instability and mutational burden [ 38 ]. Although our findings regarding the PB-KRAS subtype are highly consistent with these known roles of KRAS signaling, further in vivo studies—such as orthotopic or syngeneic mouse models—and co-culture experiments are necessary to definitively prove the causal role of PB-KRAS cells in shaping this specific immunosuppressive niche. Moreover, while the specific ligand-receptor axes identified in this study, such as TGFB2 and SPP1, represent highly promising therapeutic targets, we acknowledge that their functional significance requires further validation in follow-up translational models utilizing functional blocking with neutralizing antibodies or small molecule inhibitors in patient-derived organoid-immune co-culture systems. These insights have potential therapeutic implications. Targeting the KRAS-HNF1B axis or the immunosuppressive mediators enriched in PB-KRAS subtype may offer novel avenues for treatment. Moreover, immunotherapeutic strategies aiming to restore CD8 + T cell functionality or reprogram tumor-associated macrophages may be particularly effective in this context. Future studies should focus on elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying epithelial-immune interactions in AoV carcinoma and evaluating their druggability in preclinical models. Additionally, although the multivariate analysis yielded an inflated hazard ratio due to complete separation in our small cohort ( n  = 62), Bootstrap validation (1,000 resamples) confirmed the statistical stability and robust prognostic value of the PB-KRAS subtype. Given the limited number of patients included in the single-cell analysis, validation in larger multi-institutional cohorts will be important to further establish the generalizability and potential clinical utility of the PB-KRAS subtype classification. Conclusions Our single-cell atlas of AoV carcinoma reveals profound epithelial and immune heterogeneity and identifies a clinically relevant PB-KRAS subtype defined by KRAS-driven non-canonical stem-like features and an immunosuppressive microenvironment. These findings provide a foundation for precision classification of AoV carcinoma and suggest novel therapeutic vulnerabilities for high-risk patients. Biological entity Colon Experimental variable colorectal cancer (CRC) spec-5-gkvg Specimen Title TO_019 Sample preparation protocol Tonsil tissue sections were placed on SuperFrost PlusTM microscope slides (Thermo Scientific) for individual or combined Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression (10x Genomics) and COMET (Bio-Techne). For Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression analysis, SuperFrost Plus slides with FFPE tissues underwent deparaffinization, H&E staining, imaging and decrosslinking exactly according to the Visium HD FFPE Tissue Preparation Handbook (CG000684, 10x Genomics). After H&E staining, samples were imaged using the SLIDEVIEW VS200 slide scanner (ref, Evident) at 20x magnification. Visium HD Gene Expression libraries were then generated using the Visium HD, Human Transcriptome, 6.5mm reagents (PN: 1000675, 10x Genomics) and following the Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Reagent Kits User Guide (CG000685, 10x Genomics). Quality control and molarity calculations of the libraries were performed with Qubit 3.0 Fluorometer (#Q33216, Invitrogen) and 4200 Tapestation system (Agilent Technologies). Libraries were sequenced on the NovaSeq X+ 10B at paired-end 100bp. spec-12-hdqe-removable Specimen Title TO_017 Sample preparation protocol Tonsil tissue sections were placed on SuperFrost PlusTM microscope slides (Thermo Scientific) for individual or combined Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression (10x Genomics) and COMET(Bio-Techne). Sequential Immunofluorescence (SeqIF) staining was performed on FFPE tissue sections using COMET system from Lunaphore, according to standard protocol for proteomic applications (User manual – COMET, Revision: 006).
Briefly, SuperFrost Plus slides with FFPE tissue underwent deparaffinization and antigen retrieval using Dewax and HIER buffer, pH 9 (Epredia, #TA-999-DHBH) in the PT module (Epredia, ref) at 102°C for 1h, with pre-heating temperature set to 85°C and cool-end temperature to 65°C. Following antigen retrieval, slides were rinsed and kept in the Multistaining Buffer (BU06, Lunaphore) until loading them on to the instrument for SeqIF. SeqIF staining was performed on the COMET using the SPYRE Immuno-oncology Core Panel (Lunaphore) supplemented with pan-Cytokeratin antibody (ref). SeqIF protocol was set up on the COMET control software and sequential staining, imaging, and elution cycles were performed on the instrument as per manufacturer’s protocol. Imaging was performed with 12.5 x 12.5mm imaging area.  spec-13-3mlz-removable Specimen Title TO_018 Sample preparation protocol Tonsil tissue sections were placed on SuperFrost PlusTM microscope slides (Thermo Scientific) for individual or combined Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression (10x Genomics) and COMET(Bio-Techne)
Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Analysis post- H&E staining:

For Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression analysis, SuperFrost Plus slides with FFPE tissues underwent deparaffinization, H&E staining, imaging and decrosslinking exactly according to the Visium HD FFPE Tissue Preparation Handbook (CG000684, 10x Genomics). After H&E staining, samples were imaged using the SLIDEVIEW VS200 slide scanner (Evident) at 20x magnification. Visium HD Gene Expression libraries were then generated using the Visium HD, Human Transcriptome, 6.5mm reagents (PN: 1000675, 10x Genomics) and following the Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Reagent Kits User Guide (CG000685, 10x Genomics). Quality control and molarity calculations of the libraries were performed with Qubit 3.0 Fluorometer (#Q33216, Invitrogen) and 4200 Tapestation system (Agilent Technologies). Libraries were sequenced on the NovaSeq X+ 10B at paired-end 100bp.

Sequential Immunofluorescence using COMET:

Sequential Immunofluorescence (SeqIF 
) staining was performed on FFPE tissue sections using COMET system from Lunaphore, according to standard protocol for proteomic applications (User manual – COMET 
, Revision: 006).
Briefly, SuperFrost Plus slides with FFPE tissue underwent deparaffinization and antigen retrieval using Dewax and HIER buffer, pH 9 (Epredia, #TA-999-DHBH) in the PT module (Epredia) at 102°C for 1h, with pre-heating temperature set to 85°C and cool-end temperature to 65°C. Following antigen retrieval, slides were rinsed and kept in the Multistaining Buffer (BU06, Lunaphore) until loading them on to the instrument for SeqIF. SeqIF staining was performed on the COMET 
 using the SPYRE 
 Immuno-oncology Core Panel (Lunaphore) supplemented with pan-Cytokeratin antibody. SeqIF 
 protocol was set up on the COMET 
 control software and sequential staining, imaging, and elution cycles were performed on the instrument as per manufacturer’s protocol. Imaging was performed with 12.5 x 12.5mm imaging area. 

Post- COMET Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Analysis:

For efficient preservation of RNA integrity to enable post-COMET Visium HD Gene expression analysis, SuperFrost Plus slides with FFPE tissues underwent deparaffinization and antigen retrieval according to the recommended pre-processing protocol for multiomics applications (User manual – COMET 
, Revision: 006).
Slides were baked at 60°C for 1h, followed by cooling down for 5 mins at RT. They were deparaffinized by incubating sequentially in two coplin jars of xylene (5 min each), two jars of 100% ethanol (2 mins each), and then dried for 2.5 min at 60°C. Antigen retrieval was performed using Dewax and HIER buffer pH 9 (Epredia, #TA-999-DHBH) in the PT module at 99°C for 1h, with 85°C and 65°C as the pre-heating and cool-end temperatures, respectively. After antigen retrieval, slides were rinsed and kept in Multistaining Buffer (BU06, Lunaphore) until loading them on to the COMET 
 instrument for SeqIF 
. The time between antigen retrieval and starting the SeqIF 
 run was kept as low as possible. SeqIF 
 staining was performed using the SPYRE 
 Immuno-oncology Core Panel (Lunaphore) supplemented with pan-Cytokeratin, with imaging area of 12.5 x 12.5mm exactly as per manufacturer’s protocol. Table1 provides the complete list of primary and secondary antibodies, and staining cycle details.
After the COMET 
 SeqIF 
 run was completed, slides were unloaded from the instrument and immersed in 1x PBS to keep them hydrated. They were air-dried for 5 min at RT and then assembled into the Visium HD slide cassette as per standard protocol (CG000684, 10x Genomics). Subsequent steps including pre-hybridization, probe hybridization and generation of Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression libraries were performed using the Visium HD, Human Transcriptome, 6.5mm reagents (PN: 1000675, 10x Genomics) and following the Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Reagent Kits User Guide (CG000685, 10x Genomics). Quality control and molarity calculations of the libraries were performed with Qubit 3.0 Fluorometer (#Q33216, Invitrogen) and 4200 Tapestation system (Agilent Technologies). Libraries were sequenced on the NovaSeq X+ 10B at paired-end 100bp, pooling 2-4 libraries per lane.

For the Xenium Prime In Situ workflow, Xenium slides with …. were processed for deparaffinization and decrosslinking according to the Demonstrated Protocol: Xenium In Situ for FFPE – Tissue preparation Handbook (CG000578, 10x Genomics).
Subsequent steps including priming, RNase treatment and polishing, probe hybridization, post-hybridization washes, ligation, amplification, blocking, staining with Multi-Tissue Stain Mix  for multimodal cell segmentation, autofluorescence quenching and nuclei staining were performed using the Xenium Prime Sample Preparation with Cell Segmentation with Slides reagents (PN: 1000742, 10x Genomics), and following the Xenium Prime In Situ Gene Expression with optional Cell Segmentation User Guide (CG000760, 10x Genomics). Hybridization was carried out overnight at 50°C, in thermocycler, with the Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue and Pathways Assay Kit (PN: 1000671, 10x Genomics). Slides were imaged on the Xenium Analyzer with Xenium Prime 5K Decoding Reagents (PN: 1000740, 10x Genomics), Xenium Decoding Consumables v2 (PN: 1000726, 10x Genomics) and Xenium Reagent Bottles (PN: 1000740, 10x Genomics), and following the Xenium Analyzer User Guide (CG000584, 10x Genomics). In the overview scan performed by the instrument, ROIs were defined per slide, comprising all fields of view (FOVs) containing the tissue, while excluding the blank areas. Following the instrument run, the buffer on the slides was replaced with 0.05% PBST and slides were stored at 4°C. spec-3-w09g-removable Specimen Title tonsil_3 Sample preparation protocol Xenium In Situ workflow with Protein Staining and Cell Segmentation
For the Xenium in situ workflow with protein staining and multimodal cell segmentation, the processing of Xenium slides with tonsil tissue for deparaffinization, decrosslinking (CG000578, 10x Genomics) and subsequent steps of probe hybridization, ligation and amplification, autofluorescence quenching and nuclei staining (CG000819, 10x Genomics) were exactly the same as for standard Xenium in situ workflow. Probe hybridization was carried out with the Xenium Human Immuno-oncology Profiling Panel (PN:1000654, 10x Genomics) overnight at 50°C in thermocycler. Following amplification and before autofluorescence quenching, tissue dehydration, secondary decrosslinking, blocking, protein and multimodal cell segmentation staining, and stain enhancement were performed using the Xenium Cell Segmentation Staining Reagents (PN: 1000661, 10x Genomics) and following the Xenium in situ Gene and Protein User Guide (CG000819, 10x Genomics). Staining was performed overnight at 4°C using a mix of Human Multi-tissue stain mix (PN: 1000661, 10x Genomics) and Xenium Protein Immune Cell Subpanels: A and B (PN: 1000833, PN: 1000834, 10x Genomics, respectively). Slides were imaged on the Xenium Analyzer with Xenium RNA and Protein Detection Reagents (PN: 1000884, 10x Genomics) and Xenium Decoding Consumables (PN: 1000487, 10x Genomics), and following the Xenium Analyzer User Guide (CG000584, 10x Genomics). In the overview scan performed by the instrument, a single ROI was defined per slide, comprising all FOVs containing the tissue, while excluding the blank areas. Following the instrument run, the buffer on the slides was replaced with 0.05% PBST and slides were stored at 4°C.

title: Cellular senescence in human liver under normal aging and cancer.
xenium_reason: New profiling/generation with Xenium is stated
evidence_text: Cellular senescence in human liver under normal aging and cancer. Cellular senescence, a stress-induced program causing stable cell-cycle arrest, is a hallmark of liver aging, fibrosis, and cancer. However, the cell-type-specific mechanisms, spatial organization, and cancer-associated alterations in the liver remain unclear. We profiled 43 normal human livers spanning ages and fibrosis stages using a single-cell multiome, Xenium spatial transcriptomics, and CODEX, complemented by fibrotic mouse models and 24 colorectal cancer liver metastases. We found CDKN1A+ senescent hepatocytes, fibroblasts, cholangiocytes, and endothelial cells associated with age, liver disease, or cancer. Senescence differed between aged and fibrotic livers, with similar patterns in mice. Spatially, CDKN1A+ hepatocytes localized periportally, while SERPINE1+ aging-associated hepatocytes formed spatial clusters, potentially mediated by Claudins and THBS1. Fibrotic regions contained CXCL12+ senescent fibroblasts interacting with CXCR4+ immune cells. Chemotherapy intensified senescence in hepatocytes by 5-fold relative to aging and led to unique CDKN2A+ populations. Across conditions, senescent cells shared AP-1 activation, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and apoptosis resistance, suggesting therapeutic opportunities.

title: Spatial multi-omics and single-cell transcriptomics uncover senescence-associated cellular programs during colon adenoma to cancer progression
xenium_reason: New profiling/generation with Xenium is stated
evidence_text:
Spatial multi-omics and single-cell transcriptomics uncover senescence-associated cellular programs during colon adenoma to cancer progression Colorectal cancer develops through a normal-adenoma-carcinoma sequence, yet only 5-10% of adenomas progress to malignancy, and the cellular programs governing that sequence remain poorly defined. Here we generate a spatial multi-omics atlas of human colon adenomas, combining Visium CytAssist and protein co-detection across 24 nonadvanced and advanced tubular adenomas with single-cell resolution Xenium Prime 5K profiling of 101 patient-matched normal, adenoma, and carcinoma cores from 16 patients. Integrating whole-transcriptome and 31-plex protein data identifies nine spatial clusters and two dysplastic epithelial populations that co-express stemness, proliferation, and senescence programs. These programs occupy a shared, spatially confined epithelial niche that expands from adenoma to carcinoma. Spatial analysis revealed GDF15, a senescence-associated secretory factor, mediated the coupling between senescence and stemness in advanced adenomas, and that GDF15-high epithelium locally excludes CD8+ T cells in adenoma and, more broadly, in carcinoma. These findings position senescence as a spatially instructive rather than merely tumor-suppressive program during colorectal carcinogenesis and suggest GDF15 might be a potential candidate target for cancer prevention and interception in the colon.

Statement of Significance

Spatial multi-omics identifies spatially co-localized senescence and stemness programs in dysplastic epithelium during colorectal tumorigenesis and links GDF15-associated niches to CD8-positive T-cell exclusion, nominating GDF15 for colorectal cancer prevention and interception strategies.

evidence_text:
Explainable machine learning and multimodal single cell analysis link NR4A2 to CD8<sup>+</sup> T-cell terminal exhaustion and a CD8-adjusted prognostic signature in hepatocellular carcinoma.

Background

Terminal exhaustion of CD8+ tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes constrains the benefit of immune-checkpoint blockade in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The orphan nuclear receptor NR4A2 (Nurr1) belongs to a transcription-factor family implicated in murine T-cell exhaustion, yet its behaviour in the human HCC microenvironment has not been characterised across data modalities. We asked whether NR4A2 is specifically coupled to the terminal-exhaustion programme of human HCC CD8+ T cells, and whether that coupling is reflected in chromatin, tissue topography and bulk-tumour outcome data.

Methods

We reanalysed publicly available human HCC datasets spanning four modalities: single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq; GSE149614, GSE98638, GSE151530, GSE125449), single-cell ATAC sequencing (scATAC-seq; GSE227265), imaging-based spatial transcriptomics (10× Xenium human liver-cancer section) and bulk RNA sequencing with overall-survival annotation (TCGA-LIHC). NR4A2 was profiled across cell compartments and, at higher resolution, across CD8+ T-cell states defined from curated exhaustion, progenitor, effector and naïve gene modules. We tested NR4A2-exhaustion coupling at single-cell and pseudobulk level, examined NR4A2 motif accessibility, traced NR4A2 along a diffusion-pseudotime exhaustion axis, evaluated spatial co-localisation of exhausted CD8+ T cells with tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs), benchmarked machine-learning classifiers of the exhausted state, and compared the human NR4A2 co-expression direction with the published NR4A1/2-knockout phenotype. We additionally trained interpretable gradient-boosted-tree models with SHAP attribution to characterise the exhausted and NR4A2-high states, scored a NR4A2 co-expression regulon, related the programme to immunotherapy-relevant signatures, and modelled overall survival using a CD8-infiltration-adjusted exhaustion score.

Results

NR4A2 was broadly expressed across HCC compartments and was highest in myeloid cells rather than being T-cell restricted; at whole-compartment and bulk-tumour resolution it was not a clean exhaustion marker. At the resolution of CD8+ T-cell states, however, NR4A2 was sharply enriched in terminally exhausted cells (mean 3.62 versus 1.05; Mann-Whitney p ≈ 3.4 × 10-83) and correlated with the exhaustion module (single-cell Spearman ρ = 0.45) but not with the effector module (ρ = 0.06), arguing that NR4A2 is not a generic activation gene. NR4A2 expression increased monotonically along a diffusion-pseudotime axis toward terminal exhaustion (ρ = 0.37). In Xenium tissue, exhausted CD8+ T cells were modestly but significantly enriched in the neighbourhood of TAMs relative to other CD8+ T cells (permutation p = 0.005). The human NR4A2 co-expression direction was 83% concordant with the published NR4A1/2-knockout differential-expression direction. In bulk TCGA-LIHC, NR4A2 was lower in tumour than adjacent liver and only weakly exhaustion-correlated, consistent with hepatocyte-dominated bulk signal and reinforcing the need for compartment-resolved analysis. Interpretable machine learning attributed NR4A2-high status to an immediate-early/AP-1 activation programme, a NR4A2 co-expression regulon was selectively active in exhausted cells, and the programme tracked the T-cell-inflamed phenotype (ρ = 0.87); although raw bulk NR4A2 was non-prognostic, a CD8-infiltration-adjusted exhaustion score independently predicted shorter overall survival (hazard ratio 1.42 per standard deviation, p < 0.001).

Conclusions

A NR4A2 co-expression regulon was most active in exhausted cells; explainable modelling linked NR4A2-high status to an immediate-early/AP-1 activation programme; the programme marked immune-hot tumours; and although bulk NR4A2 was non-prognostic, a CD8-infiltration-adjusted exhaustion score was independently associated with worse overall survival (HR 1.42 per SD, p < 0.001). Across four independent data modalities, NR4A2 behaves as a resolution-dependent marker of the terminal-exhaustion programme in HCC CD8+ T cells that is spatially associated with the myeloid niche. The convergence supports NR4A2 as a candidate component of an HCC exhaustion signature and a hypothesis-generating target for functional study, while underscoring that its association is masked in bulk and whole-compartment data.
